samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
# The Street That Wasn’t There

The first time Mara found the street, she was carrying a cabbage, a replacement fuse, and a letter she had been meaning to post for eleven days.

It was raining with the persistence of an argument neither party remembered starting. Water gathered in her cuffs. The cabbage knocked against her knee.

She turned between the pharmacy and the shuttered travel agency, expecting the narrow passage that led to the tram stop.

Instead, she found a street.

It was not especially mysterious. There were parked bicycles, basement windows, a plane tree held upright by an iron grate. A man in an apron was bringing a sandwich board inside. The board said SOUP, with no further promises.

What troubled Mara was the distance.

The pharmacy and the travel agency shared a wall. She knew this because she had once rented the flat above them, where you could hear the pharmacist sneeze every morning at eight.

There was no room for a street.

She stood in the rain and considered this.

The man with the sandwich board considered her.

“Are you coming in,” he asked, “or conducting a survey?”

“Was this always here?”

“Not the board. I put it out at eleven.”

“The street.”

He looked up and down it.

“As far as I’m aware.”

Mara followed him inside.

***

The café had six tables, five customers, and a clock that had stopped at twenty past four.

“Your clock’s broken,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“Doesn’t that bother you?”

“Only at twenty past four.”

He took her cabbage without comment and set it behind the counter.

The soup was lentil. She ate it beside a window while the rain threaded silver lines down the glass.

Across the street stood a shop called VALE & DAUGHTER, MAPS AND SURVEYS. Its window displayed a globe, three brass instruments, and a map of the city.

Mara was a municipal drainage engineer. Maps interested her professionally. Errors interested her temperamentally.

She paid for the soup, collected the cabbage, and crossed over.

A bell sounded when she opened the door.

Behind a desk sat an elderly woman wearing a cardigan the color of wet sand. She was scraping something off a sheet of paper with a small blade.

“Excuse me,” Mara said. “What street is this?”

“Bellwether Lane.”

“There’s no Bellwether Lane.”

The woman kept scraping.

“Then you’ve arrived remarkably precisely.”

***

The map in the window showed the river, the railway, the old market, the hospital, the ring road.

Between the pharmacy and the travel agency was a thin line labeled BELLWETHER LANE.

Mara leaned closer.

Other lines were wrong.

A courtyard appeared behind the courthouse, where there was only a loading bay. A footbridge crossed the canal at the gasworks. A small square occupied the place where Mara distinctly remembered a multistory car park.

“This is inaccurate,” she said.

“All maps are.”

“Some more than others.”

The woman looked up with interest.

“What do you do?”

“Drainage.”

“Ah. The city underneath.”

“The city with measurable gradients.”

“That must be comforting.”

“Usually.”

The woman set down her blade.

“My name is Elin Vale.”

“Mara Venn.”

“Would you like tea?”

“I’d like an explanation.”

“We can have both.”

***

Elin made tea on a hot plate behind the desk.

The shop smelled of paper, dust, and orange peel. Maps hung from wooden rods overhead. Others stood rolled in ceramic umbrella pots. One enormous sheet covered the back wall.

It showed the city in an unfamiliar arrangement.

The river bent more sharply. Certain neighborhoods were missing. Others were dense with streets that had no names.

Mara recognized her childhood school, demolished thirty years earlier.

Beside it was the corner shop where she had bought frozen juice in plastic sleeves.

“That map is old.”

“Parts of it.”

“How old?”

“The school is 1979. The river is mostly 1840. The railway is Tuesday.”

Mara set her tea down.

Elin nodded, as though this were a reasonable response.

“Bellwether Lane doesn’t appear on every version of the city.”

“What versions?”

“The ones people use.”

“There’s one city.”

“Of course. And you know a different one from your postman.”

“That’s metaphor.”

“Generally.”

***

Mara should have left.

Instead, she spent two hours pointing at things and asking questions.

Elin answered some directly.

Bellwether Lane was accessible from several places, although not reliably. Deliveries arrived on Thursdays. The council collected the bins, but the collectors never remembered the route afterward.

Other questions produced less satisfactory answers.

“Who owns these buildings?”

“People with keys.”

“What happens if I walk to the far end?”

“Eventually, something else.”

“Why hasn’t anyone documented this?”

Elin spread her hands over the desk.

Mara disliked the theatricality of the gesture. She disliked more that it was justified.

At six, Elin said she was closing.

“Will I find it again?”

“Probably.”

“What determines that?”

“I don’t know.”

It was the first answer Mara entirely trusted.

Elin gave her a small folded map.

“Don’t study it while crossing roads.”

Outside, the rain had stopped.

Mara walked to the end of Bellwether Lane and emerged beside the pharmacy.

The passage was once again a passage.

She checked twice.

Then she went home, put the cabbage in the refrigerator, replaced the fuse, and forgot to post the letter.

***

For three weeks, Bellwether Lane refused to return.

Mara visited before work, after work, and once at midnight, which attracted the attention of a fox and a police officer.

She measured the passage.

She checked property records.

She requested historical drainage plans under a project number she could almost justify.

Nothing.

The folded map was no help. It showed Bellwether Lane clearly, but its surrounding streets changed when she wasn’t looking.

Mara tried photographing it.

The photographs showed whichever arrangement had been present at the time, so she accumulated seventeen mutually incompatible images and no useful conclusion.

Her colleague Dev asked whether she was sleeping.

“Not particularly.”

“Your culvert calculations have become very aggressive.”

“They’re correct.”

“Yes. They’re just written as though the culvert has disappointed you.”

On the twenty-third day, Mara gave up and went to buy bread.

The bakery door opened onto Bellwether Lane.

She stood holding the handle.

Behind her, someone said, “Are you going in?”

***

Elin was repairing the spine of an atlas.

“You might have warned me,” Mara said.

“About what?”

“The uncertainty.”

“I believe I did.”

Mara put seventeen photographs on the desk.

Elin examined them carefully.

“This one’s lovely.”

“It’s impossible.”

“The light, I mean.”

Mara pulled out a chair.

“I need to understand how this works.”

“Why?”

“So I can predict it.”

“Why?”

“So I can come here when I intend to.”

Elin considered that.

“Most visitors stop at wanting to prove they’ve been.”

“How many visitors?”

“Fewer lately.”

For the first time, Mara noticed the dust on the lower shelves. A pale rectangle on the wall marked the absence of a picture or a clock.

“What happened to Vale?”

“I’m Vale.”

“The other Vale.”

“My father.”

“And the daughter?”

“Also me.”

“An old sign.”

“A good one.”

***

Over the following months, Mara found the lane nine times.

She learned the café owner was named Tomas, and that the stopped clock belonged to his wife, who was alive and irritated by his refusal to repair it.

She learned the bicycle shop opened only when its proprietor felt his knees were trustworthy.

She learned Elin had once worked for the national survey.

“What happened?”

“I submitted a coastline they found objectionable.”

“Was it accurate?”

“At low tide.”

Gradually, Elin taught her to read the maps.

Not by scale or legend. Mara already understood those.

She taught her to notice which details a map considered important.

A map for children made alleys broad and grown-up roads narrow. A map for a woman with failing eyesight marked every bench between her flat and the river. A map of the city during a strike showed walking routes, public taps, and places where someone might let you use a telephone.

“These are just specialized maps,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“You say that as though it explains the street.”

“It explains why I keep the shop.”

***

One evening, Mara found Elin sitting on the floor.

A ladder lay beside her.

For several seconds, Mara thought she was dead.

Then Elin opened one eye.

“If you say anything about my age, I’ll charge you for the tea.”

Her ankle was broken.

The ambulance took forty minutes to find them. Mara stood at the entrance to the lane, waving both arms, terrified that it would disappear while she watched.

It did not.

Afterward, at the hospital, Elin gave her the shop keys.

“There are orders.”

“I don’t know how to fill them.”

“They’re labeled.”

“And the other things?”

“What other things?”

“The impossible geography.”

“Dust it occasionally.”

Elin closed her eyes.

Mara remained beside the bed until a nurse asked whether she was family.

“No,” Mara said.

Then, because it sounded like a reason to leave, she added, “I have her keys.”

***

Running the shop was initially straightforward.

A man collected a map of orchard soils. A student bought a facsimile of the city before the railway. Tomas came in to borrow tape and stayed to complain about his supplier.

Then a boy of about twelve arrived carrying a bicycle wheel.

“Do you have a map to my father?”

Mara looked up.

“Where does he live?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you know the town?”

“No.”

She sat down on the other side of the desk.

“What makes you think we’d have that?”

“Mrs. Vale said you can make maps of almost anything.”

“Almost.”

The boy spun the wheel between his palms.

“He sends postcards. Mum puts them in a drawer.”

“Are there postmarks?”

He shrugged.

Mara glanced at the maps hanging overhead. She wanted, suddenly and fiercely, for one of them to provide an answer.

Instead, she found paper.

“Tell me what you do know.”

They wrote down the last visit, the postcards, the aunt who still spoke to him.

It was not a route to his father.

It was a short list of people the boy could ask.

He folded it carefully.

“Is that a map?”

“Enough to start with.”

***

Elin returned in September, using a cane and issuing contradictory instructions about the arrangement of her desk.

Mara had taken Fridays off.

At first, she called it accumulated leave. Then she reduced her hours.

Dev was unsurprised.

“You’ve stopped arguing with the culverts.”

“I still care about gradients.”

“I never doubted it.”

That autumn, the city announced plans to redevelop the block containing the pharmacy.

The travel agency had been empty for years. The buildings above it were unsafe. There would be apartments, a supermarket, and an underground garage.

Mara brought the plans to Elin.

“They’ll close the passage.”

“Yes.”

“What happens to the lane?”

“I’m not sure.”

“Has this happened before?”

“Things have been built. Things have been knocked down.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“No.”

Mara unfolded the engineering drawings.

The new foundations cut directly through the entrance.

“I can object.”

“On what grounds?”

Mara looked around the shop.

None that would survive a meeting.

***

She tried anyway.

She wrote about pedestrian permeability, heritage value, and the importance of small commercial premises.

These were defensible arguments, which made it particularly annoying when they were dismissed politely.

The pharmacy would relocate. The passage served no essential route. The development included a public courtyard.

Mara studied that courtyard.

It was a windswept rectangle above the garage ventilation system.

She submitted calculations.

This produced a revised ventilation system.

“You’ve improved it,” Elin said.

“I haven’t saved anything.”

“Those aren’t always the same job.”

Mara went back to the drawings.

This time, she traced where people actually walked: to the tram, the school, the clinic. She brought Dev in to check the drainage implications. He complained for an hour and then found a cheaper alignment for a sewer connection.

The revised design allowed a narrow public route through the block.

The developers accepted it because it increased storefront access and reduced excavation costs.

No one mentioned magic.

Mara found this reassuring.

***

On the last evening before demolition, the residents of Bellwether Lane ate at Tomas’s café.

There were fourteen of them, plus Mara.

Someone had brought flowers. Someone else had brought a bottle with no label and strong opinions attached.

Tomas’s wife arrived carrying a new clock.

“No,” Tomas said.

“Yes,” she replied.

Elin watched them from the window table.

“Will this be enough?” Mara asked her.

“The route?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you ever find that embarrassing?”

“Constantly.”

Outside, the plane tree moved in a light wind.

Mara thought of everything she had measured in her life: flow rates, distances, pressure losses. Numbers she could defend.

She had enjoyed the work. She still did.

Now she wished she had measured the shop, too—the shelves, the doorway, the length of the desk. She wanted something she could put back exactly.

At twenty past four, Tomas took down the old clock.

Behind it, the wallpaper was brighter.

***

The passage closed for eighteen months.

During that time, Mara did not find Bellwether Lane.

She checked other entrances without success. Letters to Elin came back undelivered.

Once, she saw the boy with the bicycle wheel riding beside a woman along the canal. He waved but did not stop.

Mara kept the folded map in her desk.

It became ordinary paper.

The streets settled into a single arrangement. Bellwether Lane disappeared.

She nearly threw it away during a spring cleaning, then put it with the letter she had carried that first day.

Eventually, she posted the letter.

It was to her brother. They had quarreled over something practical after their mother died, then maintained the quarrel long after the practical matter had been resolved.

He called on a Sunday.

They talked awkwardly about his roof.

It was enough for another call.

***

The new passage opened in April.

Mara walked through on her lunch break.

There were pale bricks, stainless steel railings, three young trees. Rainwater ran toward the channels she had specified.

Halfway through, she stopped beside a bench.

A door stood opposite it.

Through the glass, she could see a desk, a hot plate, and rolls of paper.

Elin opened the door before Mara knocked.

“You’re late.”

Mara laughed once, unexpectedly.

“Eighteen months.”

“Is that what it’s been?”

Behind Elin, the shop was smaller. The great map no longer fitted the back wall. It lay rolled beneath the desk.

“Where’s everyone else?”

“Tomas is around the corner. The bicycle shop’s upstairs, which nobody considers sensible.”

Mara stepped inside.

On the desk lay a map of the new development. The passage was marked clearly. A fine line branched from it, turned twice, and continued beyond the edge of the sheet.

“Does it have a name yet?” she asked.

“Not one that’s stuck.”

Mara hung her coat on a hook.

Elin filled the kettle.

Outside, someone paused, checked a phone, and looked through the window. Mara moved a stack of atlases off the second chair.

Then she opened the door.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
# The Places Between

Our office was not permitted to put trees on maps.

Trees moved, according to the chief surveyor. Not quickly, he admitted, but they leaned, expanded, dropped limbs, and died. A maple could occupy one coordinate in April and three by September. We recorded permanent features: roadways, property boundaries, drainage channels, buildings with foundations.

“What about rivers?” I asked when I was new.

“Rivers have departments,” he said.

I found this answer satisfying for nearly twenty years.

My job was to maintain the official street map of Bellwether, a city large enough to have several terrible intersections but too small to agree on which was the worst. Every spring, I updated the master file. New roads appeared at the edges. Old factories became rectangles labeled RESIDENTIAL. Schools expanded into parking lots, then campaigned for money to plant shade trees.

I liked the work. There was pleasure in making things line up.

***

The problem began with a woman who wanted an address for an empty lot.

She arrived carrying a motorcycle helmet and a paper bag darkened with butter. She set both on my counter.

“I need you to put a place on the map.”

“Do you own the property?”

“No.”

“Are you representing the owner?”

“Absolutely not.”

I slid the bag away from an open drainage survey.

“What’s the address?”

“That’s the problem.”

She described the lot behind the former Majestic Cinema, between a locksmith and the blank wall of a furniture warehouse. I knew it. On our maps it was Parcel 18-C, zoned commercial, owned by a development company whose correspondence came from another city.

“What’s there?” I asked.

“Tuesday.”

I waited.

“People meet there on Tuesdays.”

“For what?”

“Different things.”

“That’s not usually enough to establish an address.”

She opened the bag and offered me a cheese pastry. I declined. She ate it while studying the evacuation diagram above my desk.

“Your emergency exit is wrong,” she said.

It was. A renovation had moved the stairwell six years earlier.

***

Her name was Ada Ferris. She repaired restaurant refrigerators and had the patient, suspicious manner of someone frequently told that a broken machine had been working perfectly yesterday.

The Tuesday gathering, she explained, had begun during a heat wave. A man called Mr. Vale carried a chair into the lot because his upstairs apartment was hotter than the outdoors. Someone joined him. Then someone else brought a folding table.

By autumn, people were bringing food, sewing, batteries they hoped somebody could identify, and letters they needed help understanding. A retired teacher gave lessons in the corner nearest the locksmith. A teenager sharpened kitchen knives for money until his grandmother made him stop charging her friends.

“Is it a market?” I asked.

“No.”

“A club?”

“No.”

“An event?”

“Every week for eight years.”

I opened the property record. There were no permits, public easements, or registered organizations associated with the site.

“Why do you need an address now?”

“A new woman tried to come. Her son drove her around for forty minutes. There’s no sign. The cinema entrance is on the other street.”

“Could you make a sign?”

“We did. The warehouse took it down.”

I suggested an online location pin. Ada explained that several of the people who attended did not use smartphones.

“You do print a map,” she said.

We did. Twelve thousand copies every year.

She left a pastry on the counter despite my refusal. I ate it after she had gone.

***

That Tuesday, I went to Parcel 18-C.

I intended to stay ten minutes. I even parked somewhere that required me to move the car by six.

The lot was paved unevenly, with weeds growing through a long crack that resembled an ambitious river system. There were seventeen chairs, none matching. Someone had stretched a blue tarpaulin from the warehouse’s fire escape to a pole fixed inside a bucket of concrete.

A woman was repairing the lining of a coat. Two boys were arguing over a chessboard. On a camping stove, a dented kettle made a sound like distant applause.

Ada spotted me.

“The map person.”

Everyone looked up with the mild interest generally reserved for a substitute bus driver.

I explained the address problem. Before I finished, a man wearing a wool waistcoat said, “Tell him about the ambulance.”

The previous winter, Mr. Vale had fallen. When someone called for help, the dispatcher insisted on a street number. The caller gave the locksmith’s address, but the ambulance went to the front entrance. The locksmith had closed. There had been several minutes of shouting between people who could hear one another but could not find one another.

“Is Mr. Vale all right?” I asked.

“He’s there.”

Mr. Vale raised his cup.

“Hip,” he said. “Not my best.”

I got out my notebook.

***

The easiest solution was to assign the lot a supplementary access address. We had procedures for that. Procedures were my specialty; I knew which forms could travel together and which required separate envelopes.

The difficulty was the owner.

An address change required written consent, unless emergency services requested it. Emergency services wanted evidence of regular authorized occupancy. Regular authorized occupancy required written consent from the owner.

I called the development company. After several transfers, a young man told me that nobody was authorized to occupy the parcel.

“There are people using it,” I said.

“That doesn’t mean they’re authorized.”

“They’ve been there eight years.”

He paused.

“Can you send photographs?”

I looked at my notebook, where I had written the positions of the chairs and the easiest route for a stretcher.

“What would the photographs be used for?”

“To assess the situation.”

I said I would call back.

For the first time in my career, I closed a property file without saving my notes.

***

My father had driven buses in Bellwether for thirty-one years.

He knew the city by instructions that could never appear on a street map. Wait here if the school lets out early. Take this corner wide. The old man at the third stop needs to see your face before he’ll stand.

When my mother died, he began riding buses on his days off. He claimed he was checking the new vehicles, but he always rode routes worked by drivers he knew.

After he died, I found a notebook in his kitchen drawer. It contained no private revelations, only shopping lists, football scores, and directions.

*Woman with red trolley: stop past puddle.*

*Hospital evenings: give them time.*

I kept the notebook because I could not think where to throw it away.

That night I took it from my desk and read it again. One page had a sketch of a junction that no longer existed. He had drawn a tree beside the bus shelter.

Under it he had written: *Shade until two.*

***

The following Tuesday, I brought six photocopies of the neighborhood map.

I spread them on the table between a tin of biscuits and an electric fan that Ada was dismantling.

“Show me what’s missing.”

The retired teacher, whose name was Leena, immediately added the passage through the church garden.

“That closes at dusk,” said someone.

“Only the west gate.”

“Both gates now.”

“No, that was during the roof work.”

I gave her a pencil with an eraser.

Mr. Vale marked a public toilet. The woman repairing the coat crossed it out.

“Closed.”

“Since when?”

“February.”

“Permanently?”

She shrugged. “Long enough.”

The boys added a drinking fountain. Ada marked a doorway sheltered from rain. Someone pointed out a steep stretch of pavement that looked entirely harmless when viewed from above.

Soon the sheets were crowded with arrows and corrections. The official map underneath was still accurate. The streets were where we said they were. The blocks had not changed shape.

Yet a person following it could arrive thirsty, exhausted, locked out, or on the wrong side of a wall.

At half past six, I remembered my car.

“You parked on Mercer?” Ada asked.

“Yes.”

“They don’t tow on Tuesdays. The truck’s at the livestock auction.”

“That can’t possibly be a dependable arrangement.”

She handed me a biscuit.

***

I began walking after work.

Initially, I told myself I was verifying pedestrian connections. This sounded respectable and explained the clipboard.

I found a staircase concealed beside a funeral home, a bench in a supermarket loading area, and a covered arcade that remained open all night because three businesses disagreed over who should have keys to the gates.

I found places where people had solved small problems without asking the city to name the solution.

Outside a bakery, someone had fixed a shelf to the wall at elbow height. Customers set their bags there while finding their keys. Behind the library, a low stone ledge served as a meeting point for teenagers whose parents were late collecting them. A mechanic kept a chair near his forecourt for a woman who needed to rest halfway home.

I also found shortcuts that were dangerous, benches deliberately made uncomfortable, and friendly-looking courtyards where a security guard would ask you to leave.

My notes became less confident.

I stopped writing *public seating* and started writing *chair usually available; ask Leon*.

This was not the sort of information our database had been designed to hold.

***

My supervisor noticed the new layer in the mapping software.

“What’s ‘Informal Access’?”

“Supplementary pedestrian information.”

“Who requested it?”

I considered saying emergency services, but lying to Margaret required more preparation than I had undertaken.

“Some residents.”

She pulled a chair beside mine.

Margaret had worked in the department longer than I had. She distrusted novelty, particularly novelty requiring maintenance, and could identify a poorly surveyed boundary by looking at it upside down.

We went through the entries.

At the church passage, she nodded. At the supermarket bench, she frowned. At the mechanic’s chair, she took off her glasses.

“You can’t publish a person’s kindness as a municipal facility.”

I had no answer.

“People will turn up expecting it. He’ll move the chair, and someone will complain. Or the landlord will see it and ask why he’s operating a waiting area.”

“So we leave it off?”

“Perhaps.”

“And the people who need it?”

She looked back at the screen.

“You’ve found a real problem,” she said. “That doesn’t make every solution a good one.”

***

The fence arrived on a Thursday.

Ada called me at work. I drove over during lunch and found two contractors measuring the lot. Sections of temporary fencing lay on a truck.

The development company had scheduled a site assessment. Nobody could tell Ada what that meant beyond the fact that the Tuesday gathering would have to stop.

“Did you send them anything?” she asked me.

“No photographs.”

“What did you send?”

“Nothing. I called.”

She turned toward the warehouse wall.

I began explaining the address procedure, then heard myself and stopped.

The contractors waited politely. One asked whether the chairs belonged to anyone. Ada said yes, all of them.

We carried them to the locksmith’s storeroom. Mr. Vale’s chair was heavier than it looked, with a steel frame and wooden arms polished by use. One foot had been repaired with a bolt that stuck out sideways.

The locksmith, whose name I had never learned, held the door for us.

“Put that one near the front,” he said. “He’ll want it.”

***

For several days I could not work on the map.

I completed routine amendments, answered emails, and adjusted the spelling of a cul-de-sac named after a tree that did not grow in our climate.

Then Margaret put a folder on my desk.

“Surplus highway land,” she said.

Inside was a list of small municipal properties: leftover triangles, abandoned turning areas, strips purchased for road widening that never happened.

“There’s one near your lot.”

It was a narrow rectangle beside an old pumping station, forty yards from Parcel 18-C. The station had been decommissioned, but the water department still mowed the grass.

“Could they use it?”

“Possibly.”

“What would they need?”

“Insurance. An agreement. Someone to be responsible.”

“They’re not an organization.”

“They might have to become one.”

I imagined Ada’s expression.

Margaret tapped the folder.

“And don’t promise anything before we know about the drains.”

For three weeks, we discussed drains.

***

The new place was inferior in several ways.

It had less shelter, more traffic noise, and a slight slope that made the chess pieces drift if the table was positioned badly. The water department required unrestricted access to a locked metal hatch nobody had opened in eleven years.

But it had a street number.

Ada helped form an association and hated every minute of it. Leena became secretary because she owned a printer. Mr. Vale refused to be chairperson on the grounds that he had already supplied the chair.

The locksmith donated a sign.

On the first Tuesday, it rained. Seven people came. Water gathered along the tarpaulin until Ada pushed it upward with a broom, releasing a sheet of rain onto my shoes.

We ate sandwiches from damp paper plates.

“Better drainage at the old place,” Mr. Vale observed.

Nobody contradicted him.

By June, attendance had recovered. By July, the boys had persuaded someone to level a corner for chess. In August, the warehouse manager came over carrying an electric kettle and asked whether anyone could fix it.

Ada told him to take a number.

There were no numbers.

He waited anyway.

***

We published a revised pedestrian map that autumn.

It included gradients, public toilets with opening hours, drinking fountains, sheltered waiting areas, and passages whose access we had verified. Margaret insisted on a revision date printed prominently at the bottom.

Several things stayed off it. Leon’s chair remained between Leon and the people who knew him. The teenagers behind the library asked us not to label their meeting place. A woman who let neighbors use her garden gate said she was happy with the present number of neighbors.

I learned to ask before making something easier to find.

The Tuesday gathering appeared as a small square beside the pumping station.

**Community meeting space. Tuesdays, 4–8. Step-free access.**

Ada examined the proof for a long time.

“Sounds official.”

“It is official.”

“Unfortunate.”

She took twelve copies.

***

I still maintain the street map. Buildings acquire foundations; roads reach into fields; rivers continue to have departments.

On Tuesdays I sometimes leave early, taking the route through the church garden while the gate is open. I know where the pavement rises sharply, where rain collects, and which bakery shelf is strong enough for two shopping bags.

Last week, Mr. Vale arrived late. Someone had put his chair in the sun, so I moved it beneath the tarpaulin.

He lowered himself carefully, tested the repaired leg, and nodded.

On the table lay a map, held flat by the biscuit tin. A newcomer was tracing her journey home. Leena leaned over to help, then called me across to settle a question about the evening buses.

I knew the street they meant. I did not know the stop.

We asked around.

# The Museum of Almost Nothing

The museum began with a drawer that would not close. Mara had inherited the desk from the previous superintendent of the railway station, along with three keys, a calendar eleven years out of date, and a job description that no longer described a job. Passenger trains had stopped coming in September. Freight trains still passed at night, shaking dust from the ceiling, but they never slowed. The town council kept her employed to supervise the building until someone decided what it should become. Every morning she unlocked the doors. Every evening she locked them again. Between those duties lay eight hours.

The troublesome drawer contained a wool glove, a brass screw, two foreign coins, a photograph of an unidentified dog, and a folded piece of paper bearing the words, “Don’t forget the good plates.” Mara removed everything, examined the runners, and discovered a wooden ruler wedged behind the drawer. Once extracted, it proved to have belonged to someone named E. Bell, who had carved the name carefully into one edge. She laid the objects across the desk. Without the drawer around them, they looked less like rubbish. They looked like the surviving evidence of several interrupted thoughts, none available for questioning.

At noon, a boy appeared at the ticket window and asked whether trains would ever return. Mara said she did not know. He considered this an inadequate but apparently honest answer. Then he asked what the objects were for. “I’m sorting them,” she said. “Into what?” She had not decided. The boy leaned close to the glass. He thought the brass screw might be part of a submarine. Mara thought it had probably fallen from a chair. “You can’t prove that,” he said. His name was Tomas, and he had recently reached the age at which uncertainty seemed a magnificent resource.

After he left, Mara found six unused display stands in a cupboard. They had once held timetables. She placed the glove on one and wrote a label: LEFT GLOVE. FOUND IN DESK. OWNER UNKNOWN. This pleased her less than she expected. She tried again: LEFT GLOVE. SOMEONE WENT HOME WITH ONE COLD HAND. That was worse. It pretended to know too much. Perhaps the owner had another pair. Perhaps it was summer. Finally she wrote: LEFT GLOVE. WE DO NOT KNOW WHAT HAPPENED TO THE OTHER ONE. She stood it in the ticket window and returned to work.

By Friday, three people had stopped to read the label. One laughed. One said she owned a glove like that, though not that particular glove. The third was Mr. Vale, who had repaired shoes on Market Street for forty years and now repaired them in his kitchen because the rent had become impossible. He brought Mara a small cardboard box the following Monday. Inside lay a child’s leather shoe, beautifully mended along the sole. “Never collected,” he said. “How long ago?” Mara asked. He looked toward the platform, where weeds grew between the paving stones. “Long enough to stop charging.”

She did not call it a museum until the council did. A clerk arrived to inspect the building and found the glove, the shoe, the ruler, and a chipped teacup arranged beneath the departure board. “Is this some sort of museum?” he asked, sounding worried about insurance. Mara said she supposed it might be. The clerk wrote this down. Two weeks later, an official letter informed her that unauthorized exhibitions required approval. Another letter, delivered in the same envelope, invited applications for a modest cultural grant. She filled out the application during a rainstorm and used the first letter as blotting paper.

Under “Institutional Mission,” she wrote: To preserve ordinary objects whose significance has not yet been established. Under “Target Audience,” she wrote: Anyone passing. Under “Projected Attendance,” she hesitated, then entered a number larger than three and smaller than a lie she would feel obliged to maintain. Tomas recommended calling it the Museum of Treasure. Mr. Vale preferred the Municipal Collection. Mara chose the Museum of Almost Nothing, partly because it left room for mistakes. The grant committee approved a sum sufficient for paint, additional labels, and one fire extinguisher. The extinguisher became the most valuable object in the room.

People began bringing things. Not antiques, usually. Those went to dealers. Not rubbish, exactly, though the distinction required negotiation. A woman brought the string from a parcel sent by her brother in 1968. A mechanic contributed a metal washer worn thin as a fingernail. The former school cook delivered a wooden spoon with one side burned black. Each donor arrived with an explanation and discovered, sometimes to their embarrassment, that the explanation was longer than expected. Mara learned not to interrupt the silence after a story seemed finished. Often the part that mattered came afterward, quietly, while the donor put on a coat.

The woman with the string had not seen her brother since he emigrated. The parcel contained oranges, which had spoiled in transit, and a letter, which she had lost during a move. She had kept the string because it was good string. That was what she said at first. Later, with one sleeve on and one sleeve empty, she said her brother had always tied excellent knots. Mara wrote several possible labels and rejected them. At last she asked the woman what visitors should know. Together they settled on: PARCEL STRING. THE KNOT WAS TIED BY SOMEONE WHO LIVED FAR AWAY.

The mechanic objected to this approach. “You make everything sound sad,” he told her. His washer had no tragic history. It came from a pump he had kept running for twenty-three years by refusing to believe the manufacturer’s estimate of its useful life. He wanted the label to say the washer was evidence of cheap materials and competent maintenance. Mara wrote exactly that. He returned the next day with his daughter to show her. She read the label, then looked at him with an expression Mara could not decipher. He stood a little straighter. The washer remained among the smallest exhibits.

There were disputes. A retired teacher insisted a cracked marble had belonged to her first pupil, while her sister maintained it came from a Christmas cracker. Two men disagreed over whether a particular door handle came from the demolished cinema or the demolished bank. Mara wrote both accounts on the labels. This annoyed people who expected museums to settle things. “Which is true?” they asked. “We’re still finding out,” she said. Tomas loved these exhibits best. He proposed a special cabinet for objects about which nobody agreed. They filled it within a month, though one donor disputed the cabinet’s title.

Winter exposed the building’s faults. Wind entered through the old luggage hatch. The roof leaked above Platform Two. The waiting room radiator produced a noise like cutlery being shaken inside a suitcase, but very little heat. Mara moved the exhibits away from damp walls and wore her coat indoors. Attendance fell to almost nobody. Some afternoons she wondered whether the whole enterprise was only an elaborate way of refusing to look for another job. She swept the floor, answered correspondence, and listened to freight trains pass. Beyond the windows, their lit carriages carried things somewhere people had actually requested them.

One dark Thursday, Mr. Vale arrived with soup. He had noticed that she stayed late and correctly suspected she was eating biscuits for dinner. They sat beneath the departure board, which still announced destinations nobody could reach from there. Mara asked whether he thought the museum was useful. He stirred his soup. “Useful how?” She explained that the town needed housing, buses, a dentist willing to take new patients. It probably did not need a room containing someone’s parcel string. Mr. Vale listened without disagreeing. Then he asked whether the soup needed salt. She said it did. He passed it.

A week later, he brought a sewing kit and repaired the torn seat of a waiting room chair. Mara offered to pay him from the grant, but there was almost nothing left. “Then don’t,” he said. While he worked, visitors sat nearby and talked. Someone fetched a broken lamp from home. Someone else knew how to mend its switch. By February, Thursday afternoons had become repair afternoons. The museum acquired a kettle, an extension lead, and a rule against attempting repairs on gas appliances. Nothing about this appeared in the original application. Mara sent the council photographs instead of an explanation.

The first thing Tomas repaired was a mechanical kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. He took it apart with immense confidence, lost a spring, found the spring inside his sleeve, and reassembled the mechanism so that it rang after seven minutes regardless of the setting. Its owner declared this sufficient, since she mainly used it for eggs. He wanted to exhibit the timer, but she wanted it back. Mara watched him struggle with the discovery that successful work could leave no monument. Then he drew a picture of the tomato and pinned it behind the desk, where they kept repair records.

Spring brought an email from a regional development consultant. He proposed making the museum a destination experience. There could be a branded shop, interactive storytelling stations, perhaps a wall where visitors photographed themselves holding oversized replicas of the exhibits. He particularly liked the glove. “Strong emotional accessibility,” he wrote. Mara read the proposal three times. The building still needed a roof. The consultant had identified possible funding. She could not dismiss him simply because he used phrases she disliked. They arranged a meeting, during which he asked what made the collection unique. Through the window, she watched a woman mend a curtain.

“Nothing here is unique in that way,” Mara said. The consultant smiled patiently, as though she had misunderstood her own institution. She tried again. There were other gloves, other shoes, other lengths of string. There were even other museums of ordinary life. What mattered was that people here could come back, correct a label, bring another piece of the story, or take their object home if they needed it. The consultant made notes. He asked whether this flexibility might undermine the permanence visitors expected. Mara thought of the tomato timer counting out somebody’s eggs. “Yes,” she said. “It might.”

In April, the river rose. It had risen before, and the town possessed many photographs of previous floods, along with strong opinions about which authorities had failed to learn from them. This time the water came after three days of rain in the hills. By dawn, the road under the railway bridge had disappeared. Mara reached the station wearing borrowed boots and found water entering beneath the platform doors. She began moving exhibits upstairs to the former signal office. The larger cases were too heavy. She telephoned Mr. Vale, then the council, then everyone whose number she had.

They arrived carrying buckets, towels, crates, and an astonishing variety of advice. The mechanic disconnected the electricity downstairs. The school cook organized the movement of objects with the same authority she once applied to lunch queues. Tomas carried labels in a biscuit tin. Nobody had assigned him this task, but he understood that without them the collection would become a heap of inscrutable belongings. By midday, everything portable had reached higher ground. The volunteers stood on the stairs and watched brown water spread across the waiting room floor. A paper cup drifted past the place where the glove had been displayed.

Upstairs, there was little to do but wait. Rain tapped the windows. Someone distributed sandwiches. The woman who had donated the string sat beside the mechanic, holding a crate between her knees. They had lived three streets apart for decades without speaking. Now she asked about the washer. He explained the pump in considerable detail, using his hands to indicate the movement of water through a system designed, in his view, by idiots. She listened carefully. Then she told him about the oranges. Mara, checking the crates, heard their conversation continue through the afternoon, wandering well beyond either object.

The damage was expensive rather than spectacular. Mud coated the floor. Two doors swelled shut. The grant-funded paint blistered, and the radiator, after years of threats, stopped working entirely. For several days the museum smelled of wet plaster and river weeds. The council suggested closing it indefinitely while options were reviewed. Mara received the news sitting on an overturned bucket. She was too tired to feel eloquent. That evening, she wrote a notice explaining the situation plainly and taped it to the outside wall. Beneath it she placed a second sheet: CLEANING SATURDAY. BRING GLOVES IF YOU HAVE THEM.

Thirty-one people came. Mara counted because the grant application had made her attentive to attendance, though she later forgot to record the number officially. They scrubbed, hauled, scraped, argued, and stopped for tea. A builder inspected the roof and offered a price that included more kindness than he admitted. The consultant sent a donation without mentioning branding. Someone found the brass screw beneath a cabinet and announced that the submarine had survived. Tomas, taller now, rolled his eyes but kept the screw. By evening the floor was visible again. It looked worn, ordinary, and unexpectedly handsome in the clearing light.

The museum reopened in June with fewer exhibits and more chairs. Mara had discovered that crowded displays encouraged people to move quickly, while a little space gave them permission to stop. She installed a table where visitors could write down things they knew about the objects. Most contributions were helpful. Some were jokes. One claimed the ruler had belonged to a famous explorer, which seemed unlikely, although E. Bell remained unidentified. There was also a new cabinet containing flood-damaged items: a warped label, a rusted hinge, a photograph in which water had erased half the platform but spared a stranger’s shoes.

Years later, visitors would assume the museum had been planned from the beginning. They would praise the converted station, the repair afternoons, the careful admission of uncertainty on the labels. Mara would try to explain the stuck drawer, the empty hours, the grant application, the radiator. People preferred a clearer origin. They wanted a moment in which she had seen what the place could become. She remembered mostly deciding what to do next: borrow a ladder, ask a question, replace a bulb. Once, searching for an invoice, she found her first label about the cold hand and threw it away.

On summer evenings, she sometimes left the doors open after closing. The town softened around the station: bicycle bells, kitchen windows, the faint argument of gulls above the river. People crossed the forecourt without entering, and she no longer counted them as missed visitors. Inside, the glove rested beside its patient label. The shoe held the shape of a vanished foot. The washer occupied its small, well-earned patch of felt. When the freight train passed, every case trembled slightly. Mara would steady whichever needed steadying, wait until the sound had gone, and then carry the empty cups into the kitchen.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum occupied a former railway station in a town the railway had stopped visiting. Above its entrance, carved into stone, were the words ARRIVALS and DEPARTURES. Someone had installed the museum’s name between them on a modest wooden board, so that the whole building appeared to offer three possible conditions of existence.

ARRIVALS. THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. DEPARTURES.

On wet mornings, rain traveled through the missing roof tiles and landed in a bucket beneath the old station clock. The clock had stopped at eleven seventeen. Visitors often assumed this was an exhibit.

“No,” said Ada, the curator. “That’s broken.”

They sometimes nodded as though she had said something profound.

The collection included a wedding dress with one sleeve, a chess game abandoned in 1963, the first nine chapters of a detective novel, and a wooden bird whose left wing remained trapped inside its original block.

There was a half-knitted yellow scarf. There was a map of an imaginary country whose coastline ended abruptly at a coffee stain. There was a letter beginning, *There is something I should have told you before.*

Nothing followed.

Ada had spent eleven years arranging these objects so they did not seem merely neglected. She believed there was a difference between a thing discarded and a thing held in suspension, although she had never found a satisfactory way to put that difference on a funding application.

Under “Public Benefit,” she usually wrote: *Preservation of local cultural material.*

The council seemed reassured by this.

***

Each donated object arrived with a form.

What is it?

Who began it?

Why was it not completed?

The third question caused trouble. People wrote *lack of time* when they meant divorce, *loss of interest* when they meant disappointment, and *circumstances* when they meant that the person who knew what came next had died.

Ada never corrected them.

Her favorite donation was a model sailing ship brought in by a retired dentist named Bell. It had a finished hull, three masts, and no rigging.

“I discovered,” he explained, “that I dislike string.”

He said it without embarrassment. Ada admired him enormously.

Other donors lingered. They touched the edge of a table or adjusted an object already sitting perfectly straight. One woman returned six times to visit an unfinished quilt, then stopped coming. A young man donated a screenplay and asked whether the museum could promise never to stage it.

“We don’t generally stage things,” Ada said.

“Yes, but could you promise?”

She did.

There were rules. The museum did not accept unpaid invoices, unresolved legal disputes, or living animals. It had once accepted a sourdough starter, but this created philosophical and practical difficulties.

Neither did it accept people.

That rule had been added after a man arrived carrying a folding chair and announced that he himself was the most important unfinished project in the county.

Ada offered him tea.

He stayed until closing, helped her bring in the pavement sign, and later became the museum’s accountant.

His name was Maurice.

***

The difficulty began with a chair.

It was a handsome oak chair, almost complete, except that one of its back legs was missing. Its maker had abandoned it after accepting a job in another city. A neighbor rescued it from a shed and brought it to the museum.

Ada displayed it on a low platform with a discreet support beneath the seat.

One Thursday, a girl named Nell visited with her school.

While the other children searched for answers on a worksheet, Nell crouched beside the chair.

“Why don’t you put the leg on?”

“Because then it wouldn’t be unfinished.”

“Would that be bad?”

“For this museum, it would be inconvenient.”

Nell considered this.

“Do you want things to stay wrong?”

Ada had developed answers to many questions. Was the missing sleeve lost? Had anyone finished reading the unfinished novel? Did the station clock work?

She had no prepared answer for this one.

“It isn’t always wrong for something to be unfinished,” she said.

“But that chair could be sat on.”

“Yes.”

“And nobody can sit on it now.”

“That’s true.”

Nell stood up. She looked neither victorious nor particularly interested in the damage she had done.

“My grandad makes legs,” she said.

“For furniture?”

“Mostly.”

Then her teacher called her away.

Ada remained beside the chair for several minutes. Eventually she straightened its label, although it was not crooked.

That evening, while locking up, she noticed how tired her own feet were. It was an irritating thing to notice.

***

The following week, the council sent a letter.

The museum’s grant would be reviewed in September. Attendance had declined. Heating costs had risen. The building required significant maintenance, particularly to its roof.

The council wished to see evidence of increased community engagement.

Maurice read the letter twice.

“They want more people.”

“We had more people last month.”

“How many?”

“Seventeen more.”

“Wasn’t there a school visit?”

“Yes.”

“How many children?”

“Twenty-three.”

He set the letter down.

Outside, wind pushed a crisp packet along the abandoned platform. It traveled several yards with apparent purpose, then caught beneath a bench.

“We could do an event,” Maurice said.

“We do events.”

“A different event.”

Their existing events included a lecture on abandoned canals, a reading of incomplete poems, and an annual evening at which local musicians performed movements from unfinished symphonies.

The symphony evening was poorly attended, but those who came were fiercely loyal.

“What sort of different event?”

Maurice hesitated.

“People could finish something.”

Ada looked at him.

“Not everything,” he added.

“You can’t invite people into a museum to dismantle its purpose.”

“Some museums let you grind flour.”

“They’re museums of milling.”

“Yes,” Maurice said. “I suppose those have an advantage. Milling is quite clear about what it wants.”

They sat in silence.

Rain began striking the bucket beneath the clock.

Maurice glanced toward it.

“Would fixing the roof count as vandalism?”

Ada tried not to smile. She failed, but only slightly.

“Put the kettle on,” she said.

***

That night, Ada walked through the galleries after closing.

Without visitors, the objects seemed less eager to explain themselves.

The yellow scarf lay in its case beside two knitting needles. Ada knew the donor’s story: a woman had begun it for her son before he moved to Canada. She had made it too wide, started again, grown annoyed, and bought him a coat instead.

He still lived in Canada. She still spoke to him every Sunday.

The scarf was not a tragedy. Ada had sometimes allowed visitors to think it was.

She stood before the wooden bird.

Its maker, a cabinetmaker recovering from a stroke, had carved it as an exercise. He stopped when movement returned sufficiently to his hand for him to repair a chest of drawers.

He had considered the bird a success.

Ada read her own label:

*An evocative study of arrested flight.*

For the first time, it struck her as rather rude.

In the office, she opened the donation records. Some objects had been given without conditions. Others were loans. A few carried explicit requests that they remain untouched.

She made three lists.

Things that must be preserved.

Things whose owners should be asked.

Things about which she knew too little.

The third list was longest.

At half past ten, she telephoned Maurice.

“I think,” she said, “we may have confused unfinished with waiting.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“Can we discuss this tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Only I’m in the middle of something.”

***

Nell’s grandfather arrived wearing a green sweater dusted with pale curls of wood.

His name was Tomas. He carried a canvas tool bag and approached the chair with none of the reverence Ada had come to expect in the galleries.

He turned it upside down.

Ada made a small involuntary noise.

“Loose joint,” he said.

“The missing leg is the principal issue.”

“It has more than one issue.”

The chair’s original maker had replied to Ada’s letter with surprising speed.

*Please finish it. I never liked thinking of it in that shed.*

Tomas examined the surviving back leg. He measured it, sketched its profile, and asked whether the museum had a workbench.

It did not.

“Good table?”

“Yes.”

“One you don’t mind scratching?”

“No.”

He looked around.

“We’ll need to solve that first.”

The workbench came from the school. Clamps came from a plumber. A retired art teacher offered brushes, though nobody yet needed brushes. Someone donated a sewing machine, and someone else donated a second sewing machine because, apparently, the first had started a competition.

Ada called the event “A Weekend of Possible Completions.”

Maurice shortened it to “Finish Something” on the posters.

“Your version sounds uncertain,” he said.

“It is uncertain.”

“People can discover that when they arrive.”

They established rules. Permission mattered. Historical material would remain untouched. Nobody would finish another person’s letter. Nobody would be required to complete anything.

Ada insisted on the last rule.

Tomas nodded.

“Good. Some things are a bad idea.”

***

On Saturday morning, thirty-eight people were waiting outside.

Ada counted them through the office window, then counted again.

There were bicycles chained to the old railings. A woman held a lamp with a crooked shade. Two brothers carried a small table between them, arguing about which one had damaged it.

A man arrived with a cardboard box containing most of a radio.

“We said unfinished projects,” Ada told him. “Not necessarily repairs.”

“I started repairing it in 1998.”

She let him in.

By noon, the waiting room smelled of sawdust, warm electrical components, and tea.

Tomas worked on the chair while Nell sanded a piece of scrap wood beside him. Three women discussed the yellow scarf. Its donor had authorized them to unravel it if necessary, and they were approaching that possibility with the gravity of surgeons.

At the far end of the room, Maurice helped a teenager format a résumé.

“Is that an exhibit?” Ada asked.

“No,” he said. “But neither is the roof.”

Not everyone approved.

A regular visitor named Mrs. Vale stood before the empty chair platform.

“It looks like a jumble sale.”

“Only in the waiting room.”

“The atmosphere carries.”

Ada understood. She missed the quiet herself. Someone had put a mug on a display plinth. The plumber’s radio was receiving two stations at once.

Mrs. Vale looked toward the workbench.

“What happens when everything’s finished?”

“I don’t know,” Ada said.

This answer seemed to offend her more than the noise.

***

Near closing time, a woman named Ruth brought in a small blue cardigan.

She had begun it fourteen years earlier. The sleeves remained separate from the body, pinned into place with safety pins that had darkened at their hinges.

Ada recognized her from the library.

“Would you like someone to help sew it together?”

Ruth shook her head.

“I thought I would.”

They stood beside the sewing table. Around them, people were packing tools into boxes. One of the brothers had forgiven the other about the table, provisionally.

“It was for my daughter,” Ruth said.

Ada waited.

“She’s fourteen now. Perfectly healthy. Taller than I am.”

Ruth laughed, then pressed her lips together.

“I don’t know why I brought it.”

“To finish it, perhaps.”

“Perhaps.”

Ada drew out a chair.

Ruth sat with the cardigan across her knees.

After a while she said, “I think I wanted somebody to see that I did start.”

Ada sat beside her.

Across the room, Tomas fitted the chair’s new leg into its joint. Nell watched from the floor, solemnly holding a clamp she had been told not to tighten yet.

Ruth stroked one tiny cuff with her thumb.

“Could you keep it?”

“As it is?”

“Yes.”

“We could do that.”

“Not because anything terrible happened.”

“I’ll make sure the label says so.”

Ruth considered this.

“Could it just say I got busy?”

Ada brought her a donation form.

For the third question, Ruth wrote exactly that, in careful blue letters.

***

The chair was ready on Sunday afternoon.

Tomas placed it on the floor and stepped back.

Nobody sat down.

“Go on,” he told Ada.

She lowered herself cautiously onto the seat.

It held.

A small group applauded, which embarrassed her, though not enough to make her stand immediately. The chair was comfortable. Its back supported her at precisely the angle she liked.

The new leg was lighter than the others.

“We could stain it,” someone said.

“I’d rather not,” Ada replied.

Tomas nodded as though she had passed a test he had not mentioned.

By the end of the weekend, the scarf had become two narrow scarves. The radio received one station clearly. The table stood level. Three projects had been declared beyond rescue, and their owners seemed relieved.

Several others had barely progressed.

These, Ada discovered, had produced no less conversation.

Mrs. Vale returned on Sunday carrying a biscuit tin.

Inside was a collection of fabric squares.

“I’m not promising anything,” she said.

“No one’s asking you to.”

“I simply thought someone might know what sort of pattern this was meant to be.”

Ada directed her to the sewing table.

Later, Maurice counted the donations.

“Enough for the roof?”

“Enough for someone to look at the roof.”

“That’s a start.”

“Yes,” he said. “Though we should probably avoid collecting too many of those.”

They left the workbench in the waiting room. Moving it would have required six people, and all six had gone home.

***

In September, the council renewed the grant.

Not generously, but sufficiently.

The museum opened a workshop on the first Saturday of each month. Its collection continued to grow. People still brought things they wanted preserved, things they wanted released, and things whose meaning they hoped Ada could determine for them.

She became more careful about that last category.

The wooden bird received a new label. It described the cabinetmaker’s recovery and mentioned the chest of drawers.

The detective novel remained unfinished. Several visitors offered to write an ending, but the author’s daughter declined.

“He never knew who did it,” she explained. “I think he enjoyed that.”

Ruth’s cardigan went into a case beside the yellow scarves, one of which was eventually claimed by the donor for her granddaughter.

The other remained.

The chair stood near the entrance, available to anyone who needed it. Ada kept its old label in a drawer.

A roof repair silenced the bucket. Repairing the clock proved more expensive, so it continued to show eleven seventeen. When visitors asked, Ada still told them it was broken.

One afternoon, Nell arrived without her school.

She sat in the chair and swung her feet.

“Is it still in the museum?”

“Yes.”

“Even though it’s finished?”

“Yes.”

Nell examined the pale new leg.

“Good,” she said.

Then she took a book from her bag and began reading.

Ada returned to her desk. Outside, on the unused platform, Maurice was measuring the bench. One of its boards needed replacing.

# The Office of Unspent Afternoons

On the morning the city decided to abolish wasted time, Mara found a whole summer afternoon in the pocket of a coat.

The coat belonged to a man who had been dead for eleven years. His daughter had brought it to the office in a paper shopping bag, together with a stopped wristwatch, three bus tickets, and an apology.

“I don’t know what you take,” she said.

“Neither do most people.”

Mara laid the coat across her desk. It was brown wool, shiny at the elbows, with a lining that had come loose beneath one arm. In the left pocket she found a peppermint stuck to its wrapper. In the right, behind a folded receipt, she found the afternoon.

It rested in her palm like a small, warm egg.

The daughter leaned forward.

“Is that his?”

“Possibly. We’ll have to check.”

Beyond the office window, rain stippled the courtyard. Someone had left a bicycle against the fountain, and water was collecting in its bell.

Mara held the afternoon to the light.

There was a garden inside it. A green chair. The shadow of a pear tree moving across a pair of bare feet.

“Oh,” said the daughter.

She sat down without being invited.

***

The Office of Unspent Afternoons occupied the ground floor of a municipal building that had once been a bathhouse. Its windows were tall and frosted at the edges. Beneath the carpet, the old floor still sloped toward drains.

People came there with time they had misplaced.

Usually it arrived attached to objects: a quarter of an hour inside an unopened letter, a winter evening caught in a scarf, seven minutes lodged between the pages of a cookbook.

There were rules.

Time deliberately spent could not be recovered. Neither could time slept through, however much certain employers insisted otherwise. Boredom was not proof of waste. Waiting was a disputed category and required a separate form.

Most recoverable time had been abandoned through inattention.

Someone would stand at a kitchen window, thinking about a meeting scheduled for Thursday, and fail to notice the snow beginning on Tuesday. The unnoticed interval would loosen. If nothing secured it—a smell, a touch, a sudden thought—it could slip entirely out of the day.

Such intervals drifted until they found something to cling to.

The office collected them, identified them where possible, and returned them to their owners.

Mara had worked there for twenty-three years.

She was very good at distinguishing a minute from a wish.

The daughter watched the afternoon brighten.

“I remember that chair,” she said. “He never sat in it.”

“Apparently he did once.”

“Can I have it?”

“Not quite. But you can visit.”

***

Visits took place in the former changing rooms.

Mara showed the daughter into a narrow cubicle with a wooden bench and a hook on the wall.

“You can observe,” she explained. “You can’t intervene. He won’t know you’re there.”

“How long do I get?”

“As long as it lasted.”

The daughter looked at her phone.

For a moment, Mara thought she would leave.

Then she switched it off.

Mara placed the afternoon in a shallow brass dish and closed the door.

Through the frosted glass came the soft rustle of leaves.

At her desk lay an envelope marked MUNICIPAL EFFICIENCY DIRECTORATE. Mara had been avoiding it since breakfast. Now she opened it with the blunt knife she used for extracting seconds from envelopes.

The notice was brief.

Following a comprehensive review, the city had determined that the Office of Unspent Afternoons duplicated services increasingly available through digital scheduling platforms, wellness initiatives, and private memory-preservation providers.

The office would close in thirty days.

Unclaimed holdings would be processed for civic reinvestment.

Mara read that phrase twice.

Then she went downstairs.

***

The archive occupied the old swimming pool.

Shelves stood along the tiled lanes. The shallow end held minutes, sorted by decade and weather. Hours occupied the middle. Longer intervals were stored beneath the diving gallery, where the temperature remained steady.

There were jars of railway waiting rooms, boxes of Sunday mornings, and a locked cabinet containing the last eleven seconds before a man decided not to board a ship.

Mara passed a shelf labeled DOMESTIC, MISCELLANEOUS.

Inside one jar, a woman was peeling an orange while a child explained something about dinosaurs. Inside another, two brothers washed dishes without speaking, having finally exhausted an argument that had lasted six years.

Most of these moments had never been claimed.

People tended to search for dramatic losses: the speech they should have made, the train they should have caught, the person they should have kissed.

The office could rarely help with those.

What it held instead was everything that had happened around the edges.

At the far end of the pool stood a glass vessel as tall as Mara’s shoulder.

Its contents looked like late daylight in an empty room.

The label read:

**UNATTRIBUTED**  
**SEVENTEEN MINUTES**  
**FOUND: MUNICIPAL CLOCK TOWER**  
**CAUTION: COLLECTIVE**

Mara touched the glass.

Somewhere overhead, in the visiting cubicle, a woman began to cry.

***

The efficiency director arrived the next day wearing shoes that had never encountered uncertain ground.

His name was Pell. He shook Mara’s hand with the grave friendliness of a man about to remove a tree.

“Extraordinary place,” he said.

She waited.

“I want to assure you that the transition will preserve the spirit of your work.”

“What happens to the archive?”

“The recoverable material will be consolidated.”

“Where?”

“We’re developing a central resource.”

“For what purpose?”

Pell glanced toward the courtyard.

“The city loses thousands of productive hours annually. Congestion. Administrative delays. Infrastructure interruptions. Your holdings could offset some of that loss.”

“You want to put them into traffic lights.”

“That’s one potential application.”

“People’s afternoons.”

“Unclaimed afternoons.”

Mara looked at his polished shoes. There was a bead of rain on one toe.

“You can’t make an afternoon into something useful,” she said. “It already was something.”

Pell’s expression softened, which annoyed her more than impatience would have.

“I understand this is emotional.”

“No,” said Mara. “You understand that I’m objecting.”

He left a folder containing relocation options.

One was a position in the Office of Parking Appeals.

That evening, Mara stayed after closing. She walked between the shelves until the building’s heating switched off. Around her, thousands of small intervals glimmered in the dark.

She had spent twenty-three years returning time.

It occurred to her that she had never tried to save any.

***

She began with letters.

The office records contained names, addresses, fragments of identification. Mara wrote to everyone she could find.

We may be holding something that belongs to you.

She expected very little.

People ignored notices about money they were owed. Time seemed even less likely to bring them through the door.

But by Thursday there was a queue in the courtyard.

A retired tram driver reclaimed twelve minutes of his first marriage. A violin teacher found an evening during which she had eaten soup alone and felt, inexplicably, content. A teenage boy came for forty seconds belonging to his grandmother and emerged from the cubicle smiling.

“What happened?” Mara asked.

“She swore at a pigeon.”

The local paper sent a reporter.

He wanted photographs of the jars.

Mara made him sit with eight minutes from his own childhood, recovered years earlier from a donated school blazer.

When he came out, he asked for a glass of water.

His article appeared on Saturday.

By Monday, the queue reached the street.

People brought suitcases, wedding dresses, broken radios, umbrellas, and once an entire bedside cabinet.

They brought objects they had intended to throw away.

They brought things they had been afraid to touch.

Mara worked through lunch.

On the ninth day, someone brought her own name.

***

It was written on the back of a photograph.

The photograph showed Mara at nineteen, sitting on the wall outside her mother’s house. She wore a yellow shirt and an expression of impatience.

A man from the house-clearance warehouse had found it inside a box overlooked after her mother’s death.

“There’s something stuck to it,” he said.

Mara knew before she turned it over.

An hour lay against the photograph, thin and pale as a slice of onion.

She signed the receipt.

For the rest of the day, she kept it in a drawer.

Her mother had died in November, four years earlier. Their last conversation had concerned a leaking gutter and whether Mara was eating properly.

Mara had been leaving for work.

Her mother had asked her to stay for tea.

She had said, “At the weekend.”

There were details she no longer trusted. Had her mother already filled the kettle? Had she been wearing the blue cardigan or the grey one? Grief had worked over the scene so often that memory had begun to resemble a room repeatedly searched by strangers.

After closing, Mara took the hour to a cubicle.

She set it in the dish.

The room filled with the smell of ironing.

***

It was not the last conversation.

It was an ordinary Wednesday, twenty-seven years earlier.

Her mother stood at an ironing board beside the kitchen window. A radio murmured near the bread bin. Young Mara sat at the table, reading a job advertisement.

“I could move,” she said.

“You could.”

“There’s nothing here.”

Her mother turned a sleeve inside out.

“There are some things.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes.”

Outside, someone dragged a wheelie bin over uneven paving.

Mara remembered this summer. She had applied for jobs in six cities. She had regarded her hometown as a waiting room whose magazines she had already read.

She did not remember this hour.

Her younger self went upstairs. Her footsteps crossed the ceiling.

Her mother continued ironing.

That was all.

For a long while, nothing happened.

The radio gave the weather forecast. A fly worried at the window. Her mother paused to rub the base of her thumb.

Mara found herself growing impatient.

She had expected a revelation: some private evidence of love, some sentence spoken into the empty kitchen that would settle everything.

Instead, her mother switched off the iron.

She cut a heel of bread, spread it with butter, and ate standing up.

Then she opened the back door and looked at the sky.

Mara watched her.

For the first time in years, her mother was not dying, not remembered, not required to mean anything.

She was deciding whether the washing would dry.

***

Two weeks before closure, Pell returned.

The newspaper had complicated matters.

“There may be scope for a heritage model,” he said. “Volunteer staffing. Limited opening hours. A representative collection.”

“What happens to the rest?”

He said nothing.

Mara took him downstairs.

At first he appeared impressed. Then concerned. Finally he adopted the look of someone calculating the cost of shelving.

She stopped before the tall glass vessel.

“What is that?” he asked.

“Seventeen minutes.”

“Rather a large container.”

“They belonged to the whole city.”

Forty years earlier, during repairs to the clock tower, the municipal clocks had stopped together. For seventeen minutes, no public clock had advanced.

People continued living, of course. Bakers baked. Buses ran late without official confirmation. Children waited for bells that did not ring.

But the city, considered as a single administrative entity, had failed to account for those minutes.

They had collected in the tower.

The office had removed them with considerable difficulty.

“What would happen if you released them?” Pell asked.

“I’m not certain.”

“Then I would strongly advise against it.”

“So would I.”

He looked relieved.

Mara studied the label.

The old archivist had added a note in pencil beneath the warning.

**Must be returned at point of origin.**

***

On the final Friday, Mara closed the office early.

There were still hundreds of jars downstairs.

They had returned what they could. Volunteers had traced families, repaired records, and carried chairs into the courtyard. Someone had supplied sandwiches every day without leaving a name.

But there was too much.

There had always been too much.

At five o’clock, a municipal van arrived for the archive.

At four forty-five, Mara was already in the clock tower.

She had borrowed a handcart from the market.

The climb had taken three people, two ropes, and language unsuitable for the teenage volunteer helping at the bottom.

Pell found her beside the mechanism.

“You cannot do this,” he said, breathless from the stairs.

“I’m returning municipal property.”

“You don’t know what will happen.”

“No.”

Below them, buses crowded the square. Office windows burned against the gathering dusk. People hurried toward crossings, shops, stations, home.

Pell stepped forward.

Then he stopped.

Perhaps he understood. Perhaps he was merely tired.

Mara loosened the lid.

The seventeen minutes rose without light or sound.

The clock’s second hand paused.

Across the square, a woman stopped searching in her handbag.

A cyclist put one foot on the ground.

Someone looked up.

***

Nothing stopped.

That was what people argued about afterward.

Cars still moved. Rain still fell. A dropped cup still broke against the pavement outside the café.

But for seventeen minutes, nobody in the city felt late.

A surgeon continued operating. A cleaner finished a corridor, then stood beside its long window. A father listening to his daughter’s elaborate account of a playground disagreement stopped preparing his reply.

In the square, the woman found her keys and stayed where she was.

Pell sat on the tower steps.

“I used to come up here with my brother,” he said.

Mara waited, but he said nothing more.

When the second hand moved again, the van was still parked outside the office. The transfer order was still valid. Pell made a telephone call and postponed it until Monday.

That gave them a weekend.

By Monday, the library had offered a basement, and three retired clerks had offered mornings. The council took longer. Eventually, after meetings, revisions, and one remarkably ill-tempered vote, it approved a smaller office.

Mara spent the winter packing.

She kept her mother’s hour until the last day. Then she visited once more.

The ironing was there, and the bread, and the uncertain weather.

This time, when her mother opened the back door, Mara noticed washing already hanging at the far end of the garden.

One sleeve had worked loose from its peg.

Her mother went outside to fasten it.
