# The Office of Lost Time

On her first morning at the Office of Lost Time, Mara was given a brass key, a green cardigan, and a warning about Thursdays.

“The key opens your desk,” said Mr. Bell. “The cardigan is because the building never warms up. On Thursdays, people lie.”

“Only Thursdays?”

“Other days too. But Thursdays they’ve usually rehearsed.”

He showed her the public counter, the kettle, and the shelves behind the frosted glass partition. The shelves held jars of different sizes, each labeled in a careful hand.

**NINE MINUTES. WAITING FOR A PLUMBER.**

**FOUR SECONDS. NAME FORGOTTEN DURING INTRODUCTION.**

**ONE SUMMER. CLAIM DISPUTED.**

Some jars were clear. Others contained a grayish vapor, or light that moved as though something had passed in front of a distant window.

“Don’t open anything without the claimant present,” Mr. Bell said.

“What happens if I do?”

“You’ll find out what it was like to wait for somebody else’s plumber.”

---

The office occupied the ground floor of a municipal building scheduled for demolition since 1974. Upstairs were the Department of Weights and Measures and a room containing obsolete street signs.

Mara had applied because the advertisement said no experience was necessary, only legible handwriting and a willingness to sit with people who could not explain themselves.

She had recently spent eight months caring for her father. After his death, people kept suggesting occupations that would be meaningful.

She did not want meaningful work. She wanted a chair, a salary, and instructions.

For the first week, these were enough.

A woman collected twenty-three minutes she had lost looking for her glasses. A boy reclaimed the pause between dropping a plate and hearing it break. He wanted to use it during a mathematics exam.

“You can’t transfer it that way,” Mara told him, reading from the handbook.

“Why not?”

“The circumstances have to be reasonably similar.”

“So I have to drop a plate during the exam?”

Mr. Bell, passing behind her, said, “We neither encourage nor prohibit creative applications.”

There were forms for everything except the question most people eventually asked.

Could they have the good parts again?

No, Mara learned. Those had not been lost.

---

Time arrived overnight through a slot in the rear wall.

Nobody knew who delivered it. Mr. Bell had stayed late once, with sandwiches and a crossword, and fallen asleep at eleven. In the morning, the sandwiches were gone and the slot was full.

“Could have been a coincidence,” he said.

Each delivery came wrapped in brown paper. Mara unwrapped the parcels, measured their contents using an instrument resembling a kitchen scale, and entered them in the ledger.

Lost time was heavier than she expected.

A wasted afternoon could make her wrists ache. Years sometimes weighed almost nothing.

“People misunderstand the measurements,” Mr. Bell explained. “Duration isn’t the same thing as weight.”

One Tuesday, she found a parcel no larger than a matchbox that required both hands to lift.

Inside was a moment in which someone had almost said something.

She put it on the lowest shelf.

By the second month, Mara had learned to recognize certain kinds without reading the labels: the sour metallic chill of bureaucracy, the dusty warmth of indecision, and, most common, the faintly electrical sensation of having entered a room and forgotten why.

They stored that last category in a drawer.

---

The man with the eleven minutes came in during rain.

He was very tall and wore a hat that had been repaired with thread of the wrong color. He stood just inside the door until Mara looked up.

“I’m told you might have something of mine.”

“What have you lost?”

“Eleven minutes. Approximately.”

“When?”

“Forty-six years ago.”

Mara took out the long-term claim form.

The man’s name was Elias Venn. He had been a piano tuner. On a particular afternoon in November, he had gone to buy oranges while his wife waited at home.

There had been a queue. Then a conversation with the shopkeeper about a broken awning. Then a small confusion over change.

“When I got back,” he said, “she was sitting by the window.”

Mara waited.

“She said something. I answered without listening. I was putting the oranges in a bowl.”

“Do you remember what she said?”

“No. That’s the difficulty.”

“And the eleven minutes?”

“If I hadn’t wasted them, perhaps I’d have been settled when she spoke.”

Mara lowered her pen.

“Is your wife—”

“She died in February.”

Outside, a bus went past with its interior lights on.

“I don’t want the years,” he said. “I understand about those. I only thought you might have the queue.”

---

They found the eleven minutes in a squat jar behind a school assembly and two hours spent on hold with an insurance company.

Mara recognized the shop immediately: damp coats, oranges, a bell above the door. A tiny length of striped awning moved inside the glass.

She carried it to Mr. Bell.

“He wants to get home earlier.”

“Then he’ll be disappointed.”

“Couldn’t it change what happened?”

“No.”

“What can it do?”

“Give him back eleven minutes in the queue.”

She looked at the jar.

“That seems cruel.”

“It isn’t cruel. It’s eleven minutes in a queue. We must be careful not to promise more.”

Mr. Venn received the explanation without protest. He turned his hat in his hands.

“Would I remember buying the oranges?”

“You would experience it again.”

“And then?”

“Then you’d be here.”

“May I sit down?”

Mara brought a chair.

He unscrewed the lid. The room smelled briefly of citrus peel and wet wool.

For eleven minutes, he sat with his eyes open, occasionally shifting his weight. Once he put a hand into his pocket.

Then the smell vanished.

“Well?” Mara asked before she could stop herself.

“The shopkeeper’s name was Arun,” he said. “I’d forgotten.”

He thanked her and left.

She watched him negotiate the wet pavement, placing his feet carefully between the puddles.

---

After that, Mara began checking the arrivals for her father’s name.

It was against policy to search personal claims during working hours, so she did it at lunch.

Her father had been a bus mechanic. He saved screws in tobacco tins and read the last page of a novel before deciding whether to begin it. During his illness, he had become particular about toast.

Not too dark. Not too pale. Butter all the way to the edges.

One morning, after a night in which neither of them had slept, he sent a slice back.

She had said, “It’s toast, Dad. It doesn’t matter.”

He had looked at the plate.

“No,” he said. “I suppose not.”

She wanted the minute before that exchange. She wanted to stand again beside the toaster, tired and angry, knowing what she knew now.

She found other things.

Seven minutes he had spent waiting outside a dance hall in 1968. An afternoon lost to a carburetor incorrectly described as compatible. A whole Sunday during which he had intended to telephone his brother.

Nothing from the kitchen.

“Was it wasted?” Mr. Bell asked when he discovered her searching.

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

She was so angry with him that she could not answer.

He left her alone with the ledger.

---

In October, a notice arrived from the council.

The building would be demolished in March. The Office of Lost Time would close at the end of February. Outstanding claims would be transferred to an online portal.

“What does an online portal do with the jars?” Mara asked.

“Nothing,” said Mr. Bell.

“What happens to them?”

“Disposal.”

The attached guidance described lost time as a nonhazardous residual product.

Mr. Bell took off his spectacles and rubbed the bridge of his nose.

“They’ve wanted to do this for years.”

“Can they?”

“They own the building.”

Mara spent the afternoon imagining a truck loaded with years reversing toward an incinerator.

She asked the council for clarification. The council sent her a link to the notice she had already read.

She wrote again.

This time, she received an acknowledgment with a reference number.

The acknowledgment took four days to arrive. On the fifth morning, those four days appeared through the slot, neatly wrapped.

Mr. Bell examined the parcel.

“At least they’ve processed something.”

Mara did not laugh.

There were nine thousand jars in the office, and fewer than five months to find their owners.

---

They began with letters.

Most came back marked unknown, deceased, or insufficient address. Some people replied that the office must be mistaken. They had lost no time. Their lives had been extremely full.

Others arrived carrying lists.

A retired headmistress wanted every meeting she had ever attended. A young man asked for the three years of a failed relationship.

“Was all of it lost?” Mara asked.

“At the moment it feels that way.”

“Perhaps wait a little.”

He looked relieved to be given something to do.

Mr. Venn came back near Christmas. He brought a paper bag of oranges.

“I read about the closure.”

“We’re trying to return as much as we can.”

“Could I help?”

Mara gave him envelopes to address.

He came on Wednesdays after that. His handwriting was excellent. Sometimes he spoke about his wife, whose name was June and who had once been banned from a hotel for taking cuttings from its ornamental plants.

“Were they valuable?”

“Only to the hotel.”

He never again asked about the words he had missed.

Once, while licking an envelope, he said, “Arun let us pay at the end of the month when work was slow. I remembered that afterward.”

Mara peeled an orange. Its skin came away in one long piece.

---

In January, they opened the unclaimed storage room.

It contained everything too vague to assign: time lost by crowds, by committees, by people who had forgotten their own names.

There were crates of delayed trains and postponed decisions. Along one wall stood large stoneware vessels labeled simply **BETWEEN**.

Mara rested her hand on one.

She felt herself standing outside a hospital lift, neither arriving nor leaving.

She moved to another.

A child’s bedroom after the child had grown up.

Another.

The weeks after sending an application and before receiving an answer.

“Who owns these?”

“Sometimes nobody in particular,” Mr. Bell said. “Sometimes too many people to list.”

“Can they be used?”

“Under the original charter, unclaimed intervals can be released for public benefit.”

“What benefit?”

He went upstairs and returned with a bound volume and dust on his cardigan.

They found the clause between regulations concerning tram horses and public clocks.

**For the relief of persons hurried beyond reasonable endurance.**

There was no application procedure.

There was no prohibition either.

Mara read the sentence three times.

Then she asked Mr. Venn whether he knew anyone who could build a bench.

---

His brother had been a joiner. His nephew still had the tools.

They put the bench in the little paved square beside the office, where people ordinarily stopped only to shake rain from umbrellas.

It was sturdy, with a back high enough to lean against and arms that made getting up easier.

Underneath it, Mr. Bell installed a brass fitting from the oldest part of the storeroom.

“Standard interval regulator,” he said.

“Why do we have one?”

“We used to maintain waiting rooms.”

“What happened?”

“Someone decided waiting was inefficient.”

They connected the first vessel on a Monday morning.

Nothing flashed. The pigeons remained unimpressed.

Mara sat down.

The traffic continued. Across the street, a woman was trying to fold a pushchair. Somewhere, a delivery driver sounded his horn.

Yet the urgency drained out of these things.

Mara could hear the horn without feeling that she ought to move. She noticed a loose thread on her cuff and broke it carefully rather than pulling.

After a while, she stood.

The clock above the pharmacy had advanced less than a minute.

She sat down again.

This time, she cried.

Mr. Bell stayed by the office door. When she raised her hand, he came over with a tissue and sat beside her.

---

They put up a sign.

**PLEASE SIT IF YOU NEED A MOMENT.**

The first person to use the bench was the delivery driver. He ate a sandwich, checked his watch twice, and left looking suspicious.

Then came a nurse between shifts, a woman with two shopping bags, and a teenager who sat with his hands pressed against his knees.

Word spread without settling into an explanation.

People called it the quiet bench, though the square remained noisy.

A council inspector arrived with a clipboard.

“Is this an authorized installation?”

“We’re acting under the charter,” Mara said.

He examined the clause.

“This predates the current street furniture policy.”

“It does.”

“Has a risk assessment been completed?”

Mr. Bell offered him a seat while Mara fetched the forms.

When she returned, the inspector was still there. His clipboard lay beside him.

“My daughter’s getting married,” he said.

“Congratulations.”

“I’ve been worrying about the parking.”

Mara waited.

“I suppose someone else could do that.”

He approved the bench provisionally for six months.

In February, they ran a pipe beneath the pavement to a storeroom in the pharmacy. The pharmacist agreed to turn the valve when a vessel emptied.

“What does it need?”

“Checking occasionally,” Mr. Bell said. “Nothing complicated.”

---

On the office’s final afternoon, Mara packed her father’s unclaimed intervals into a small cardboard box.

She had permission now. Mr. Bell had signed the form.

At home, she opened the seven minutes outside the dance hall.

Cold air touched her face.

She stood inside her father’s impatience, young and badly dressed, watching the door. Music leaked through the brickwork. He had borrowed a comb and was afraid the person he was meeting would notice.

Mara almost laughed.

She did not learn anything useful. There was no message, no hidden explanation of his life.

Only cold feet, cheap hair cream, and the astonishing fact that he had once been waiting for a future that included her.

Afterward, she put the empty jar on her kitchen shelf.

The toaster clicked.

She buttered two slices without examining their color.

In March, the building came down.

The bench remained.

Mr. Venn visited on Wednesdays. Mr. Bell claimed retirement disagreed with him and took responsibility for polishing the brass regulator.

Mara found work at the railway station.

Sometimes, on her way home, she stopped in the square. Usually someone was already sitting there, and she kept walking.

One evening, a little boy was on the bench beside his mother, carefully undoing a knot in his shoelace.

She held their bags.

He worked slowly, using both hands.

Nobody helped him.

Nobody told him to hurry.

# The Department of Almost

The Department of Almost occupied the fourth floor of a building that had never received its final coat of paint. From the street, it looked less like a government office than a thought someone had been interrupted while having.

Mara found it on a Thursday, after the rain had stopped but before the city had decided whether to dry.

She had been carrying the letter for eleven years.

It was not a remarkable letter. Three pages, blue ink, an envelope softened at the corners. She had written it to her brother during the last winter of their mother’s life, and she had never sent it. Then her brother had moved, and then she had moved, and then not sending it had become a kind of arrangement.

The department’s address appeared on the back of a receipt from a bakery she did not remember entering.

**For matters nearly settled**, it said.

Inside the building, the lift offered buttons for floors one, two, three, and eventually.

Mara took the stairs.

On the fourth-floor landing stood a rubber plant, a clock without a minute hand, and a receptionist eating an orange with great concentration.

“I’m not sure I belong here,” Mara said.

The receptionist placed a strip of peel on a napkin.

“That’s our most common opening statement.”

“I have a letter.”

“Sent or unsent?”

“Unsent.”

“Good. Sent letters are downstairs, in Consequences.”

She slid a form across the desk.

At the top, in neat black type, it read:

**WHAT WERE YOU ABOUT TO DO?**

---

The waiting room contained six people and an aquarium full of water.

No fish. Just water, circulating faithfully through a little stone castle.

A young man in a wedding suit held a single running shoe. An elderly woman had brought a cake under a glass dome. Beside the window, a boy was trying to remember a tune, producing the same five notes over and over.

Mara sat near a man whose briefcase was leaking sand.

“First visit?” he asked.

She nodded.

“Don’t agree to a permanent solution straight away.”

“What kind of solution?”

He tilted the briefcase upright.

“I nearly became a geologist.”

Before she could ask what that meant, a door opened and a clerk called her name.

The clerk was tall and narrow, with sleeves rolled to precisely equal heights. His identification badge read **ELIAS, PROVISIONAL**.

His office contained two chairs, a desk, and shelves of objects that seemed unconnected: a chipped mug, a ballet slipper, a tiny brass cannon, a jar of dark water.

“Please,” he said, indicating the chair without a stack of newspapers on it.

Mara placed the letter on his desk.

Elias did not touch it.

“What outcome are you seeking?”

“I thought you might tell me.”

“That’s possible, but expensive.”

“How expensive?”

“Usually several years.”

Mara almost smiled.

“I’d like to stop carrying this around.”

“In your bag?”

“In general.”

He nodded, as if the distinction mattered.

“Before we proceed,” he said, “I should explain that we do not remove the past. We have tried. It affects the plumbing.”

---

Elias opened a drawer and took out a small wooden tray.

“Set it here.”

Mara laid the letter in the tray. The envelope shifted slightly, like something settling into sleep.

“How does the department work?” she asked.

“Unfinished actions accumulate. Most disperse naturally. You consider buying pears, buy apples instead, and the pear intention evaporates by supper. But certain things persist.”

“Because they matter?”

“Sometimes because they matter. Sometimes because they were interrupted at an unfortunate angle.”

He gestured toward the shelves.

“That mug belongs to a woman who was about to ask her husband whether he was happy.”

“What happened?”

“The kettle boiled.”

“And then?”

“Thirty-seven years.”

Mara looked at the mug.

It was ordinary white ceramic, with a faded picture of a duck.

“Did she ever ask?”

“She came here last month.”

“What did you do?”

“Helped her decide whether she still wanted the answer.”

From somewhere beyond the wall came the sound of applause, abruptly cut off.

“Unmade speeches,” Elias explained.

“Do you keep everything here?”

“Certainly not. We’d need a much larger building. We maintain representative objects. The rest is stored in the city.”

“Where?”

“Wherever there’s room. The pause before a traffic light changes. The space under an unused chair. The last second of a song after someone turns off the radio.”

Mara glanced at the letter.

“So this has been taking up space?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

Elias put on his glasses.

“That’s what we’re about to find out.”

---

He unfolded the pages carefully.

Mara watched his eyes move.

She remembered writing the letter at her kitchen table, beside a bowl of oranges going soft. She remembered the thrill of arranging her anger so that it looked like evidence. Every paragraph had seemed reasonable. Every reasonable paragraph had contained a concealed knife.

Her brother, Daniel, had not visited enough.

He had not called enough.

He had said their mother sounded better on the telephone because he could not hear what it cost her to sound that way.

All this was true.

There were other true things she had left out.

Elias finished reading.

“Well?” Mara said.

“It’s a very efficient letter.”

“That sounds bad.”

“It accomplishes several things at once. It accuses him, defends you, remembers your mother, and requests an apology without admitting that an apology is what you want.”

Mara folded her arms.

“You said you weren’t going to tell me what outcome I wanted.”

“I said it was expensive.”

He turned the last page toward her.

At the bottom, beneath her signature, was a sentence she did not remember writing.

**You were supposed to know I needed you.**

The ink looked fresh.

“That wasn’t there.”

“No,” Elias said.

“Did you write it?”

“No.”

She touched the words. They did not smear.

For eleven years she had remembered the letter as a record of Daniel’s failures. The new sentence made her want to take it back from Elias.

Outside, a bus hissed at the curb.

---

“There are three standard options,” Elias said.

He took out a brochure so old that the woman pictured on its cover was holding a telephone attached to a wall.

“Completion, release, or conversion.”

“What’s conversion?”

“We turn the unfinished matter into something else.”

“Such as?”

“A garden. An unreasonable dislike of a particular song. Expertise in restoring antique clocks. It depends on the material.”

“And release?”

“You accept that it will remain unfinished.”

“That sounds like doing nothing.”

“It can look similar from a distance.”

Mara stood and went to the window.

Below, a cyclist waited at a red light despite there being no cars. A delivery driver rearranged parcels in a van.

“I can’t send that letter,” she said.

“You can.”

“It would be cruel.”

“Possibly.”

“And it’s too late.”

“For that version of the conversation, certainly.”

She turned.

“What does that mean?”

Elias considered her.

“Would you like to see storage?”

“Will it help?”

“I don’t know. But most people find the brochure disappointing.”

He lifted the wooden tray. The letter had become heavier; Mara could tell by the adjustment of his wrists.

They went through a door behind his desk into a narrow passage lined with coat hooks.

Each hook held a different shadow.

“Unaccepted invitations,” Elias said.

One shadow raised a hand as they passed.

Mara nearly raised hers back.

At the end of the passage, Elias unlocked a green door with a key that looked freshly cut.

Beyond it was an enormous railway station.

---

The station roof vanished into a bright, overcast distance.

Platforms extended in every direction. Some held trains. Others held houses, dinner tables, hospital beds, or stretches of empty road.

There were announcements, but Mara could understand only fragments.

“Passengers intending to explain themselves—”

“Due to an unexpected act of kindness—”

“The service originally scheduled for last November—”

On the nearest platform, a man repeatedly approached a woman sitting on a bench. Each time he came within a few steps, the scene reset. He was back beside a vending machine, adjusting his coat.

“Is he trapped?”

“No. He’s at home watching television. This is the approach he never made.”

“Who is she?”

“Someone he thought he recognized.”

“Did he?”

“We don’t collect outcomes that never happened.”

They walked past a field where a house had been marked out with stakes and string. Past a classroom full of raised hands. Past a restaurant in which a waiter held a bottle above two empty glasses.

Then Mara saw a kitchen.

Her mother’s kitchen.

The yellow curtains were there, and the calendar from the insurance company, and the burn mark on the counter shaped vaguely like a country.

Daniel stood beside the sink.

He was younger than she remembered him being, which unsettled her.

“What is this?”

Elias looked at the tray.

“An associated matter.”

In the kitchen, Daniel took a telephone from his pocket.

He looked at its screen.

He put it away.

Then he took it out again.

---

“That doesn’t prove anything,” Mara said.

“No.”

“He could have been calling anyone.”

“Yes.”

Daniel leaned against the sink. Through the kitchen doorway, Mara could see the narrow bed they had brought downstairs for their mother.

She remembered that afternoon.

She had gone to the pharmacy, then driven past the house and parked beside the river. She had sat there for forty minutes with the medicine on the passenger seat.

When she returned, Daniel said he had to leave.

She had hated him for having somewhere to go.

In the station kitchen, he pressed something on the telephone and lifted it to his ear.

The scene stopped.

“Can you make it continue?” Mara asked.

“This is where the unfinished part ends.”

“But what was he going to say?”

“We don’t know.”

“Surely someone knows.”

“Perhaps your brother.”

She watched his still face. He looked exhausted. She had forgotten that, or had never noticed.

It did not cancel anything. He had left. She had stayed. Their mother had needed things in the night, and Mara had been the person who heard.

She waited for the scene to provide more: a message on the screen, a word from him, something she could use.

Nothing moved.

“People sometimes stay here for hours,” Elias said.

“Does it change?”

“No.”

Mara glanced at him, annoyed by how gently he had answered.

“I’d like to go back.”

He turned toward the green door, carrying the tray between them, and she followed without looking into any of the other platforms.

---

Back in the office, Elias put the letter on the desk.

Mara sat with her coat still on.

“Does your family know what you do?” she asked.

“My daughter thinks I work in permits.”

“Do you have unfinished things?”

“Of course.”

“Can’t you fix them?”

“Being employed here is not the same as being good at it.”

He straightened the brochure.

“I have been meaning to apologize to a friend for nine years.”

“What happened?”

“I was funny at his expense in a room where he needed me to be kind.”

“Why haven’t you?”

“For a while I thought explaining my intentions would help. Then I realized I was waiting until I could apologize without feeling ashamed.”

He put the brochure back in the drawer.

Mara took her telephone from her bag.

Daniel’s number was still there.

They exchanged birthday messages. At Christmas, photographs. He had a dog she had never met and a wife she liked but did not know well enough to telephone independently.

Once, two years earlier, he had sent a picture of a badly assembled bookshelf.

**Mum would have called this modern**, he wrote.

Mara had replied with a laughing face.

She remembered almost adding something else.

Now she opened their messages.

The blank field looked very small.

“What should I say?”

Elias shook his head.

“That part isn’t a service we provide.”

She typed, deleted, and typed again.

**I found an old letter I wrote to you. I don’t think I should send it. But could we talk about that winter sometime?**

She read it twice.

Then she pressed send.

---

Nothing happened.

The shelves did not tremble. The jar of dark water remained dark. Somewhere outside the office, a printer jammed.

Mara looked at the screen.

“I thought—”

“Yes,” Elias said. “People often do.”

“Was that completion?”

“That was a message.”

She laughed, unexpectedly, and had to wipe her eyes.

He passed her a box of tissues without commenting.

After a while she asked what would happen if Daniel did not answer.

“You’ll decide what to do then.”

“And if he answers badly?”

“The same.”

The letter lay between them.

She had imagined, without admitting it, that relinquishing it would make the eleven years available again. There would be some relief large enough to account for the time.

Instead, she was tired. She needed lunch. She had sent her brother a message she could no longer edit.

She folded the pages and returned them to the envelope.

“I think I’ll keep it for now.”

“All right.”

“Is that allowed?”

“It belongs to you.”

When Elias handed it over, it felt like three sheets of paper.

At reception, the woman was clearing away her orange peel.

“Settled?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

The receptionist nodded and reached for the next form.

Mara went down the stairs. On the second-floor landing, she stopped to check her telephone. There was no reply.

She put it in her bag rather than carrying it in her hand.

Outside, water was still dripping from the scaffolding. She stepped around a puddle and went looking for somewhere to eat.

---

Daniel called that evening while Mara was washing a pan.

She let it ring twice, dried her hands, and answered.

“Hello.”

“Hello,” he said.

For a moment, both listened.

Then Daniel said, “Is this a bad time?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“The pan can wait.”

He laughed. It was the same laugh, older.

They did not settle everything. Daniel remembered some things differently. He said something defensive, and Mara answered sharply. There was a silence during which she considered ending the call.

Then he asked, “What was in the letter?”

She sat down.

“Some things I still mean,” she said. “Some things I wouldn’t say now.”

“Will you tell me?”

So she began.

Later, she would remember the conversation imperfectly. She would remember the refrigerator switching on. A car door outside. Daniel telling her that on the afternoon she went to the pharmacy, he had nearly called to ask her to come home.

“Why didn’t you?”

“I thought you needed a break.”

“I did.”

“I know.”

“No,” she said, then stopped. “I don’t think you did.”

This time, he let her explain.

They spoke until the kitchen window reflected only the room.

The following week, Mara passed the unfinished building. A dentist occupied the fourth floor. On the landing below, someone had left a rubber plant with a note asking whoever took it to give it plenty of light.

She carried it home on the bus.

It fitted beside her kitchen window.

She watered it, then moved the letter to a drawer.

# The Department of Unclaimed Hours

The office stood between a locksmith and a shop that sold lamps nobody ever seemed to buy. Its window displayed a clock without hands and a notice printed in blue:

**IF YOU HAVE LOST TIME, PLEASE TAKE A NUMBER.**

Mara went inside because it was raining. That was what she told herself afterward, although the rain had been light and she had owned an umbrella.

Behind the counter, an elderly man was eating an orange with a knife. He wore a waistcoat, and his sleeves were secured with silver bands. On the wall behind him hung hundreds of keys, each labeled with a date.

“Have you an appointment?” he asked.

“No.”

“Then you’re early.”

He set down the knife.

Mara looked around. There were three wooden chairs, a filing cabinet, and a large brass bell beneath a glass dome. Somewhere beyond the wall, machinery made a sound like a person thinking before answering.

“What is this place?”

“The Department of Unclaimed Hours.”

“Is that a business?”

“Not by any useful definition.”

She should have left. Later, she would identify this as the last moment when leaving would have been simple.

Instead, she closed her umbrella.

The man examined her with mild interest.

“Most people come looking for something specific,” he said. “A summer. A conversation. Tuesday.”

“I don’t think I’ve lost Tuesday.”

“People rarely notice immediately.”

He slid a form across the counter. At the top, beneath her name, which was already printed there, someone had written: **SUITABLE FOR EMPLOYMENT.**

***

Mara had been unemployed for seven weeks.

Before that, she had worked for an insurance company, explaining to people why the particular disaster that had happened to them was different from the disaster they had paid to be protected against. She had been competent. Competence had made the job worse.

“What would I do?” she asked.

“Receive claims. Assess losses. Return what can be returned.”

“And the salary?”

He named a sum that was modest but possible.

“Pension?”

“Complicated.”

“Holiday?”

“Strongly encouraged.”

His name was Mr. Vale. He had managed the department for thirty-four years, although he admitted there were discrepancies.

He showed her the rooms behind the counter.

The building was considerably larger inside, but not in a grand way. It expanded into the kind of space usually occupied by municipal records: low ceilings, humming lights, corridors with scuffed paint.

There were shelves of glass jars. Some held a pale golden substance. Others were cloudy, greenish, or almost black.

“Hours,” he said.

Mara picked up a jar labeled **WAITING FOR THE PLUMBER, FEBRUARY 1998**.

It was surprisingly heavy.

“Wasted time?”

“Not necessarily. Unclaimed time.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Sometimes an hour passes without anyone being fully present for it. Sometimes people abandon an hour deliberately. Sometimes they cannot bear to remember it, but cannot bear to let it disappear.”

“And it ends up here?”

“Some of it.”

He took the jar from her and replaced it carefully.

“Don’t open anything until you’ve read the handbook.”

The handbook was six pages long. The final page contained only one sentence:

**You cannot give someone an hour they are unwilling to live.**

***

Her first customer was a retired bus driver named Mr. Anwar.

“I’ve lost about nine years,” he said.

Mara glanced at Mr. Vale, who was polishing the glass dome over the bell.

“Can you be more specific?”

“Traffic.”

Mr. Anwar placed a notebook on the counter. He had calculated his average daily delays across thirty-one years of employment, adjusted for holidays, illness, and unusually clear roads.

“I haven’t counted red lights,” he said. “I consider those legitimate.”

Mara admired his restraint.

They found eleven minutes.

The minutes had occurred on a November evening when his bus had been stationary beside a school playing field. A fox had appeared under the floodlights, carrying what looked like a white glove.

Mr. Anwar had watched it cross the grass.

“I remember that.”

“Did you enjoy it?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know. I was late.”

The jar brightened in her hands.

He took the minutes home in a paper envelope. Two days later, he returned the envelope empty.

“My wife watched with me,” he said. “She thought it was a sandwich bag.”

After he left, Mara asked how two people could share eleven minutes without reducing them.

“Not everything divides the way you expect,” said Mr. Vale.

Other customers were less satisfied.

A woman demanded the return of six years spent learning the violin before realizing she hated it. A man wanted every minute he had spent apologizing.

The department could do little for either.

The violinist, however, recovered an afternoon when she had played badly and happily with her sister.

She accepted it without enthusiasm.

***

By the third week, Mara understood several rules that were not in the handbook.

People exaggerated the time they had wasted and underestimated the time they had loved.

Children rarely came in.

Nobody ever asked for an hour spent doing the washing up, though the shelves held thousands of them, warm with kitchens and radio music.

The most difficult claims concerned the dead.

A widower wanted the last evening before his husband entered hospital. The hour existed, but it contained an argument about money.

“Can’t you remove that part?”

“No,” Mara said.

“Then what good is it?”

She had no answer that would have helped.

He left without taking it. A month later, he came back.

Mara learned not to describe an hour before handing it over. Her descriptions were always inadequate. An apparently ordinary breakfast might contain the exact scrape of a chair that someone had spent twenty years trying to hear again.

An hour that looked radiant might be unbearable.

There was a room at the end of the longest corridor where the jars had no labels.

Mr. Vale kept it locked.

“What’s in there?”

“Hours nobody survived to claim.”

Mara looked at the door.

“Who are we keeping them for?”

“I don’t know.”

It was the first time he had said this to her without disguising it as a joke.

That evening, she walked home instead of taking the bus. She bought bread from a bakery she usually passed after closing.

She ate half the loaf before reaching her flat.

***

Her mother had been dead for four years.

Mara had not mentioned this during her interview. Mr. Vale had not asked.

The illness had lasted eighteen months. During the final six, Mara had learned to organize her feelings around practical tasks. Prescriptions. Appointments. Soup. The washing of sheets.

Afterward, people told her she had been wonderful.

She found this difficult to forgive.

One Thursday, while searching for a missing anniversary, she discovered a jar bearing her mother’s handwriting.

Not her mother’s name. Her handwriting.

Mara knew the open loops of the letters, the hurried crossbar of the t.

The label said:

**AFTER THE RAIN, BEFORE THE SHOPS.**

Inside was a thin, clear light.

She stood holding it until Mr. Vale appeared at the end of the aisle.

“Oh,” he said.

“You knew?”

“I knew there might be something.”

“Can I take it?”

“Yes.”

“Just like anyone else?”

“Exactly like anyone else.”

She wanted him to be kinder, or more solemn. Instead, he asked her to sign the ledger.

At home she set the jar on the kitchen table.

For three nights she left it there.

She tried to place the hour. Perhaps they had been on holiday. Perhaps it belonged to a Saturday when she was small and her mother still worked at the library.

She could remember several shopping trips, none worth preserving.

On the fourth night, Mara made tea, washed her cup, and unscrewed the lid.

The kitchen disappeared.

She was standing beside her mother at a bus stop.

***

Her mother was forty-three, younger than Mara remembered her being.

She wore a red coat with one loose button. In her hand was a shopping list written on the back of an electricity bill.

“Well,” she said, looking down the road. “That’s not coming.”

Mara knew immediately that she was seventeen.

She also knew she was thirty-six.

Neither knowledge displaced the other.

Water dripped from the shelter. Across the street, a man was struggling to lift the shutter of a hardware shop.

“We could walk,” her mother said.

“It’s miles.”

“It’s twelve minutes.”

“In your shoes.”

Her mother looked at Mara’s boots.

“I did warn you.”

They began walking.

Mara had expected revelation. Instead, her mother talked about a colleague who microwaved fish, the price of curtains, and whether their neighbor’s new dog was actually new or merely the old dog clipped differently.

Mara listened desperately.

She tried to say, You will get ill.

What came out was, “We need milk.”

“Yes, it’s on the list.”

She tried to stop walking.

Her feet continued.

At the crossing, her mother took her arm, an absent little pressure through the sleeve. Then she released it to search for a tissue.

There was a small disagreement about which shop to visit first.

Her mother wanted the butcher.

Mara wanted a magazine.

They compromised badly and went to the chemist.

When the hour ended, Mara was back at her table, reaching toward something no longer there.

The jar was empty.

She sat until morning.

At work, Mr. Vale gave her the quieter desk.

***

Winter came.

The office windows misted over. Customers stamped their feet on the mat and brought in smells of wet wool, cold pavement, cigarettes.

Then the unclaimed hours began arriving faster.

Usually, they appeared overnight on a receiving shelf. Now Mara would turn around and find jars crowded along the floor.

Whole afternoons accumulated beneath the stairs.

Hours abandoned in hospital corridors. Hours spent refreshing messages. Hours from night shifts when the machinery ran smoothly and the worker stood beside it, feeling themselves become machinery too.

Mr. Vale ordered more shelving.

The shelving filled.

“Has this happened before?”

“Yes.”

“What did you do?”

“Ordered more shelving.”

The machinery behind the walls grew louder.

One morning, a crack appeared in the ceiling above the public counter. Golden dust fell onto a claim form.

Mr. Vale looked suddenly old.

“We’ll have to inspect the reservoir.”

Below the basement was another basement.

Below that was a staircase whose bottom Mara could not see.

They descended for a long time.

The reservoir was a cavern filled with slow-moving light. Walkways extended over it, supported by pillars inscribed with dates.

Far below, hours shifted against one another.

Mara heard laughter, a dropped pan, someone calling a dog.

The light had almost reached the walkways.

“What happens if it overflows?”

“People begin receiving time they didn’t ask for.”

“That sounds manageable.”

“While driving. During surgery. While carrying a child downstairs.”

Across the cavern, a wave struck a pillar.

For an instant, Mara smelled burning toast and heard someone shout her name.

Mr. Vale took her elbow.

“We should go.”

***

There was, naturally, a procedure.

Mr. Vale retrieved it from a red cabinet.

**EMERGENCY RELEASE OF SURPLUS TEMPORAL MATERIAL.**

The procedure allowed the department to empty the reservoir into a period where nobody would notice the additional time.

Historically, this had meant remote winters, long sea voyages, and certain committee meetings.

“The destination must have sufficient capacity,” Mr. Vale explained.

“What does that mean?”

“Someone has to live it.”

Mara reread the document.

At the bottom was a list of previous custodians.

The most recent had received forty-seven years.

“What happened to them?”

“They grew old.”

“While everyone else—”

“Yes.”

She put the paper down.

“You’ve done this.”

“A smaller release.”

“How much?”

He straightened the pages.

“Eleven years.”

The discrepancies.

Mara looked at his hands.

“Were you alone?”

“For most of it.”

The department was silent around them, except for the strained machinery.

“There must be another way.”

“There may be. We haven’t found it.”

Mara spent the afternoon reading old incident reports.

There were failed attempts to burn hours, bury them, distribute them through public clocks.

Each experiment had returned the time to the reservoir.

Near closing, she found a note in the margin of a report dated eighty years earlier.

**Small voluntary allocations successful. Scheme discontinued: insufficient participation.**

“Why didn’t you tell me about this?”

Mr. Vale read the note.

“Because I’d forgotten.”

For the first time since meeting him, she wanted to shout.

Instead, she fetched a blank sheet of paper.

“What are you doing?”

“Changing the sign.”

***

The new notice read:

**AN HOUR AVAILABLE. NO EXPERIENCE NECESSARY.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**You may encounter boredom, grief, unexpected pleasure, or ordinary weather.**

The first volunteer was the lamp seller next door.

“Does it cost anything?”

“Your attention,” Mara said.

“That’s usually the expensive part.”

He took an hour spent repairing a bicycle with someone’s father.

The next morning he returned and asked for another.

Then came the locksmith, two students, a nurse after her shift, and Mr. Anwar with his wife.

Not everyone liked what they received.

One student found herself waiting for exam results that never arrived within the allotted hour. She came back furious.

A man cried in the doorway and would not explain why.

Mara stopped calling the allocations gifts.

She called them hours.

People could refuse after reading a brief description. Nobody could choose the ending.

Within a week, there was a queue.

Within two, there were arguments in the queue.

Someone suggested premium appointments.

Someone else tried selling an unopened envelope outside the station.

The department added three rules and hired a woman named Ruth, who had managed a public swimming pool and was afraid of nobody.

The reservoir fell by the width of a finger.

It was not enough.

But at lunchtime, Mara found Mr. Vale in the back room, eating an orange.

He had removed his waistcoat.

“I think,” he said, “we should open on Saturdays.”

“You’ll need another employee.”

“Yes.”

“And you’re taking a day off.”

He considered this.

“Wednesday,” he said.

***

By spring, the queue had shortened, but it had not disappeared.

Some volunteers never returned. Others came monthly, fitting an unfamiliar hour between errands.

The reservoir stabilized.

Mara still visited it every Friday. She measured the level against a mark on a pillar and entered the result in a ledger. Progress looked less impressive written in millimeters, but she preferred it that way.

She never found another hour belonging to her mother.

Occasionally she searched.

Once, she nearly opened a jar because the label mentioned a red coat. She put it back.

Her own empty jar stood on her kitchen windowsill. In April, she used it for cuttings. Roots appeared in the water, pale threads branching against the glass.

One Wednesday, Mr. Vale came into the office carrying a paper bag.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” Ruth told him.

“I’ve brought lunch.”

“That’s how it starts.”

He left the bag and went out.

Through the window, Mara watched him hesitate at the corner. He looked toward the station, then toward the park.

For a moment, he seemed unable to choose.

Then the light changed. Other pedestrians crossed around him. A cyclist rang her bell.

He turned toward the park.

Mara returned to the counter, where a young woman was waiting with her hands tucked beneath her arms.

“I don’t know if this is the right place,” she said.

“What have you lost?”

The woman thought.

Outside, the locksmith raised his shutter. Next door, someone switched on every lamp.

“I’m not sure yet.”

Mara pulled out a chair.

“That’s all right,” she said. “Tell me what you remember.”

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

On my first morning at the Museum of Unfinished Things, the director handed me a key, a pencil, and half a biscuit.

“The key is for the front door,” she said. “The pencil is for the register. The biscuit is because I thought I wanted a whole one.”

Her name was Mrs. Vale. She wore a yellow cardigan whose left cuff had been repaired with green wool. In a museum devoted to incompletion, this seemed an unexpectedly firm statement.

The building had once been a railway station. Trains no longer stopped in our town, but the waiting room remained, along with its brown benches and a clock that showed twenty past four. Whether it was morning or afternoon had been debated by volunteers for years.

“We don’t mend the clock,” Mrs. Vale explained.

“Because it’s an exhibit?”

“Because the electrician quoted nine hundred pounds.”

I had applied for the job after leaving the planning office, where I had spent eleven years approving extensions to houses I would never enter. The museum offered less money, uncertain heating, and the possibility that work might occasionally surprise me.

“What exactly do we collect?” I asked.

Mrs. Vale led me past the ticket window into a room crowded with cabinets.

“Things people couldn’t finish. Things they wouldn’t finish. Things they simply stopped wanting.”

“And how do you tell the difference?”

“Usually we can’t.”

She gave me the larger portion of the biscuit.

“That,” she said, “is why we keep a register.”

I opened it carefully.

***

Our first exhibit was a model ship without a mast. Its donor, a retired dentist, had worked on it every Sunday for fourteen years before discovering that he preferred Sundays without it.

Beside it stood a wedding cake made of painted plaster. The baker had intended it for her shop window, then abandoned the business to become a driving instructor. According to her donation form, this had worked out extremely well.

There were unfinished novels, incomplete chess games, a quilt consisting of seventeen beautiful squares, and a brass instrument that three visiting musicians had failed to identify.

One cabinet contained a single glove.

“Surely that’s lost property,” I said.

“Look closer.”

It had six fingers.

In the former parcel office, shelves held things that people had asked us not to display: letters, sketchbooks, a dissertation, a list of baby names. These were wrapped in plain paper and identified only by numbers.

“Why keep them if nobody sees them?”

“People like knowing there’s somewhere they can be.”

I thought she meant the objects. Later I wondered.

My duties were modest. I dusted, catalogued donations, answered questions, and persuaded visitors not to complete the crossword displayed beneath glass.

One man came every Thursday to inspect a half-carved wooden fox. He never spoke or paid admission, which was voluntary anyway.

“Did he make it?” I asked.

“No.”

“Does he know who did?”

“I don’t think so.”

“What does he want?”

Mrs. Vale watched him through the doorway.

“A fox, perhaps. Must everything be complicated?”

***

After six weeks, I brought something of my own.

It was a blue cardigan my mother had begun knitting when I was nineteen. The back was finished, along with one sleeve and most of the front. The remaining wool lived in a plastic bag from a supermarket that no longer existed.

I had carried that bag through four flats, a marriage, a divorce, and the purchase of a small house whose dining room I used for drying laundry.

My mother was alive and well in a coastal town, where she attended swimming classes and complained about the price of cherries. Yet the cardigan had acquired, in my mind, the solemnity of something recovered from a shipwreck.

“She stopped when her hands got bad,” I told Mrs. Vale.

“Have you asked whether she wants it back?”

“She’ll only feel guilty.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

I telephoned my mother that evening.

“The blue thing?” she said. “Good heavens. Have you still got that?”

“I thought you might want me to keep it.”

“Whatever for?”

“Because you made it.”

“I also made a fish pie on Tuesday. You needn’t preserve that.”

I sat down on the stairs.

“Was it your hands?”

“What?”

“Why you stopped.”

“Oh, darling, no. The pattern was horrible. Those enormous shoulders. You’d have looked like a municipal building.”

For years I had imagined her setting down the needles in pain, reluctantly conceding something to age.

Outside her kitchen window, somebody called her name.

“Must go,” she said. “We’re going dancing.”

***

The closure notice arrived in November, folded into thirds.

The council owned the station. The roof leaked, the heating system was failing, and fewer than eight hundred people had visited the museum that year. Of these, Mrs. Vale admitted, several hundred might have been schoolchildren counted enthusiastically.

We had until the end of March to present a viable plan or vacate the premises.

I read the letter twice.

“They can’t just close it.”

“They can,” Mrs. Vale said. “It belongs to them.”

“But these things matter.”

“Yes. So does the roof.”

I wanted an adversary with polished shoes and no imagination. Instead, the council sent a woman called Denise, who arrived on a bicycle and kept her coat on throughout the meeting.

She inspected the damp patch above the quilt.

“My son made a castle out of cereal boxes,” she said. “It lived in our hall for three years. Eventually it had to go.”

“This isn’t a cereal-box castle,” I said.

“No,” she replied. “It’s a building with asbestos in the boiler room.”

After she left, I complained that she hadn’t understood us.

Mrs. Vale was putting a saucepan beneath a fresh leak.

“I think she understood us perfectly.”

That was worse.

I spent the afternoon drafting a statement about cultural memory. It contained the words *irreplaceable*, *community*, and *legacy* several times.

Mrs. Vale read it without expression.

“Will it bring in money?”

“Probably not.”

“Will it stop rain?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps begin again.”

I disliked her intensely until about half past five.

***

My first idea was a sponsored finishing marathon.

Local craftspeople would complete selected objects while visitors watched. We would auction the results, attract newspaper coverage, and prove that the collection possessed practical value.

Mrs. Vale asked who would choose what should be finished.

“We would.”

“Why?”

“Because we’re the museum.”

She waited.

I heard myself.

The second idea was worse: visitors could pay to have their abandoned ambitions ceremonially absolved. I had even written a slogan before realizing we would essentially be selling expensive permission slips.

For three days I sulked behind the ticket window.

Then the man who visited the fox approached my desk.

“Are you closing?”

“Possibly.”

“What happens to everything?”

“We don’t know.”

He looked toward the carving.

“My brother had one like that.”

“A fox?”

“A knife.”

He showed me with his hands: the length of the blade, the shape of the handle.

“We used to carve things behind the garage. Mostly terrible things.”

“Does your brother still carve?”

“He lives in Perth. I should ask.”

That evening I called a meeting of the volunteers. Seven people came, bringing nine packets of biscuits. I abandoned my prepared speech.

“What would you miss?” I asked.

“The people,” said Arthur, who polished the display cases.

“The quiet,” said Leila, who ran school visits.

“The excuse to leave the house,” said someone else.

Mrs. Vale said nothing.

Finally, I asked her.

She glanced around the room.

“I’d miss having somewhere to put things while I decide.”

I wrote that down too.

***

We held our first sorting day in January.

Not a finishing marathon. Not an auction. We invited donors, relatives, craftspeople, librarians, and anyone who had ever wondered what became of something they gave away.

The invitation said: **Help us decide what happens next.**

I expected twenty people. Sixty-three arrived.

The retired dentist reclaimed his ship. He had acquired a grandson who enjoyed wrecks.

The driving instructor took the plaster cake for her new office.

“It’ll make people ask questions,” she said.

A woman identified the mysterious brass instrument as part of a milking machine.

There was disappointment, followed by considerable relief.

The letters proved more difficult.

Some donors wanted theirs returned unopened. Others authorized us to destroy them. One man stood beside the shredder while I fed in eleven pages addressed to his former business partner.

“Do you want to say anything?” I asked.

“No,” he said. “That was the problem originally.”

We shredded them.

By lunchtime, I understood that I had been treating every object as a promise whose maker had failed to keep it.

But here were people recovering materials, correcting records, changing their minds.

The woman who had donated the quilt squares inspected them with a frown.

“These are good,” she said.

“They’re beautiful.”

“I know. I’d forgotten.”

She took twelve home and gave five to the school.

At four, the fox visitor returned with a photograph of his brother, aged twelve, holding something that might have been a wooden submarine.

“He says hello,” the man told me.

***

Not everyone approved.

A columnist accused us of dismantling the town’s heritage under the guise of public participation. A woman called to say museums were supposed to preserve things, not invite people to take them home.

She had a point.

We had already declined to destroy the notebooks of a local botanist, despite his nephew’s request. The incomplete observations contained the earliest recorded appearance of a marsh orchid in the county.

The nephew said his uncle would have preferred a clean desk.

The county ecologist said otherwise.

For a week, the notebooks sat between two chairs in my office while I tried to find a policy that could settle the matter. There wasn’t one. We arranged a meeting.

Mrs. Vale seemed almost cheerful.

“Now you’re doing museum work.”

“I thought I was doing that before.”

“Before, you were dusting.”

At the meeting, the nephew admitted that he had never read the notebooks. The ecologist admitted that she wanted them mainly for six pages. We agreed to digitize those pages, offer the originals to the county archive, and return the family photographs tucked into the covers.

Nobody got everything they wanted.

Afterward, Denise visited again. I showed her the lists: objects returned, transferred, retained, destroyed. She spent a long time reading the notes.

“How much space would you need,” she asked, “if you stopped trying to keep everything?”

I looked around my office. For the first time, it seemed possible to answer with a number.

I found a ruler in the desk.

***

The library had a room behind its local history shelves.

It was smaller than our parcel office, with fluorescent lights and a view of the supermarket loading bay. There was no ancient clock, no ticket window, no beautiful echo when rain struck the station roof.

It was dry.

Denise offered us the room for a year, provided we found volunteers and accepted a strict limit on storage.

Mrs. Vale measured it herself.

“We’ll fit,” she said.

“The collection won’t.”

“No.”

I waited for her to explain how this was secretly good.

She didn’t.

We spent February making choices. Some were easy. Others felt like betrayals, particularly when nobody wanted an object whose label I knew by heart.

A half-built dollhouse went to the recycling centre after three charities declined it. Its wallpaper had been cut from real wallpaper samples. Inside a tiny kitchen cupboard, I found a pencilled shopping list.

Milk. Bread. Apples.

I kept the cupboard longer than I should have, then asked a volunteer to drive me to the tip.

That night I took my mother’s cardigan out of its bag.

The wool was softer than I remembered.

I could finish it badly, pay someone to finish it well, or continue storing it until another person inherited the decision.

Instead, I rang my mother.

“Would you mind if I unravelled it?”

“Not at all. Save the buttons.”

“There aren’t any buttons.”

“Well, that shows how much I remember.”

We talked while I worked. Her evening class had started ballroom.

***

Unravelling required more patience than I expected.

The wool caught at seams and broke where moths had found it. Some sections came apart with a steady pull; others resisted until I laid them flat beneath a lamp and examined each knot.

My mother told me about her dance partner, a widower who counted aloud and apologized to furniture after bumping into it.

I told her about the museum.

“Are you disappointed?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Will you keep the job?”

“Some of it. Fewer hours.”

“Can you manage?”

“I think so.”

She did not tell me that everything happened for a reason. This was one of her better qualities.

By midnight, I had six uneven balls of wool and a small heap of unusable scraps.

I donated four balls to the library’s knitting group. I kept two, without a plan for them.

On the station’s last open day, we served tea in paper cups. People walked through the remaining exhibits, noticing spaces where familiar objects had stood.

The fox was still there.

Its Thursday visitor had declined to take it.

“I liked coming to see it,” he explained. “Having it on my mantelpiece wouldn’t be the same.”

We had agreed to bring it to the library.

Near closing time, Mrs. Vale stood beneath the broken clock.

“Will you miss this place?” I asked.

“Very much.”

She reached into her bag and produced a screwdriver.

“What are you doing?”

“Taking out the battery.”

“You said it was broken.”

“It is. Still no reason.”

***

We opened the new room on a Tuesday.

The library gave us a cabinet, two tables, and a noticeboard. Our name occupied a modest sign beside the door: **The Unfinished Room**.

Mrs. Vale insisted we were no longer large enough to call ourselves a museum.

Arthur insisted that size had nothing to do with it.

Their argument continued through lunch, which made the place feel settled.

We kept the fox, the six-fingered glove, the botanist’s digitized pages, and a changing selection of objects borrowed rather than acquired. There was a shelf for materials people could take, and a monthly afternoon when volunteers helped mend things.

Not everything was eligible. We learned to say no.

A boy brought in a cardboard bridge he had abandoned because his guinea pig refused to cross it.

“Do you want to finish it?” I asked.

“No. He can just walk around.”

“What would you like us to do?”

He considered this.

“Have you got any scissors?”

We cut the bridge into pieces suitable for making a tunnel.

Across the room, the fox visitor was telling Arthur about his brother’s garden in Perth. Mrs. Vale sorted buttons into an old biscuit tin. Outside, a delivery driver reversed toward the supermarket, his warning signal audible through the closed window.

At five, I entered the day’s donations in our new register.

Under the bridge, I wrote: *Returned to owner, altered.*

Then I put away the pencil, checked that the windows were shut, and went home before it got dark.

# The Office of Unclaimed Afternoons

The office occupied the narrow space between a locksmith and a shop that sold expensive lamps. People looking for either business sometimes opened our door by mistake. They would glance at the green carpet, the numbered counter, the clock with its hands removed, and apologize. Occasionally someone stayed. There are rooms that make you remember why you left the house, and rooms that make you realize you have forgotten something more important. Ours was the second kind. Above the counter, in letters individually cut from brass, a sign read: LOST TIME IS NOT NECESSARILY WASTED TIME.

I had worked there for eleven years when the woman with the yellow gloves arrived. It was February, raining with the halfhearted persistence of a task nobody wanted. She closed her umbrella carefully, wrapped its strap around it twice, and stood beneath the sign. Most visitors asked whether we were a joke, a government department, or some kind of church. She asked whether we kept Thursdays. I said we kept whatever came in. “Then I’m looking for a Thursday,” she said. “Late summer. There would have been a small boy.”

We were not permitted to promise anything. This was the first rule in the employee handbook, followed by regulations concerning fire exits and the storage of eclipses. I gave her a claim form. Name, approximate date, duration, distinguishing features. Under circumstances of loss, she wrote, *I thought there would be more.* I had seen this answer before. Usually it referred to childhood holidays, evenings with aging parents, the months after someone moved into a first apartment. Once it had referred to a bus journey during which two strangers almost spoke. I did not ask her to elaborate.

Her name was Mara Venn. The Thursday had taken place nineteen years earlier, give or take two summers. Her son would have been six. Possibly seven. They had gone somewhere with water, but not the sea. She remembered buying him an ice cream and being annoyed when he dropped it. “Was he upset?” I asked. “I don’t know.” She pulled at the fingers of one glove. “That’s part of the trouble.” Beyond the partition, a drawer slid open by itself. This happened when someone described a missing afternoon accurately enough. We both turned toward the sound.

The public imagined our storage rooms as something grand: endless shelves vanishing into darkness, glass vessels filled with golden weather. In fact, the main archive resembled the basement of an underfunded library. There were gray cabinets, handwritten labels, and a kettle that needed descaling. The mornings were filed eastward, the evenings westward. Lunch hours had their own annex because they were disproportionately lost and seldom claimed. Whole years were kept downstairs, although I had never been authorized to handle one. My supervisor said they were structurally unstable. “You open 1987 carelessly,” she told me, “and suddenly everyone has opinions about wallpaper.”

Her name was Mrs. Vale, and she had worked there since before the installation of the carpet. She possessed the formidable calm of someone who had watched generations invent new ways to be late. She was also the only person I knew who could identify a decade by listening to its rain. When I brought her Mara’s form, she put down her sandwich. “Water, dropped ice cream, yellow light,” she said. “Have you checked municipal parks?” I had not mentioned yellow light. She read my expression and shrugged. “August Thursdays usually have it. Unless they’re indoors. Then they have dust.”

We began with reservoirs, paddling pools, ornamental lakes. The archive did not organize time by date alone. Dates were useful, but less reliable than certain smells. Freshly cut grass could take you directly to a week that a calendar would never find. We searched under sunscreen, warm railings, duckweed, the rubber lining of a child’s sandal. At three o’clock we found a promising afternoon in a box labeled MINOR DISAPPOINTMENTS, OUTDOORS. It was wrapped in tissue paper and gave off the faint sound of a lawn mower. Mrs. Vale held it close to her ear. “No,” she said. “Golf.”

Mara returned the following day. People often did, though we specifically told them we would telephone. She sat in the waiting area with her gloves folded on her lap and watched the door. After an hour I brought her tea. She thanked me, then asked if anyone ever found what they were looking for. “Sometimes.” “And does it help?” That was not a question covered by the handbook. I said it depended on what they expected. She turned the cup in its saucer. “I don’t expect to change anything.” Then, after a moment: “At least, I know I must say that.”

Her son was alive. I learned this because she told me, quickly, as though correcting a diagnosis. He lived in another country and designed ventilation systems for large buildings. They spoke on the first Sunday of each month. He was kind, she said. Busy, but kind. There had been no quarrel, no slammed door, no scene she could point to as the beginning of their distance. He had simply grown into a life in which she appeared occasionally. “I can remember his birthdays,” she said. “School plays. The holiday when he broke his wrist. But I want an ordinary day.”

I understood this better than I admitted. The archive contained many ordinary days, and on quiet shifts I sometimes handled them longer than necessary. A November morning spent choosing buttons. Twenty minutes listening to a neighbor practice the clarinet badly. An evening during which a man repaired a drawer while his wife read aloud from a magazine about whales. Nothing happened in these intervals that anyone would have thought to photograph. Their owners had often retained the argument before them or the bad news afterward. We kept what lay between, carefully separated by sheets of acid-free paper.

My own missing time was a Tuesday. I had never filled out a form. Employees were allowed to make claims, but Mrs. Vale discouraged it during working hours, and outside working hours I had other excuses. The Tuesday involved my mother, a pot of soup, and a telephone I would not stop checking. She was telling me something about the house she had lived in as a girl. I remembered a staircase. Or perhaps she had been describing a tree. Six months later she died, and the story lost its only reliable address. Since then, every staircase had looked faintly accusatory.

On Mara’s third visit, the drawer opened again. This time I was standing close enough to read its label: MOMENTS MISIDENTIFIED AS INTERRUPTIONS. It was not a large drawer, but it was very deep. Inside were parcels bound with cotton tape. A child asking to be watched. A friend calling during a deadline. Someone stopping in a doorway to say, “You’ll never guess.” I lifted out a thin packet that smelled of river mud and vanilla. From somewhere inside it came a boy’s voice, fierce with discovery: “No, look. Properly.” Mara stood so suddenly that her chair struck the wall.

We took her to the viewing room. It held two chairs, a small table, and a window looking onto whatever weather the recovered time required. I explained the conditions. She could enter once. She could remain until the afternoon ended. She could not alter an event, introduce information, or take any object away. “Will he see me?” she asked. “He’ll see who you were.” “And will I be who I was?” “Mostly.” This was the least satisfactory answer we gave, and the most accurate. People entered lost time carrying everything that had happened since. The door was wide enough for that.

Before I opened the packet, Mrs. Vale called me into the corridor. “There’s a complication.” She held the form beneath the light. Along its lower edge, words had appeared in the paper’s fibers: SECOND PARTY INTEREST. Mara’s son had a claim on the same afternoon. He had not submitted it here, necessarily. Other offices operated in other cities, and some requests reached us without paperwork. “What does he want?” I asked. Mrs. Vale read further. “The moment his mother laughed.” We stood quietly. From the viewing room came the scrape of Mara moving her chair closer to the unopened window.

Shared claims required a slightly different procedure. We could not release the afternoon unless both versions remained intact. Memory was not a recording that two people could borrow in turn. One person’s recollection could crowd out another’s, especially when it arrived armed with certainty. Mrs. Vale brought a second packet from a cabinet I had thought was locked. This one smelled of hot pavement. The same Thursday, differently kept. Through the wrapping I heard a woman laugh, then a splash. “Will they be there together?” I asked. “They were there together,” she said. “That’s what makes this difficult.”

We explained the complication to Mara. At first she looked frightened, then embarrassed. “He remembers it?” “Some of it.” “Did he say I was angry?” We told her that claims were confidential. She nodded, but her hands worked against each other. For nineteen years she had been carrying an afternoon in which she was impatient, distracted, ungenerous. Somewhere else, her son had been carrying one in which she laughed. Neither account canceled the other. I could see that she wanted his recollection to acquit her. I could also see her beginning to understand that it had not been made for that purpose.

She asked for a few minutes alone. Mrs. Vale returned to her lunch, now technically an early supper. I went to the staff kitchen and stood beside the kettle. Above it, someone had pinned a notice reminding us not to use the good teaspoons for measuring historical snowfall. I thought about my mother’s soup. I remembered deciding that the next message on my phone would be the last one I answered. Then another had arrived. There had been bread on the table, still in its paper bag. For years I had remembered the phone more clearly than anything she said.

When Mara called us back, she had removed her gloves. “I’d like to go,” she said. “Even if I was awful.” Mrs. Vale placed the two packets side by side and untied them. The window filled with light. A narrow river appeared beyond it, brown and slow, with willows along the opposite bank. There was a bench, a litter bin painted dark green, a path shimmering in the heat. The smell of rain vanished. Mara took one step forward, then stopped. “How long will I be gone?” “Until closing,” Mrs. Vale said. “For us.”

While she was inside, I dealt with a man who had lost forty minutes in a supermarket and wanted them refunded. He had spent most of them comparing breakfast cereals. I explained that indecision was not, by itself, grounds for reimbursement. He asked to speak to my supervisor. Mrs. Vale listened patiently and offered him a leaflet on prospective attention. After he left, she sat at my counter. “You’ve never claimed anything,” she said. I pretended to check the appointments book. She waited. One advantage of working where we did was that waiting rarely seemed like the worst use of time.

I told her about Tuesday. Not everything; just the kitchen, the phone, the story. She asked whether I wanted a form. I said I was afraid of discovering that the story had been unimportant. Mrs. Vale rubbed a mark from the counter with her thumb. “It may have been.” Outside, the lamp shop began switching on its displays. “Your mother might have forgotten it herself by Wednesday.” I laughed, though I had not expected to. Mrs. Vale rose carefully, favoring one knee. “You don’t have to decide tonight,” she said. Then she brought me a form and left it facedown.

Mara returned at six minutes past five. There was mud on one shoe, which faded while we watched. She looked tired and slightly sunburned. For a while she said nothing. Then she asked for water. We waited as she drank it. “He dropped the ice cream because he was showing me something,” she said. “A beetle on the railing. I didn’t look. I was counting coins.” She set down the glass. “Later he took off his shoes and went into the river. I told him he’d cut his feet. Then I went in after him.”

The riverbed had been slippery. She fell, not dangerously, but completely, with the sort of undignified commitment that children admire. Her son laughed. She laughed too. They walked to the bus stop with her skirt dripping and his sandals tied together over her shoulder. “I remembered the ice cream,” she said. “All this time.” I asked about the beetle. “Green. Very shiny. He said it looked expensive.” She smiled, and for a moment I could see the wet young woman by the river without opening either packet. Then she put on her coat and asked whether the afternoon would remain in storage.

“We keep the original,” I said. “You’ll remember what you saw, though not perfectly.” She seemed relieved. At the door she paused. “I suppose I should telephone him.” I offered our telephone, but she shook her head. “It’s the middle of his working day. I’ll ask when he’s free.” She wrapped her umbrella strap twice around the folded cloth. Before leaving, she looked back at the window, which had returned to its usual view of a brick wall. “There was a bus driver,” she said. “He wouldn’t let me sit down. I’d forgotten him too.”

Afterward I completed my form. Under distinguishing features, I wrote: *Soup. Bread in a paper bag. A story that may involve stairs.* I left circumstances of loss blank for a long time. Then I wrote, *I was answering messages*, because that was what I had done. Mrs. Vale accepted it without comment. As she filed it, a drawer opened somewhere downstairs. She listened, her head tilted. “Not yours,” she said. “A honeymoon. We get a surprising number.” She locked the cabinets while I rinsed our cups. Mine had left a brown ring on Mara’s claim.

I had soup for dinner that night. It was not my mother’s recipe; I had never asked for it. I ate at the kitchen table with my phone in the bedroom, where I could still hear it vibrate once against the chest of drawers. Outside, somebody was teaching a child to ride a bicycle. Their instructions rose through the open window: pedal, keep going, look ahead. I carried my bowl to the sink, then went to watch. The child traveled four wobbling yards before putting a foot down. They wheeled the bicycle back and tried again.
