# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum stood between a locksmith and a shop that sold only blue objects. Nobody could remember what had occupied the building before it became a museum, although the locksmith insisted it had once been a narrower building. From the street, it appeared to have three floors. From the staircase, it had seven, provided you did not count the landing where it was always raining.

Admission was free. The opening hours were written on a brass plate:

**TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY  
WHENEVER YOU ARE READY**

On Mondays, the museum was closed for dusting and regret.

Mara had worked there for twenty-three years. Her official title was Keeper of Incomplete Acquisitions, though she was also the ticket attendant, archivist, electrician, and person responsible for explaining why visitors could not finish the crossword in Gallery Four.

“But I know seventeen across,” they would say.

“That isn’t the point,” Mara would reply.

Occasionally, someone would fill it in when her back was turned. By morning, the letters were gone. The pencil, however, would have become slightly shorter.

This was one of the museum’s gentler defenses.

***

The collection had begun with a sweater.

It was green, or had intended to be green before its maker changed yarn halfway through the chest. One sleeve was complete. The other ended just below the shoulder in a fringe of loose wool. It arrived folded in a paper bag, accompanied by a note:

*My mother was making this for my father. Then she decided to leave him. Neither event explains the other as much as you might think.*

There was no signature.

Mara displayed the sweater on a wooden chair rather than a mannequin. She thought it looked less accused that way.

Other things followed.

A chess game abandoned in 1964, with black in an apparently winning position. A doctoral thesis on the sleeping habits of bees. The foundations of a house, somehow delivered in a shoebox. Three bars of a melody that made everyone who heard it turn toward the nearest window.

There were unfinished meals, unfinished migrations, and one unfinished Tuesday.

The Tuesday required refrigeration.

Mara liked practical objects best. A chair without a seat made no attempt to disguise its situation. A half-carved spoon was pleasantly specific about what had happened to it. Letters were more difficult. They often believed they were finished, especially the cruel ones.

The museum had a room full of letters that ended, *And another thing—*

Visitors rarely stayed there long.

***

Every acquisition received a label.

**OBJECT 114: WOODEN BOAT**  
**Maker unknown**  
**Abandoned before the mast was fitted**

At first, Mara had written longer descriptions. She had speculated about interruption, poverty, illness, distraction. She had used phrases such as *the pressures of ordinary life* and *a testament to thwarted ambition.*

Then a carpenter visited the museum and studied a cabinet whose drawers had never been installed.

“Could just be he got sick of cabinets,” the carpenter said.

After that, Mara restricted herself to facts.

Even facts could be troublesome. The boat, for example, had been donated by a woman who said her husband died before he could finish it. Six months later, the husband appeared, very much alive, and asked for it back.

“She tells people that when she’s angry,” he explained.

Mara returned the boat. Two weeks afterward, it arrived again, now with a mast but no sail.

This time the note said:

*He has taken up pottery.*

***

The boy came on a wet Thursday in November.

He was perhaps twelve, with a serious face and a schoolbag that appeared to contain bricks. He stood just inside the entrance until Mara looked up from repairing a label.

“Is this where you keep things people didn’t finish?”

“Some of them.”

“Who decides which ones?”

“Usually the stairs.”

He considered this without smiling.

“I’ve brought something.”

He took a small black recorder from his bag and placed it on the desk. It was the sort journalists once carried, with physical buttons and a wrist strap. A strip of masking tape on the back read **DAD**.

Mara did not touch it.

“Would you like to tell me about it?”

“My father used to record things. Birds. Trains. Our refrigerator when it was making a noise. He said machines were easier to understand if you listened before you opened them.”

The boy pressed play.

There was a click, a breath, and the distant scrape of a chair.

Then a man’s voice said, “Eli, there’s something I should have told you before—”

The recording stopped.

Outside, a bus sighed at the curb.

“Is there more on the tape?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Do you know what interrupted him?”

“He turned it off.”

***

Mara had learned not to ask certain questions too quickly.

She offered the boy a chair. He remained standing.

“He died in February,” he said. “Not while recording it. Later.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Everyone is.”

He looked around the entrance hall, where an unfinished portrait seemed to be listening with its one completed ear.

“Can you find out the rest?”

“No,” Mara said.

The speed of her answer surprised him.

“You haven’t tried.”

“I know what the museum can do.”

“What can it do?”

“Keep it safe. Give you somewhere to leave it.”

“I have a drawer.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “You do.”

The boy put the recorder back in his bag.

She expected him to leave, but he looked at the staircase.

“What’s upstairs?”

“Things people thought they would come back to.”

“Did they?”

“Some.”

He shifted the bag onto both shoulders.

“I’ll look.”

***

He returned the next Thursday, and the Thursday after that.

His name was Eli. He disliked being asked how school was. He liked the refrigerated Tuesday, particularly the sandwich suspended halfway between a plate and an absent mouth. He spent a long time with a model railway whose tracks stopped at the edge of a meticulously painted village.

“Why didn’t they make the rest?”

“Space, perhaps.”

“They could have made a smaller village.”

“Perhaps they liked the village.”

He bent until his face was level with the tiny station.

“There’s nobody waiting.”

“No.”

“That’s good.”

By December, Mara had begun keeping biscuits in the desk. She pretended they were for everyone, although the museum’s other regular visitor, a retired surveyor, could not eat wheat.

Eli noticed.

“You could buy him something else.”

So she did.

The surveyor accepted his almond biscuit with solemn gratitude and then asked, for the ninth time, whether the unfinished map on the top floor represented an actual place.

Mara gave her usual answer.

“Not yet.”

***

The map was hers.

She had drawn it at nineteen, when she and her sister planned to cross the country on bicycles. It showed back roads, cheap campsites, public fountains, and a town where someone reportedly sold the best peaches in the world.

Their route ended at the sea.

Three weeks before departure, their father fell down the cellar stairs and broke his hip. Their mother had been dead for years. Mara stayed to help. Her sister, Lena, went alone.

That was the simple account.

The less simple account contained a quarrel beside a kitchen sink, six months of unanswered letters, a postcard Mara tore in half, and a sentence spoken with such precision that she could still remember the shape of her sister’s mouth afterward.

She had brought the map to the museum during her first week of employment.

The previous keeper hung it without asking questions.

Mara had been grateful to him.

She had never considered whether gratitude was the right response.

***

One afternoon, Eli found her on the top floor replacing a lightbulb.

“Did you make that?”

He pointed to the map.

“Yes.”

“Why did you stop?”

“Family trouble.”

“Did the trouble stop?”

Mara tightened the bulb a little too firmly.

“Eventually.”

“Then why didn’t you go?”

She climbed down from the stepladder.

“By then, other things had happened.”

“What things?”

“A job. Responsibilities.”

He waited.

“I got older,” she said.

“My teacher cycled to France. She’s sixty.”

“Your teacher sounds energetic.”

Eli examined the map again.

“You drew a ferry.”

“Yes.”

“There isn’t any sea.”

“I hadn’t got that far.”

He traced the route without touching the paper.

“So you finished the journey before you finished the map.”

Mara opened her mouth, then closed it.

The bulb above them gave a small, satisfied click.

***

In January, the museum began misbehaving.

This was distinct from its normal behavior.

The incomplete Tuesday developed a Wednesday along one edge. The green sweater grew three stitches overnight. In Gallery Four, seventeen across filled itself in.

The answer was **MERCY**.

Mara checked the security cameras. They showed nothing except the retired surveyor standing very still before the map, eating an almond biscuit from his coat pocket.

Then the wooden boat returned.

It appeared on the entrance desk on a Monday morning, though the doors had been locked. There was still no sail. Instead, its maker had fitted a small electric motor.

Attached was a note:

*Apparently this counts.*

Mara was still reading it when someone knocked.

A woman stood outside carrying a canvas toolbox.

“Building inspection,” she said.

“We had one last spring.”

“You had a fire inspection. I’m here about the other problem.”

“What other problem?”

The woman looked up.

A fourth-floor window had appeared above the third.

“Your premises are becoming definite.”

***

The inspector’s name was Mrs. Vale. She wore muddy boots and carried a measuring tape that occasionally measured things before she asked it to.

She examined the sweater, the crossword, and the refrigerated Tuesday.

Then she sat at Mara’s desk.

“How many objects have been reclaimed in the past year?”

“Seven.”

“How many acquired?”

“Four hundred and twelve.”

Mrs. Vale wrote something down.

“Do you conduct reviews?”

“Of what?”

“The objects. Their circumstances. Whether they still belong here.”

“They’re unfinished.”

“Yes. When did you last check?”

Mara looked toward the galleries.

Mrs. Vale set down her pen.

“A place like this can hold things while people decide what to do with them. It can hold them for a very long time. But you have several thousand objects here, and hardly anyone seems to know they’re allowed to take them home.”

“It says so on the donation form.”

“Where?”

Mara fetched a form.

The sentence was on the reverse, beneath the insurance exclusions.

***

That evening, Mara stayed late.

She opened the acquisition ledger and began reading.

The thesis on bees belonged to a woman who had become a successful baker. The abandoned chess game had been interrupted by the players deciding to marry. The half-carved spoon was one of eighty-seven attempts made by an apprentice who had subsequently become a master.

Mara had all this information. She had recorded it herself.

Yet the labels said only *unfinished.*

She went upstairs to the map.

The route remained exactly as she had drawn it: hopeful, economical, avoiding steep hills.

In the margin, Lena had sketched a fish wearing a crown.

Mara had forgotten that.

She stood there until the automatic lights went out, then waved one hand to bring them back.

***

Eli arrived the next day to find the entrance hall crowded with empty boxes.

“Are you closing?”

“I’m reviewing the collection.”

“Did someone complain?”

“Yes.”

“Who?”

“The building, apparently.”

He helped her sort correspondence. Together they wrote to makers, donors, descendants. Some addresses no longer existed. Some names had changed. One letter came back with the handwritten explanation, *Gone sailing. Try in June.*

A woman collected an unfinished wedding dress.

“Are you going to finish it?” Eli asked.

“No. I want the silk.”

A man reclaimed a half-written novel and read the first page while standing at the desk.

“Oh, good lord,” he said.

“Would you like some privacy?” Mara asked.

“I’d like a recycling bin.”

She showed him where it was.

For the first time in years, the museum’s windows opened.

***

Eli brought the recorder again in March.

By then, the refrigerated Tuesday had thawed into an ordinary afternoon. Mara had eaten the sandwich. It had been cheese and pickle, and she considered it one of the collection’s more successful departures.

The boy placed the recorder on the desk.

“I asked my mother.”

“About the message?”

He nodded.

“She didn’t know. She got upset because I thought she did.”

Mara waited.

“He forgot my birthday once. Not the whole day. Just in the morning. He went to work without saying anything, then came back with a cake from a petrol station.”

Eli turned the recorder over.

“Maybe he was going to tell me something important. Maybe he was going to tell me where he’d put something.”

“Yes.”

“I hate that.”

“I know.”

He pressed play.

*Eli, there’s something I should have told you before—*

This time, after it stopped, he did not immediately rewind it.

Instead, he opened a side pocket of his bag and took out a second tape.

“This one’s the refrigerator.”

***

Mara telephoned her sister on a Sunday.

She had found the number through a cousin, which required a conversation she had been avoiding for almost as long as the call itself.

Lena answered on the fifth ring.

“Hello?”

Mara had prepared several openings. All of them now sounded like museum labels.

“It’s me,” she said.

“I know.”

In the background, someone was chopping vegetables.

For a moment, neither sister spoke.

Then Mara said, “Do you remember the fish you drew on our map?”

“The king of the herrings.”

“Was that what it was?”

“Obviously.”

Mara laughed. The sound startled her.

“I still have it.”

“The fish?”

“The map.”

The chopping stopped.

“Oh,” Lena said.

“I’m sorry,” Mara said.

There was a long pause.

“About which part?”

It was a fair question. Mara sat down.

They spoke for forty minutes. Some of it went badly.

Before hanging up, Lena gave Mara her address.

***

By summer, the museum had become smaller.

The rainy landing disappeared, leaving behind a damp umbrella nobody recognized. Gallery Six became a cupboard. Gallery Seven returned a pair of spectacles Mara had lost eleven years earlier and then ceased to exist.

There were still plenty of exhibits.

Some things needed keeping.

The three bars of music remained, as did the house foundations and several letters whose owners were not ready to touch them. Mara changed the labels where she could.

**Set aside.**

**No longer needed.**

**Awaiting a decision.**

The crossword stayed unfinished. Visitors still complained.

Eli came less often once school ended. On his last visit before a holiday, he brought Mara a recording of the museum: footsteps, the clock, a drawer sticking, rain against the front window.

Near the end, Mara could hear herself asking whether he wanted a biscuit.

Then came his answer, perfectly clear.

She kept the tape in her desk.

On Sunday evening, she took down the map. Her train ticket was tucked into its fold, beside the crowned fish.

At the door, she paused to straighten the opening-hours plaque.

The locksmith was closing up next door.

“Off somewhere?”

“To see my sister.”

“Far?”

“A fair way.”

He offered to check the building while she was gone.

“Just the windows,” Mara said.

“What about the rest?”

She looked back at the museum. Upstairs, a light went out.

“The rest can wait.”

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

On the morning the museum received its first cloud, Mara was trying to repair the kettle.

The cloud arrived in a wooden crate marked THIS SIDE UP, although the delivery driver admitted that nobody at the depot had agreed which side that meant. He had brought it on a handcart, beneath a tarpaulin, and now stood in the museum doorway with his cap dripping rain onto the tiles.

“Signature,” he said.

“What is it?”

“According to the form, an atmospheric remainder.”

Mara looked past him at the weather. The street was full of atmospheric remainders. They ran down the windows and collected in the pothole outside the pharmacy.

“We didn’t order one.”

“Nobody orders anything anymore. They just inherit it.”

He held out the clipboard.

The museum occupied a former railway station at the edge of a town that no longer had trains. Its official name was the Municipal Repository of Incomplete Endeavors, but somebody had stolen enough brass letters from the sign to leave MUNICIPAL POSITORY, and the council had declined to fund replacements.

Inside were forty-three unfinished paintings, a bridge that had never reached its opposite bank, nine doctoral theses, a knitted sleeve, the blueprints for a machine intended to translate birdsong, and a wedding cake preserved beneath glass.

The wedding had happened. The marriage, according to the donor, had not.

Mara signed for the cloud.

***

Her predecessor had left three instructions in a notebook.

First: Do not finish anything.

Second: Keep accurate records.

Third: The north window sticks in damp weather. Lift before pushing.

Mara considered the third instruction the most useful.

She had taken the job because it included a small apartment upstairs and because, after eleven years of restoring furniture, she had developed a pain in her right wrist that made precise work difficult. The museum required very little precision. Mostly it required dusting around people’s intentions.

Visitors were rare. Schoolchildren came in November, when their teachers had exhausted the town’s other educational attractions. Occasionally someone arrived with a parcel and the expression of a person bringing an animal to the vet.

“Would you take this?” they asked.

Mara always asked what it was meant to become.

A symphony. A business. A better kind of umbrella.

Sometimes they knew everything about the intended result. Sometimes they had forgotten.

The museum did not accept ordinary broken things. A broken chair had once succeeded in being a chair. An unfinished chair remained in negotiation with the idea.

Mara liked the distinction, though she understood why the council struggled to put it on a tourism leaflet.

She set the kettle aside and opened the crate.

Inside, suspended above a shallow copper tray, was a cloud approximately the size of a sleeping sheep. It smelled faintly of hot pavement.

A folded note lay beneath it.

*This was supposed to be rain.*

***

The note was unsigned.

Mara searched the packing straw and found an address in a village thirty miles north, a railway ticket dated seventeen years earlier, and a photograph of a woman standing beside an orchard.

The woman held a hose. Behind her, the trees were white with blossom.

Mara entered the acquisition in the ledger.

**Object 718: Cloud. Intended function: precipitation. Reason for incompletion: unknown.**

She hesitated over the condition report, then wrote:

**Restless.**

Throughout the afternoon, the cloud shifted inside its crate. It flattened when buses passed. It rose into a narrow tower when someone rang the museum bell. Once, while Mara was eating a sandwich, it produced a small internal flash.

“Absolutely not,” she told it.

The flash did not recur.

At four o’clock, a boy named Ivo came in carrying a violin case. He was twelve and visited every Thursday while his grandmother attended an appointment across the square.

He had been bringing the violin for six months. Mara had never heard him play it.

“What’s that?”

“A cloud.”

“I know. Why’s it indoors?”

“It hasn’t finished being something.”

Ivo considered this explanation with the courtesy children sometimes extend to adults who appear to be doing their best.

“Maybe it’s finished being a cloud.”

“Apparently it was supposed to rain.”

“That’s what people always say about clouds.”

He put the violin case behind the desk and went to look at the bridge.

***

The bridge occupied the old waiting room.

It had been built at one-twentieth scale by an engineer who spent thirty-two years proposing a pedestrian crossing over the river. There were drawings, surveys, traffic assessments, revised surveys, and a correspondence with the council so extensive that it required its own cabinet.

The engineer died before construction began.

Two years later, the council installed stepping-stones.

Ivo liked to lie on the floor and look through the model’s arches. Mara suspected he was imagining water where the carpet lay.

“Have you ever finished anything?” he asked that afternoon.

“Lots of things.”

“What?”

“Tables. Cabinets. A very ugly chest of drawers.”

“Did finishing make it less ugly?”

“No. But it made the ugliness more permanent.”

He nodded.

From the entrance hall came a soft pattering sound.

They hurried back.

The copper tray was dry, but the cloud had shed a handful of tiny white pellets. Mara picked one up. It melted against her palm.

“Hail,” she said.

“Close enough.”

“Not according to the note.”

Ivo looked at her. “Who gets to decide?”

Before she could answer, his grandmother appeared at the door. She was a small woman with a magnificent purple coat.

“Come along,” she said. “The doctor has decided I should walk more.”

“Is that bad?”

“It’s inconvenient. I’ve spent seventy-eight years learning where to sit.”

After they left, Mara moved the cloud away from the wedding cake and placed a second tray beside the first.

***

The council letter arrived on Monday.

It explained, across three pages, that the museum’s operating costs were disproportionate to measurable public benefit. The building would be repurposed at the end of summer.

Mara read the phrase *repurposed* several times.

There was no mention of what would happen to the collection.

She telephoned the number at the bottom of the letter and spoke to a man who called the objects “legacy holdings.”

“Some of them are quite large,” she said.

“We anticipate a disposal process.”

“There’s a bridge.”

“Is it functional?”

“No.”

“Then that should simplify matters.”

After the call, Mara walked through the rooms.

The unfinished paintings leaned toward landscapes that would never receive their skies. A half-built mechanical fox watched from its shelf with one glass eye. In a case by the stairs lay a letter beginning, *I have tried several times to tell you*, followed by three inches of blank paper.

She had always assumed that saving these things was useful.

Now she wondered whether she had merely arranged a comfortable place for them to disappear slowly.

Upstairs, her own belongings fit into seven boxes, though she had never packed them. There were clothes, books, dishes, tools she no longer used, and a small walnut drawer she had begun making before her wrist grew bad.

It had no cabinet to belong to.

She went downstairs and placed the council letter in the ledger.

The cloud had turned the color of a bruised peach.

***

On Thursday, Ivo found her writing to the address from the crate.

“Who’s that for?”

“Whoever sent us the cloud.”

“What are you asking?”

“How to look after it.”

“Ask why they stopped.”

“Stopped what?”

“Trying to make it rain.”

Mara crossed out a sentence.

Ivo opened his violin case.

The instrument inside was ordinary except for a patch of lighter varnish near the chin rest. He lifted it carefully, tightened the bow, and stood beside the desk.

“I’m supposed to be learning a piece,” he said.

“All right.”

“It’s not ready.”

“All right.”

He played six notes. The seventh squeaked. He began again.

Mara returned to her letter, which seemed to make it easier for him. After several attempts, he reached a phrase that rose unexpectedly and then stopped.

“That’s as far as I know.”

“It’s a good place.”

“It isn’t the end.”

“I noticed.”

He lowered the violin.

“My teacher says I keep starting over because I like the beginning best.”

“Do you?”

“I like knowing what happens.”

Outside, a bus sighed at the stop where trains had once discharged passengers. The cloud stirred.

“Could I leave it here?” Ivo asked.

“The violin?”

“The piece. Until I learn the rest.”

“We don’t usually take performances.”

“You took a cloud.”

This was difficult to dispute.

Mara found a blank card and wrote:

**Object 719: A piece of music, currently arriving.**

Ivo read the label twice.

Then he asked her not to mention it to his grandmother.

***

The reply came in a green envelope.

The writer was named Ada Vale. She had once worked in agricultural engineering. During a drought, she had developed a device to gather moisture from the air and release it over small areas.

It had worked, in a limited sense.

*The difficulty was persuading the moisture to let go,* she wrote.

The orchard in the photograph belonged to her sister. By the time Ada produced the cloud, the trees had already died.

*I kept it because I thought I might still solve the problem. Then I kept it because I had kept it so long.*

There were practical instructions: avoid enclosed cupboards, loud machinery, and excessive heat.

At the bottom, Ada had added:

*It responds to music, though not predictably. Please don’t consider that an explanation.*

Mara read the letter beside the cloud.

“You’re late,” she told it.

The cloud drifted against the lip of its crate.

That evening she carried the walnut drawer downstairs. She placed it on the reception desk, opened her tool roll, and examined its joints.

Her wrist hurt before she had done anything.

She put the tools away.

Then she took them out again and sharpened a pencil.

On a sheet of paper she drew a cabinet large enough to hold the drawer. She disliked it immediately.

She drew another.

At midnight, she had six bad designs, a sore hand, and an appetite. She made toast beneath the kitchen grill, burned one corner, and ate it standing up.

***

Mara did not begin with a campaign.

She made a sign.

**THURSDAY EVENINGS: BRING SOMETHING YOU HAVE NOT FINISHED.**

Beneath that, in smaller letters:

**You may also come without it.**

The first evening, nobody arrived until seven twenty, when the woman from the pharmacy brought a jigsaw puzzle in a biscuit tin.

“There’s a piece missing,” she said.

“That might be a different category.”

“I haven’t looked under the sofa yet.”

Mara admitted her provisionally.

Next came a retired bus driver with three chapters of a detective novel. Then Ivo and his grandmother, who brought nothing and explained that she intended to finish other people’s biscuits.

They sat around the long table in the former parcel office.

Mara had expected conversation about projects. Instead they talked about heating bills, a dangerous junction, and whether the bakery had changed its flour.

The bus driver read two pages aloud.

In his novel, a woman discovered a body in a greenhouse. The pharmacist interrupted to ask why someone with a greenhouse would buy tomatoes in February.

“Because she’s about to discover a body,” he said.

“That doesn’t affect the planting schedule.”

He made a note.

Ivo played the beginning of his piece. This time he continued beyond the place where he usually stopped, moving slowly through several uncertain bars.

From the hall came a faint rumble.

Everyone listened.

“Plumbing,” Mara said.

It was easier than explaining.

By closing time, the pharmacist had assembled the border of her puzzle.

She left it on the table.

***

The evenings grew without becoming popular.

Eight people came, then fourteen, then nine. Someone repaired a radio. Someone unraveled a jumper she no longer wanted to finish. A young father spent forty minutes writing a job application while his daughter arranged wooden offcuts into a town.

Mara brought out the unfinished chair.

“Are we allowed to touch the exhibits?” the father asked.

“I’m reconsidering the policy.”

She found her predecessor’s notebook and reread the first instruction.

Do not finish anything.

Below it, in a different ink, he had written something she had overlooked:

*Unless there is a good reason.*

Mara laughed so loudly that everyone turned.

There were arguments. The bus driver disliked suggestions that his detective should have a mobile phone. A woman who brought a box of fabric objected when someone called it clutter. Two friends stopped attending after a disagreement that had nothing to do with the museum.

But things happened.

The radio spoke.

The chair acquired a seat.

The pharmacist found her missing puzzle piece inside a slipper and seemed almost disappointed.

Mara’s drawer remained on the desk. One evening, a carpenter examined her sketches.

“This one’s possible,” he said.

“It’s awkward.”

“So’s the alcove upstairs. Measure it.”

They discussed tools she could hold without hurting herself.

Meanwhile, visitors signed a petition against the closure. Mara delivered it to the council with attendance figures, photographs, and a proposed budget.

She omitted the cloud from the photographs.

Its legal status seemed uncertain.

***

Ada Vale came in August.

She arrived carrying a canvas bag and wearing shoes whitened by road dust. Mara recognized her from the photograph, though her hair had shortened and gone gray.

“I thought I ought to see where it ended up.”

The cloud was over the long table. They had finally coaxed it out of its crate by moving Ivo’s music stand a little farther away each Thursday.

Ada stood beneath it.

“Oh,” she said.

Mara left them alone and put the kettle on. A volunteer had replaced its switch in June.

That evening, Ivo played the whole piece.

He made mistakes. He frowned through a difficult passage and hurried near the end. His grandmother sat with her handbag clasped firmly on her knees.

On the final note, the cloud contracted.

A drop struck the table.

Then another.

“Paper,” Mara said, and everyone scrambled.

The detective novel was rescued. The job applications were lifted clear. Someone moved the radio. Rain fell steadily onto the empty biscuit plate.

Ivo began to laugh but kept his violin beneath his jacket.

Ada held out her hand.

For perhaps a minute, the old waiting room smelled of wet stone and leaves.

Then the cloud thinned until there was nothing left to watch.

Mara fetched towels.

Ada dried the table with the others. When they finished, she sat down heavily.

“Seventeen years,” she said.

Nobody tried to improve on that.

Later, she asked for a copy of the photograph from the acquisition file.

***

The council granted the museum another year.

It was not a victory anyone could frame. The funding was reduced, and Mara spent September learning to write grant applications.

She changed the cloud’s ledger entry from “restless” to “dispersed” and invited Ada back. Then she left the door open until closing time.

# A Place to Sit

On the morning the bench disappeared, Ada arrived seven minutes early and had nowhere to put her anger.

Usually she sat on it.

The bench stood outside the old post office, beneath a plane tree that shed bark in thin, pale plates. Its wooden slats had been painted green so many times that the paint had softened their edges. One of the iron legs resembled a lion’s paw, though the other three did not. Nobody knew whether this was intentional.

Ada had been sitting there every Tuesday for eleven years, waiting for the number sixteen bus.

Now there were four pale rectangles on the pavement.

She examined them with the attention usually reserved for footprints at a crime scene. Then she looked up and down the street, as if the bench might have wandered a short distance and become confused.

The bus arrived.

“Bench has gone,” she told the driver.

“Morning to you too.”

“Did you see who took it?”

“I’m more concerned with people taking buses.”

Ada boarded, but she did not consider the matter closed.

***

At home she telephoned the council.

The first person transferred her to Street Furniture. Street Furniture transferred her to Public Realm. Public Realm explained that seating fell under Assets, unless it was commemorative seating, in which case she wanted Parks.

“There’s no plaque,” Ada said.

“Are you certain?”

“I’ve had eleven years to read it.”

Assets asked for an asset number.

“It was a bench.”

“Yes, but which bench?”

“The one that isn’t there.”

There was a silence in which Ada could hear somebody opening a packet of crisps.

Eventually a young man named Lewis agreed to investigate. He sounded tired in a way she associated with people who had recently begun working for a living and already suspected an administrative error.

“Could you describe its condition?” he asked.

“Absent.”

“Before that.”

Ada considered.

“It wobbled if someone large sat on the left.”

Lewis typed something.

“And the surface?”

“Green.”

“Was there exposed timber?”

“It was a wooden bench. I hope so.”

He promised to call back.

Ada wrote his name on the pad beside the telephone. Underneath it she wrote BENCH, pressing hard enough to leave an impression on the next three pages.

Her daughter called that evening.

“What have you been doing?”

“Trying to find some furniture.”

“Are you finally replacing that armchair?”

“No.”

“The spring is coming through.”

“It knows where I sit.”

Her daughter lived four hours away and had developed a habit of treating everything in Ada’s house as a warning. The armchair was a warning. The stairs were a warning. A jar of marmalade with a stubborn lid was practically a medical event.

Ada did not mention the bench again.

She knew how the story would sound: an old woman becoming upset about a minor alteration to a street. She had heard such stories herself, and had not always been patient with them.

***

Lewis called on Thursday.

“The bench was removed following a condition assessment.”

“By whom?”

“A contractor.”

“What condition did they assess?”

“There was a structural concern.”

“What concern?”

“I don’t have the full report.”

“Where is it now?”

“The report?”

“The bench, Lewis.”

He said he would find out.

Meanwhile, Ada began asking questions.

The newsagent had seen a flatbed truck at half past six. The woman who swept the post office steps had assumed the bench was being repainted. A cyclist claimed it had been dangerous for years, though under questioning he admitted he had never sat on it.

At the pharmacy, Ada found an ally.

“Mrs. Bell used that bench,” the assistant said. “She could get here from her flat if she rested halfway.”

“Where does she rest now?”

“She doesn’t come. Her neighbour collects.”

Ada bought a notebook.

On the first page she wrote: WHO SAT THERE?

She disliked petitions. People signed them to get you off the doorstep, and then you were left with a damp clipboard and the illusion of support. She wanted particulars.

She learned that the kitchen porter from the hotel ate his evening meal there before catching the bus home. His staff meal came in a plastic tub. He preferred to eat outside because the hotel basement smelled of hot laundry.

Two schoolgirls waited there for one girl’s grandfather, who was always late and always brought a dog.

A man from the betting shop used the bench because his wife believed he had stopped smoking.

“I’m not putting that in the notebook,” Ada told him.

“Much appreciated.”

There was a courier who changed his socks there when it rained.

There was a woman who had once sat down crying and been offered a satsuma by a stranger.

There was a stranger who remembered offering a satsuma and had worried ever since that it was an absurd thing to do.

Ada found these last two separately, which pleased her.

By Sunday she had filled nine pages.

She also discovered that almost nobody knew anybody else’s name. They described one another by coats, dogs, shopping bags, times of day.

“The tall one with the careful shoes.”

“The fellow whose dog sits on his feet.”

“That woman who laughs before answering the phone.”

The bench had apparently been running a modest neighbourhood without informing the authorities.

***

Lewis arrived the following Tuesday wearing a council lanyard and shoes too thin for the weather.

Ada was standing beside the pale rectangles.

“You came,” she said.

“I had another site visit nearby.”

She let him have this.

He carried a tablet, which he consulted before looking at the pavement.

“The support brackets were corroded.”

“Could they have been repaired?”

“Possibly.”

“Then why weren’t they?”

“It may not have been economical.”

“Compared with what?”

He shifted the tablet into his other hand.

Ada had spent thirty-four years ordering stock for a hospital kitchen. She knew that “not economical” sometimes meant a thing had been carefully costed. At other times it meant nobody wanted to telephone a welder.

Lewis explained that the bench had entered the system as a removal rather than a replacement.

“How does it become a replacement?”

“A request has to be raised.”

“Consider it raised.”

“There’s a process.”

“I’m beginning to admire its stamina.”

He smiled despite himself.

She showed him the notebook.

At first he read it with the expression of a man being handed evidence of somebody else’s enthusiasm. Then he slowed down.

“Mrs. Bell,” he said. “Is that the woman in the flats on Mercer Street?”

“You know her?”

“My gran knows her.”

“Your gran probably knows everyone.”

“She makes a serious effort.”

He read another page.

Ada watched a bus pull in. A woman carrying two bags paused near the tree, looked at the empty pavement, then leaned against the post office wall.

Lewis saw her too.

“There might be a small accessibility budget,” he said.

“Would that buy a bench?”

“It might buy part of one.”

“Which part?”

He laughed, then caught himself.

“I’ll see what I can do.”

Before leaving, he crouched to photograph the old fixing holes. His trouser cuff touched a puddle, and he stood up with a dark crescent around one ankle.

Ada felt a small, unexpected sympathy for him.

When she had been his age, she too had imagined that doing a job meant being allowed to do it.

***

The replacement proposal arrived three weeks later.

It showed a silver bench with three separate seats divided by metal bars. It looked like equipment for testing obedience.

Ada telephoned Lewis.

“Why are there fences on it?”

“Armrests.”

“Between every person?”

“They help people stand.”

“So do ordinary armrests.”

“It’s a standard approved model.”

“Can you sit next to someone?”

“Yes.”

“Comfortably?”

“That depends on the people.”

She studied the drawing again.

The old bench had held four adults when necessary, or three adults and a child whose feet stuck straight out. This one permitted exactly three people, each in an assigned territory.

“Is there another model?”

“There are several.”

“Send them.”

There were twelve. Some had no backs. Some were made of perforated metal. One was described as a perch and seemed designed by someone morally opposed to sitting.

Ada made tea.

She laid the printed pages across her kitchen table, moving a bowl of oranges to the windowsill. Then she called Mrs. Bell.

They had met twice by then. Mrs. Bell possessed a walking stick, a sharp laugh, and extensive opinions about the paving outside the chemist.

“Come and look at something,” Ada said.

“I can’t walk that far.”

“I’ll get you a taxi.”

“That seems extravagant.”

“Yes,” Ada said. “It’s a very important bench.”

Mrs. Bell arrived wearing lipstick and carrying biscuits.

They chose a wooden model with a back, end supports, and one central armrest. It was not beautiful, but it looked willing.

Then they discussed placement.

The drawing put the bench directly beneath the tree.

“Birds,” Mrs. Bell said.

They moved it a little to the right.

The new position faced the road.

“Nothing to look at,” Ada said.

They angled it toward the post office doors and the corner where people appeared from the market.

For twenty minutes they debated the winter sun.

Neither had expected to spend an afternoon designing somewhere to sit. By the time the taxi came, the biscuit plate was empty and the oranges were back on the table.

***

In April, the project stalled.

The pavement belonged to Highways. The tree pit belonged to Parks. The old post office was privately owned, and the proposed bench position might interfere with an access route that nobody had used since the building’s side entrance was bricked up in 1987.

Lewis sent an apologetic email.

Ada went to the library and asked for old street photographs.

The librarian, who loved a question with edges, produced local history books, archived planning documents, and a photograph of the post office opening ceremony.

There was the mayor, wearing a chain large enough to anchor a boat.

There were children holding flags.

And there was the bench.

It had originally stood farther from the tree, almost exactly where Ada and Mrs. Bell wanted the new one.

The photograph was dated 1954.

Ada turned it over, though of course there was nothing on the back except a library stamp.

She had been seven then.

Her mother might have walked past that ceremony. Her father might have complained about the traffic. The bench had existed through all the years when Ada had been too busy to notice benches: school, work, marriage, babies, her husband’s long illness, the bewildering paperwork afterward.

She took a copy to the council office.

Lewis came downstairs.

“I’m not sure historical placement establishes current permission,” he said.

“No,” Ada replied. “But it establishes that the world did not collapse.”

He pinned the photograph above his desk.

She knew because he sent her a picture.

Later that week, he found a retired highways officer who remembered the bricked-up entrance. The officer found a reference number. The reference number led to a document. The document established that the access route had ceased to be an access route thirty-six years earlier.

The permission took two more weeks.

During this time, the plane tree opened its leaves.

***

The bench arrived on a Monday, which Ada considered inconsiderate.

Lewis called at ten.

“They’re installing it now.”

She put on her coat over her gardening clothes and went out with soil still beneath her nails.

Two workers were unloading wooden slats. A third was measuring the pavement.

The new bench was lighter than the old one, honey-coloured rather than green. Its supports were plain. None resembled a lion’s paw.

Ada felt, to her annoyance, disappointed.

After all that work, she had wanted the lost thing returned, not replaced by a reasonable alternative.

One worker glanced up.

“You the bench lady?”

“Apparently.”

“Where do you want it?”

She pointed.

He checked the plan.

“That’s where it says.”

“I’m glad we agree.”

By noon it was bolted down.

There was no ceremony. The workers collected their tools and left behind a little pale dust, which one of them swept into a pan.

Ada stood looking at the finished bench.

“Go on,” Lewis said.

He had come over during his lunch break with a sandwich still in its packet.

“You first,” she said.

“I’ve got to get back.”

“So have I.”

Neither moved.

Then Mrs. Bell appeared around the corner, walking slowly with her stick.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake,” she said.

She lowered herself onto the bench, tested the central armrest, and shifted until she was comfortable.

“Yes,” she said. “That’ll do.”

Ada sat beside her.

Lewis took a photograph for the project record, being careful to ask permission first. Mrs. Bell told him to wait while she straightened her collar.

***

By June, the wood had lost its raw brightness. Someone spilled coffee. A child drew a tiny blue star beneath one armrest, invisible unless you bent down. The hotel porter returned with his plastic tub.

Ada still caught the Tuesday bus, though sometimes she let one pass.

She had begun meeting Mrs. Bell there on Fridays. They discussed groceries and occasionally people. Neither called it an arrangement.

One afternoon, a man lowered himself onto the far end with a sigh.

“Good to have this,” he said.

“Yes,” Ada replied.

“Council finally did something useful.”

She considered explaining about Lewis, the notebook, the photographs, the biscuits, and the retired highways officer.

Instead she watched a girl waiting at the crossing, holding a dog’s lead in one hand and two ice creams in the other.

“Yes,” she said again.

The man leaned back and closed his eyes.

Ada moved her shopping bag to give him a little more room.

# The Map of Small Repairs

The first time Mara saw the city disappear, she was waiting for a kettle to boil.

Across the courtyard, the upper windows of the yellow house went blank. Not dark, not empty: blank, as if someone had rubbed them off a drawing. The roof followed. Then the chimney, with its crooked television aerial and the gull that habitually stood there looking disappointed.

Mara blinked. The kettle clicked.

The house returned.

She stood holding an unopened tin of tea until a man in one of the restored windows pulled his curtains shut.

By morning, she had decided not to mention it.

***

At sixty-three, Mara repaired maps for the municipal archive. Mostly this involved flattening folds, removing old adhesive, and persuading people that lamination was not preservation.

“Lamination,” she told a councilman once, “is something you do to a lunch menu when you’ve stopped believing in the future.”

He had laughed uncertainly and taken his proposed conservation budget away.

Her workshop occupied the narrowest room in the old customs building. From its window she could see the river, a loading dock, and a tree growing out of a drainpipe with the persistence of a legal dispute.

That Tuesday, a parcel lay on her desk.

There was no sender’s address. The paper smelled faintly of rain.

Inside was a map of the city.

It was beautifully drawn and entirely wrong.

***

The river curved east where it should have curved west. Streets crossed without intersections. A railway station demolished forty years earlier occupied three whole blocks, while the hospital appeared as a small square labeled, in precise black letters, SOMEBODY WILL COME.

Mara fetched her magnifying glass.

Other labels were less reassuring.

A footbridge bore the words NOT YET FORGIVEN.

The central market was marked ASK AGAIN ON THURSDAY.

Across the site of the yellow house, in ink so pale she nearly missed it, someone had written:

HINGE, THIRD FLOOR, COURTYARD SIDE.

She looked up.

The house was visible beyond the tree. Its windows flashed in the morning sun.

On the reverse of the map was a single instruction:

*Begin with something you can carry.*

***

She assumed it was an elaborate joke by Ivo, the youngest archivist, who collected obsolete street signs and believed institutional morale could be improved with riddles.

Ivo denied everything.

“Is it valuable?”

“Possibly.”

“Then definitely not me.”

She showed him the yellow house.

He examined the label, then turned the map sideways.

“Maybe it’s a treasure map.”

“Treasure maps usually promise treasure.”

“Maybe someone’s managing expectations.”

At lunchtime Mara crossed the courtyard with a screwdriver in her coat pocket.

She told herself she was checking a detail.

The yellow house had been divided into flats so awkwardly that its doorbells resembled an argument. The third-floor tenant was a young father holding a sleeping child against his shoulder.

“Your window,” Mara said. “Is there a problem with the hinge?”

He stared at her.

“I reported that in October.”

“May I see it?”

***

The hinge had worked loose from rotten wood. Whenever the wind caught the casement, it struck the frame hard enough to wake the baby.

Mara could not repair the wood. She could, however, tighten the remaining screws and wedge a folded piece of cardboard beneath the hinge plate.

“It won’t last,” she said.

The father opened and closed the window.

For the first time, it made no sound.

He did it again.

“What department are you from?”

“The archive.”

He nodded, too tired to question the arrangement of municipal responsibilities.

On her way down, Mara found a small brass screw on the stairs and put it in her pocket.

Back at work, the yellow house occupied its proper place on the map.

The pale inscription was gone.

***

For three days, she ignored this.

She had a seventeenth-century boundary survey requiring urgent attention. Its owner had attempted to clean it with an orange-scented kitchen product.

But on Friday, the map changed.

A short street near the river vanished from the paper. In its place appeared:

BENCH. ONE BOARD. TWO BOLTS.

Mara knew that street. Her husband had preferred it on their walks home because it took them past a bakery that gave away broken biscuits at closing.

He had been dead for seven years.

She went after work.

The bench stood beneath a plane tree. One board was split, exposing a rusted bolt at a height calculated to punish anyone sitting down.

Mara tied a scarf across it to warn people.

On Saturday, she returned with timber.

***

She was not especially skilled with tools.

Her first measurement was wrong. Her second was less wrong. At the hardware shop, a woman wearing a green apron listened to her description and said, “You want the wood to fit between the supports, not achieve independence from them.”

The woman cut another board.

Her name was Sal.

“Council bench?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“They paying you?”

“No.”

Sal wrote a lower number on the receipt.

Mara spent an hour kneeling in damp leaves. Three people passed without comment. A fourth asked whether she was removing the bench.

“No.”

“Good,” he said. “My wife stops here halfway from the clinic.”

He waited while she tightened the last bolt, then sat down carefully, testing it on his wife’s behalf.

***

That evening, the street reappeared on the map.

Something else had changed.

A thin blue line connected the bench to the yellow house. Mara could not find it on any ordinary plan of the city. It crossed buildings and a canal, ignoring geography.

She held the paper to the light.

More lines lay hidden in its fibers, thousands of them, as intricate as veins in a leaf.

She thought of the father closing the window. The man testing the bench. The peculiar relief people showed when a small, familiar difficulty stopped asking for their attention.

Her husband, Daniel, had once spent an entire holiday fixing a gate at a rented cottage.

“We’re leaving tomorrow,” she had told him.

“Yes,” he said, “but someone’s arriving.”

***

The requests continued.

A shop door needed a handle tightened.

A public drinking fountain required a washer.

At a crossing near the primary school, a branch obscured the green pedestrian signal.

Mara could manage the handle. Sal helped with the washer. The branch required a phone call, three transfers, and an email containing photographs.

When the tree crew finally came, Mara watched from the opposite pavement with a satisfaction she usually reserved for lifting a stain without disturbing the ink beneath it.

The map did not distinguish between work done by hand and work brought about through persistence.

It merely recorded whether the thing had been done.

This, she thought, made it more sensible than most administrative systems.

***

Then the map asked for something she could not buy.

In the square beside the bus station, a little circle appeared around a name:

ELIAS VENN. LISTEN WITHOUT IMPROVING.

Mara searched the municipal directory. Nothing.

She tried the telephone book kept beneath the workshop sink for absorbing spills. Nothing there either.

At the bus station, she asked a driver.

“Accordion,” he said.

“What?”

“Old fellow. Plays an accordion with a red strap. Usually by the coffee stand.”

Elias Venn was there on Wednesday, playing a tune that seemed to have lost confidence halfway through.

Mara bought two coffees.

“I’m looking for Elias.”

“You’ve found the remaining portion.”

She offered him a cup.

He moved his accordion from the chair beside him.

***

She nearly failed.

When he complained about his landlord, she suggested the housing office.

When he mentioned pain in his hands, she began to recommend a clinic.

He looked at her over the coffee lid.

“Are you selling something?”

“No.”

“Then you can stop working so hard.”

Mara sat back.

He told her about his sister, who used to sing while he played. She had died in another country. He had not gone to the funeral because his passport had expired, although he admitted this was not the whole reason.

“What was the rest?” Mara asked.

He rubbed a finger along a cracked accordion key.

“I didn’t want to meet everybody who knew her after I did.”

A bus pulled away behind them.

Mara let him take his time.

***

By December, the city had acquired a second geography.

There were the streets everyone knew, and then there were the routes on Mara’s map: a missing stair rail connected to an unanswered letter; a broken laundrette clock linked to a woman who no longer trusted herself to leave home.

Some requests were practical. Others were troublingly vague.

RETURN THE BLUE BOWL.

ASK WHAT HAPPENED TO THE DOG.

DO NOT SAY “AT LEAST.”

Mara began carrying a notebook.

She also began missing deadlines.

“You’re distracted,” her supervisor said.

“Yes.”

“Is everything all right?”

Mara considered telling him the truth. Instead she looked at the stack of survey maps awaiting treatment on her bench.

“No,” she said. “But I can finish these by Friday.”

***

In January, a whole neighborhood faded.

It happened during the morning rush. Mara was on a tram when the houses beyond the cemetery became translucent. For a moment, she could see the distant gasworks through kitchens, bedrooms, and the wall of a school.

No one screamed.

A boy looked up from his phone and frowned. An elderly woman pressed her shopping bag to her chest.

Then the conductor announced a delay, and everyone returned to familiar grievances.

At the workshop, Mara unrolled the map so quickly she tore one corner.

The neighborhood was almost white.

Across it lay hundreds of tiny instructions.

She sat down.

Until then, she had believed the map was giving her a manageable task.

Now she understood that it had only been showing her what she might attempt.

***

For two weeks, she tried to do everything.

She replaced batteries, drafted letters, delivered groceries, argued about streetlights, and found a locksmith willing to work on a Sunday.

She forgot to eat lunch. She left washing in the machine until it smelled of a cellar.

The map became more crowded.

One evening Sal found her outside the hardware shop, crying because she had bought the wrong sort of screw.

Sal took the packet from her.

“What’s actually broken?”

Mara laughed once, without amusement.

“How long have you got?”

Sal unlocked the shop again.

They sat among buckets, hose fittings, and bags of compost while Mara explained the disappearing houses.

Sal listened without interrupting.

Then she said, “Show me.”

***

The map looked different to Sal.

Where Mara saw a tangle of instructions around the fading neighborhood, Sal saw five clear marks and a list of measurements.

“This one’s a gutter,” she said. “That’s a handrail. Those steps need edging.”

“You don’t see the names?”

“What names?”

Mara pointed.

Sal shook her head.

They carried the map to Ivo the next morning.

He saw undelivered messages, an inaccessible council website, and a box of photographs whose owner had died without anyone identifying the people in them.

For the first time in weeks, Mara felt hungry.

She bought three large sandwiches.

Over lunch, they agreed not to establish an organization.

“Organizations need chairs,” Ivo said.

“We have chairs,” Sal replied.

“Different kind.”

***

They met on Thursdays in the workshop.

By February, there were eleven of them.

A retired nurse saw journeys that required company. A bicycle courier saw things that needed carrying. Two schoolgirls saw places where younger children were frightened and adults had failed to notice.

An accountant named Priya looked at the map for a long time.

“Well?” Mara asked.

Priya sighed.

“Forms.”

Nobody’s map was complete.

They developed rules after making mistakes.

Ask permission.

Do not mistake access for entitlement.

A person declining help is not a broken object.

If a repair requires expertise, find it.

If the same thing keeps failing, investigate what surrounds it.

The last rule proved especially useful for a drain blocked every week by waste from a café whose owner had never been given a proper bin.

***

Mara had kept Daniel’s coat on the hook beside her front door for seven years.

It was a good coat, dark wool with a repaired lining. In one pocket remained a train ticket; in the other, a peppermint fused to its wrapper.

She did not think of it as a shrine.

It was simply his coat, and moving it had seemed like an action for which no suitable day existed.

In March, she brought the map home.

She spread it on the kitchen table while waiting for the kettle.

A tiny mark appeared at her own address.

She leaned close.

COAT. ASK FIRST.

Mara looked toward the hall.

“No,” she said aloud.

The mark remained.

For several days, she left the map rolled up.

***

Her daughter came on Sunday.

They ate soup and discussed a neighbor, a rising electricity bill, and whether either of them truly liked the expensive bread Mara kept buying.

Then Mara said, “Would you want your father’s coat?”

Her daughter put down her spoon.

“I thought you wanted it.”

“I did.”

“And now?”

“I don’t know.”

They stood together in the hall.

Her daughter slipped the coat on. The shoulders were too wide. She put her hands in the pockets and found the train ticket.

“Oh,” she said.

Mara had expected grief to arrive in its usual form.

Instead, they spent twenty minutes trying to remember the journey. Neither could. Her daughter took the coat home, and Mara kept the ticket.

The hook remained empty.

***

Spring brought repairs that did not hold.

The drinking fountain was damaged again. Elias stopped coming to the bus station. A landlord removed the handrail Sal had installed because he objected to its appearance.

The map offered no praise and no assurance.

At one Thursday meeting, Ivo asked whether they were accomplishing anything.

Priya looked up from a benefits appeal.

“Yes.”

“How do you know?”

“This woman’s heating is on.”

He gestured toward the map.

“But the larger thing.”

Priya took off her glasses.

“I’m very fond of the larger thing. It doesn’t make her flat warm.”

They continued.

Mara visited Elias in hospital. He asked whether she had brought coffee.

“Not the good kind,” she said.

“Excellent. I’d hate to recover unrealistic expectations.”

***

In May, the map went blank.

Mara tried raking light, transmitted light, and every safe method of examination she knew.

Nothing.

She called the others.

They gathered around the empty sheet.

“Finished?” one of the schoolgirls asked.

Beyond the window, a delivery driver was struggling to maneuver a trolley over the customs building’s broken threshold.

Sal went downstairs to help.

Nobody suggested they were finished after that.

For a month, Mara kept the blank map on her workbench. Eventually she placed it in a clean folder and recorded its dimensions, condition, and uncertain provenance.

Under *Description*, she wrote:

*Map of the city, showing selected dependencies. Intermittently legible.*

Then she returned to the boundary survey damaged by orange cleaner.

***

Years later, people disagreed about what had happened.

Some remembered a winter of unusual fog. Others recalled problems with their eyesight. A few insisted that houses had briefly vanished, but usually softened the claim if anyone laughed.

The Thursday meetings continued, though sometimes on Tuesdays.

Mara never discovered who had sent the parcel.

She occasionally examined the paper, hoping for a watermark she had overlooked. Once, she thought she saw a blue line near the lower edge, but it might have been a fiber catching the light.

One evening, walking home, she stopped at the bench beneath the plane tree.

The board she had fitted had weathered to match the others.

Someone had replaced her bolts with better ones.

She sat for a while, then went home before her tea got cold.

# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a desk, a brass key, and a sandwich wrapped in yesterday’s newspaper.

“The desk is yours,” said Mr. Vale. “The key is communal. The sandwich belongs to someone who never came back from lunch.”

“How long ago?”

“Tuesday.”

It was Thursday. Mara set the sandwich aside.

Mr. Vale looked relieved. Apparently this had been a test, although she could not tell whether she had passed.

The department occupied the upper three floors of a building that appeared, from the street, to have only two. Visitors generally arrived by accident. They took the stairs looking for a dentist, or followed the smell of coffee through a door marked ELECTRICAL, and emerged among the filing cabinets with an expression Mara would soon recognize: embarrassment complicated by hope.

Her job was to receive their unfinished things.

Not objects, exactly. Objects could be donated elsewhere. The department accepted what remained attached to them.

A woman brought the first chapter of a novel and the seventeen years during which she had meant to write the second. A retired electrician delivered an apology, folded so often that it had become soft as cloth. A boy arrived carrying an empty aquarium.

“The fish died,” he explained.

“We don’t generally handle bereavement,” Mr. Vale said gently.

“I know. But I was going to teach it a trick.”

They accepted the aquarium.

***

The work was less sorrowful than Mara had expected.

There were unfinished feuds, which arrived hot and had to be handled with tongs. There were abandoned diets, mostly harmless, though one spent a week whispering insults from a biscuit tin. A proposed opera about municipal drainage occupied a cupboard and occasionally produced a tremendous chord.

Then there were the unfinished conversations.

These were stored in glass jars, each labeled with a date and the words that had actually been spoken. Mara learned never to open one without first reading the label.

WELL, IF THAT’S WHAT YOU THINK contained thirty years of marriage.

DID YOU GET HOME ALL RIGHT? contained a love affair that neither participant had recognized.

One tiny jar, scarcely bigger than a thimble, was labeled DAD?

Mr. Vale caught her looking at it.

“Some things take up less room than they should,” he said.

He was an elderly man with impeccable cuffs and the distracted manner of someone listening for a kettle in another building. He had worked at the department for forty-three years. Before that, he said, he had intended to become an architect.

“What happened?”

He tapped the desk between them.

Mara thought he meant that the job had happened. Later, opening the wrong drawer, she found a small white city beneath a blue sky. Its streets smelled of rain. Tiny trams moved between buildings whose windows caught the light.

She shut the drawer carefully.

Her own unfinished thing was at home, in a green envelope beneath a stack of takeaway menus.

It was a letter to her younger brother, Daniel.

They had not spoken in six years.

People assumed there must have been an argument of corresponding size: an inheritance, a betrayal, an unforgivable sentence delivered at a funeral. In fact, the original argument had concerned a ladder.

Their mother had needed her gutters cleared. Daniel had promised to do it. He had forgotten. Mara had done it herself, fallen from the third rung, and broken her wrist.

When Daniel called, she said he always left her to deal with things.

He said she never let anyone forget a mistake.

Both statements had sufficient truth in them to do damage.

Afterward, each waited for the other to become a different sort of person.

Their mother died eighteen months later. They managed the funeral with the brittle politeness of strangers sharing a railway compartment. Daniel took the photographs. Mara took the crockery. Neither asked whether the other had wanted something else.

The letter began: I don’t think either of us meant for this to last so long.

She had written that sentence three years ago.

At the department, she became particularly efficient with unfinished correspondence. She could sort a hundred letters in an hour, arranging them by recipient, urgency, and likelihood of containing money.

She did not bring in her own.

***

In November, the city announced an inspection.

The notice arrived on thick paper and contained the phrases asset utilization, legacy provision, and measurable public benefit.

Mr. Vale read it twice.

“They mean to close us,” he said.

“Does it say that?”

“Not yet. First they ask us to explain why we exist. Then they discover that our explanation doesn’t fit in the box.”

For a week, they prepared.

Mara counted unmade journeys. Mr. Vale checked the seals on the conversations. Together they moved a stalled revolution away from a radiator.

The inspector arrived on a wet Monday. Her name was Mrs. Bell, and she wore sensible shoes. Mara had expected someone sharp and bloodless, but Mrs. Bell looked tired. She accepted tea and took a biscuit without apologizing for it.

“How many cases do you resolve annually?” she asked.

“Resolve?” said Mr. Vale.

“Complete. Return to use. Dispose of satisfactorily.”

“We preserve them.”

“Yes. I understand the storage function.”

“It isn’t simply storage.”

Mrs. Bell waited.

Mr. Vale described the aquarium. He showed her a half-knitted cardigan that was still warm from the lap of the woman who had started it. He opened a box containing someone’s intention to learn the names of trees.

Mrs. Bell touched a paper leaf.

“My husband used to know them,” she said.

Then she withdrew her hand and returned to her forms.

“What happens if these things remain unfinished?”

“Usually,” Mr. Vale said, “they remain here.”

“For how long?”

He looked toward the cabinets.

The inspection lasted four hours. At its conclusion, Mrs. Bell gave them thirty days to demonstrate a viable completion pathway for the collection.

Otherwise, the department would be consolidated.

“Into what?” Mara asked.

“That hasn’t been determined.”

After she left, Mr. Vale sat very still.

Mara began gathering the teacups. Behind her, the drainage opera sounded a muted, apprehensive note.

For the first time, the department seemed less like a refuge than a place where things had been left because leaving them was easier.

***

That evening, Mara took the green envelope out from beneath the menus.

She read her sentence.

Then she wrote another.

I still think you should have done the gutters.

She stared at it, appalled, and began to laugh.

The laugh was unpleasant at first, almost a cough. Then it loosened something. She laughed until her eyes watered, alone at the kitchen table, with the letter in front of her and a cold cup of tea beside her elbow.

She crossed out the new sentence.

Then she uncrossed it, as far as that was possible.

She added: But I probably didn’t need to make it a theory of your entire character.

By midnight she had written four pages. Three were explanations of why she had been right. She put those in the recycling.

The remaining page was awkward and incomplete. It said she missed him. It asked whether he still lived at the same address, which was not a useful question to put inside a letter sent to that address.

She posted it anyway.

The next morning she asked Mr. Vale whether anyone ever came back for something.

“Occasionally.”

“What do we do?”

“Locate the item. Verify ownership. Obtain a signature.”

“Could we invite them?”

He removed his glasses.

“Some people have entrusted us with things they cannot bear.”

“Some people may have forgotten where they put them.”

“And you propose to remind them?”

“I propose to ask.”

They argued until lunchtime. It was their first argument, and Mara was surprised by how much she disliked seeing him unhappy. He was surprised, apparently, that she could disagree without preparing to leave.

Finally, he unlocked a cabinet marked OUTREACH.

Inside was a telephone directory, a box of stamps, and a proposal dated thirty-one years earlier.

The proposal was his.

“I couldn’t decide how to phrase the invitation,” he said.

They used the paper from the back of it.

***

The invitations were brief.

*You left something with us.*

*You do not have to finish it.*

*You are welcome to come and decide what should happen to it next.*

Mara insisted on the middle sentence. Mr. Vale insisted on adding the opening hours.

They sent two hundred invitations before running out of stamps.

On Saturday, eleven people came.

The novelist arrived first. She was older than Mara expected, brisk and well dressed, with a shopping bag containing leeks.

“I don’t want to write it,” she said, as soon as Mara produced the manuscript.

“That’s allowed.”

“I wanted to have written it. That’s quite different.”

She read the first page, smiled at something, and asked for a pencil. For twenty minutes she made small corrections. Then she folded the pages and put them beside the leeks.

“My granddaughter likes stories,” she said. “Perhaps she’ll enjoy how dreadful this is.”

The retired electrician took his apology away unopened.

The aquarium boy returned with his father. He had grown tall enough that Mara barely recognized him.

“I thought it might be for another fish,” he said. “But I don’t really want another fish.”

They discussed it seriously. Eventually he decided to grow something in the tank.

Mr. Vale found a packet of seeds in an abandoned plan for self-sufficiency.

Other visits went less well.

A woman came for a conversation with her sister, listened to three words, and asked them to put it back. A man accused the department of stealing his youth. Someone opened a failed business proposal and immediately tried to borrow money from the electrician.

By four o’clock, Mara had a headache.

“This isn’t much of a completion pathway,” she admitted.

Mr. Vale was sweeping soil from beneath the reception desk.

“No,” he said. “But it’s considerably more interesting than counting.”

Near closing time, Mrs. Bell appeared.

She stood in the doorway, holding one of their invitations.

“I didn’t send you one,” Mara said.

“I know.”

The paper was old and yellow, with a different letterhead. Mrs. Bell smoothed it against her coat.

“My husband brought something here. Years ago. I found the receipt.”

Mr. Vale took it from her.

He read the number and went upstairs without speaking.

While they waited, Mrs. Bell explained that her husband had planned to build a boat. Not a large boat. Something wooden, with a little sail.

“He bought books. Measured the garage. Talked about it every winter.”

“What stopped him?”

“The usual things. Work. Children. Then his hands.”

Mr. Vale returned carrying a shallow wooden tray. Inside lay a stretch of water beneath an evening sky. A small boat rested against a jetty. Its sail was furled.

Mrs. Bell put her fingers to her mouth.

For a long time, nobody said anything.

“Can I?” she asked.

Mr. Vale nodded.

She touched the boat with one finger. It rocked, making a quiet wooden sound against the jetty.

“He would have loved that,” she said.

Then, after a moment: “I wouldn’t. I get terribly seasick.”

She laughed once, and wiped her face with the heel of her hand.

She did not take the tray home. Instead, she asked whether someone else might want it.

***

Daniel’s reply arrived on a Wednesday.

It was a postcard showing a lighthouse neither of them had visited.

On the back he had written:

*I absolutely should have done the gutters.*

*I’m free Sunday.*

Mara carried it in her pocket all day. Twice she took it out to verify that the words had not changed.

Sunday was not a reconciliation of the sort people describe afterward as inevitable. Daniel arrived late. Mara had chosen a café he disliked, having forgotten that he disliked it. They hugged with their shoulders rather than their arms.

For the first ten minutes they discussed parking.

Then Daniel asked about her wrist.

“It’s fine.”

“Does it hurt when it’s cold?”

“Sometimes.”

He nodded. She watched him turn his cup by the handle. His hair was thinner. There was a small scar on his chin she didn’t remember.

“I missed quite a lot,” she said.

“Me too.”

They talked for an hour. Their mother came into the conversation and stayed there. Daniel remembered things Mara had forgotten; Mara corrected him twice and managed not to correct him a third time.

When they left, nothing had been settled about who had done more or cared more or suffered more.

But Daniel had offered to bring the photographs next Sunday.

Mara had said she would cook.

At work, the thirty days passed.

Mrs. Bell submitted a report recommending that the department remain open for a six-month trial, with revised procedures and quarterly reviews.

Mr. Vale complained about the quarterly reviews for an entire afternoon. Then he went out and bought better tea.

They changed the forms. After NAME and DESCRIPTION, Mara added WHAT WOULD YOU LIKE US TO DO WITH IT? There were four boxes: KEEP, RETURN, OFFER TO SOMEONE ELSE, and I DON’T KNOW YET.

Most people ticked the fourth.

The new arrangements did not empty the department. By spring, they needed another cabinet. But things moved now. A teacher took the proposed boat to a school beside the reservoir. The drainage opera found a brass band willing to attempt its overture. The electrician came back to say that his apology had not been accepted, but he was glad to have delivered it.

Mr. Vale began taking Fridays off.

In the drawer beneath his desk, the small white city acquired a railway station. Later, a park appeared beside it, with benches positioned where afternoon sunlight would fall.

One evening, Mara found him studying a blank patch beyond the tiny river.

“Another building?” she asked.

“Possibly.”

“What kind?”

“I haven’t decided.”

He closed the drawer, put on his coat, and turned off the lamp.

Downstairs, someone was waiting on the landing with a parcel.

Mara opened the door.

“Am I too late?” the visitor asked.

She glanced at Mr. Vale. He shrugged and took off his coat again.

“Not tonight,” she said. “Come in. What have you brought?”
