samples.result:
# The Office of Unnecessary Bridges

The bridge arrived on a Thursday, folded into a brown envelope.

Mara found it between a complaint about pigeons and the quarterly invoice for municipal string. The envelope bore no return address, only the words **FOR THE ATTENTION OF WHOEVER STILL CARES**, which technically made it somebody else’s responsibility. Mara had cared quite a lot when she joined the Department of Roads and Crossings twenty-three years earlier, but recently she had been conserving it.

She opened the envelope with a ruler.

Inside was a bridge, approximately six inches long, made of pale stone. Three arches supported a narrow roadway. Along one side stood seven lampposts, each no bigger than an eyelash. A patch of moss grew beneath the middle arch.

There was also a note.

*It belongs on Bellwether Street. You will know where.*

Mara looked out at Bellwether Street.

It contained a bakery, a shuttered cinema, two bus stops, and a man wrestling a rolled carpet into a taxi.

There was nothing to cross.

***

At eleven, she took the bridge to her supervisor.

Mr. Venn was eating a pear with a knife, a practice Mara considered unnecessarily threatening in a person who controlled annual leave.

“Promotional object,” he said.

“It has moss.”

“So do some promotional objects.”

“One of the lamps is on.”

He leaned closer.

The fourth lamppost emitted a warm yellow light. Beneath it, something moved: a person, perhaps, though too small to resolve.

“Electrical,” said Mr. Venn.

“There’s no battery.”

“Solar.”

“It came in an envelope.”

“Residual.”

Mara put the bridge on his desk. A faint breeze passed through the room, carrying the smell of river mud.

Mr. Venn set down his knife.

For a moment, neither spoke.

Then he opened a drawer and removed a blue form.

“Unsolicited infrastructure,” he said. “We haven’t had one in years.”

***

The form required the bridge’s dimensions, composition, likely load-bearing capacity, and reason for existing.

Mara filled in the first two. For the third, she wrote *unclear*. For the fourth, after some consideration, she wrote *crossing*.

Mr. Venn returned it.

“Too general.”

“That’s what bridges are for.”

“That is what authorized bridges are for. We cannot assume.”

By lunchtime, the bridge had grown to the length of her keyboard.

Mara moved her sandwich.

By three, it occupied most of the desk, and water had begun collecting beneath the arches. Not much: a shallow ribbon running over the scratched laminate, disappearing before it reached the edge.

A tiny leaf floated through.

At four, the telephone rang.

“Department of Roads and Crossings.”

“Has it arrived?” asked a woman.

“Who is this?”

“Is the fourth light working?”

“Yes.”

“Oh, good.”

“Did you send us a bridge?”

“Not exactly. I sent it back.”

“Back from where?”

The woman was silent long enough that Mara thought the connection had failed.

“From a place I couldn’t stay,” she said.

Then she hung up.

***

There was a municipal archive beneath the west staircase, in a room the building directory described as Storage B.

Mara knew the archivist, Mr. Ilyan, because he had once helped her locate the original dimensions of a roundabout that had become gradually oval through successive repairs.

He listened without interruption.

Then he said, “Stone or iron?”

“Stone.”

“Number of arches?”

“Three.”

“Any lamps?”

“Seven.”

He stood so suddenly that his chair rolled into a filing cabinet.

“Don’t let them classify it as surplus.”

“Why?”

“They auction surplus.”

From a shelf above the radiator, he retrieved a narrow ledger bound in green cloth. Its spine read **CROSSINGS: NON-GEOGRAPHICAL, 1881–1914**.

Inside were drawings of bridges spanning alleys, bedrooms, market stalls, and, in one alarming case, a dining table.

“Before the reorganization,” he said, “we maintained all sorts.”

“Bridges to where?”

“Not where. Across.”

He turned a page.

The drawing showed Mara’s bridge at full size on Bellwether Street. Beneath it, instead of a river, the artist had drawn an empty rectangle.

A handwritten caption read:

*For distances not measurable by the surveyor.*

***

Mara had been a competent person for most of her life.

At school, she remembered permission slips. At work, she caught errors before they became expensive. When her mother grew ill, she learned the names of medications, the schedules of specialists, and which supermarket sold the soup her mother would still eat.

Competence had carried her through those months and the weeks afterward.

There were calls to make, a flat to clear, and a dispute with the gas company. Her younger brother, Tomas, came on the second weekend. They worked well together until they reached the kitchen.

He wanted their mother’s chipped yellow kettle.

Mara said it was unsafe.

He said he would not use it.

She said there was no point keeping broken things.

He said she had already thrown away everything that mattered.

The argument lasted eighteen minutes. Its consequences had lasted eleven years.

Now they exchanged birthday messages consisting of complete sentences without questions.

Occasionally Mara opened their conversation on her phone and studied the blank space beneath the latest message. Then she put the phone away.

***

When she returned from the archive, the bridge had displaced her monitor and one filing tray.

Mr. Venn stood beside it with two people from Procurement.

“We’ve identified a storage solution,” he announced.

“No,” Mara said.

All three looked at her.

Mara almost apologized.

Instead, she opened the ledger.

The Procurement people examined the drawings. One asked whether the archive contained a competitive quotation.

By six, everyone had gone home except Mara and the cleaner, who mopped around the growing structure without apparent surprise.

“Had one of those in my aunt’s garden,” the cleaner said.

“What happened?”

“My uncle crossed it.”

“And?”

“He came back with an apology.”

“Did it work?”

“The apology? Eventually.”

She wrung out her mop.

“Don’t stand under it when it gets bigger.”

At half past six, Mara called Tomas.

He answered on the fifth ring.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

A pause.

“Are you sure?”

“I wanted to ask you something.”

“All right.”

“Do you remember Mum’s kettle?”

The silence became so complete that she heard him breathing.

Then he said, “I’m not doing this tonight.”

The line went dead.

On the bridge, a second lamp came on.

***

Moving a bridge without authorization required a handcart, two loading ramps, and someone willing to hold a door.

Mr. Ilyan held the door.

The cleaner brought the ramps.

Mara pushed.

At the curb, the bridge slid off the handcart and settled onto the road with a sound like a heavy book being closed. Its arches rose. Its roadway lengthened. The seven lamps climbed until their glass lanterns hung above Mara’s head.

The eastern end stopped outside the bakery.

The western end stopped outside the cinema.

Between them, Bellwether Street bent downward into a space that had not been there a moment earlier.

It was not a hole. Mara could still see the white lane markings below. But the distance between the two pavements had become difficult to judge. The far side looked both thirty feet away and unreachable.

A cyclist braked.

“Roadworks?”

“Temporarily,” Mara said.

“How temporary?”

She checked her watch, though this was no help.

The cyclist dismounted and walked onto the bridge.

“Wait,” Mara called.

Halfway across, he stopped.

He stood with one foot on a pedal for nearly a minute. Then he turned around, came back, and took out his phone.

“Dad?” he said. “Have you got a moment?”

***

By morning, there were barriers.

By nine, there was a crowd.

By ten, a local news outlet had published a photograph under the headline **MYSTERY BRIDGE CAUSES PARKING CONFUSION**.

People crossed with mixed results.

A woman in a red coat reached the other side, sat on the pavement, and laughed until someone brought her water.

A delivery driver walked across twice and reported nothing except mild disappointment. On his third crossing, he remembered where he had put the spare key to his father’s house. He seemed pleased, though he would not explain why he had been looking for it.

Two schoolchildren ran across backward. One emerged carrying a conker. The other claimed to have heard the sea.

An elderly man approached the first arch, removed his hat, and went home without crossing.

The bridge did not charge admission or offer instructions.

Mara stayed beside the barriers with a clipboard, because holding a clipboard allowed her to remain close without being asked to leave.

At noon, a woman with silver hair came up beside her.

“The fourth light,” the woman said. “Still working?”

Mara recognized the voice.

“You sent it.”

The woman nodded.

“Why?”

“I was finished with it.”

***

Her name was Sera. She had once owned the cinema.

“My husband and I ran it for thirty-seven years,” she said. “After he died, I kept opening every evening. Even when nobody came.”

They sat on the bakery step.

A bus waited behind the bridge. Its driver had turned off the engine and was eating something from a paper bag.

“One night,” Sera continued, “I went upstairs to the projection room. There it was, between the projector and the wall. Small enough to step over.”

“What was on the other side?”

“A room in a house by the sea.”

“A real house?”

“It had a damp patch over the window. That seemed convincing.”

“Was your husband there?”

“No.”

Mara waited.

“I was rather angry about that,” Sera said. “But there was a bed made up, and something to eat in the kitchen. I stayed three days.”

“When you came back?”

“I still missed him. I also wanted to go somewhere else.”

She had sold the cinema, moved to a coastal town, and joined a choir despite possessing, by her own account, a voice like a cupboard being dragged.

“Why Bellwether Street?” Mara asked.

Sera pointed toward the dark cinema doors.

“It started there. I thought someone else nearby might need it.”

***

At two, Mr. Venn arrived with an engineer and a removal order.

The engineer tapped the stone, inspected the arches, and lowered a measuring tape over the side.

The tape descended twelve feet.

Then twenty.

Then forty.

The engineer wound it back up very carefully.

“I can’t certify this,” she said.

“Unsafe?” Mr. Venn asked.

“I didn’t say that.”

“Safe?”

“I didn’t say that either.”

Mr. Venn turned to Mara.

“It is blocking an adopted highway.”

“Yes.”

“It has no planning approval.”

“No.”

“We have received six complaints.”

“How many about the bridge?”

“Four. Two were about pigeons, but the timing suggests a connection.”

He handed her the order.

Mara looked toward the middle arch.

Five lamps were lit now.

“What happens when all seven come on?”

Sera, still sitting nearby, answered.

“It leaves.”

“With anyone on it?”

“No. Mine waited for me.”

Mr. Venn rubbed his forehead.

For the first time that day, Mara noticed how tired he looked.

“Give it until evening,” she said.

He looked at the engineer.

“I wouldn’t attach machinery to it,” the engineer said.

“Evening,” he conceded.

***

Tomas arrived just after five.

Mara saw him standing outside the pharmacy, hands in his coat pockets. He looked older than he did in photographs. So, presumably, did she.

“You said there was something I should see.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the bridge.

“Right.”

They stood together while a teenager crossed carrying a violin case.

On the other side, the teenager opened the case, took out the violin, and began tuning it.

“Is this some sort of apology?” Tomas asked.

“No,” Mara said.

His face closed.

“I mean, the bridge isn’t. I am.”

The violin produced a long, uncertain note.

Mara gripped the clipboard.

“I shouldn’t have thrown the kettle away.”

“It wasn’t about the kettle.”

“I know.”

“No,” he said. “You keep saying that, but I don’t think you do.”

She almost explained the hospital bills and the clearance deadline. She almost reminded him how little time they had and how much she had already done.

Instead, she asked, “What was it about?”

He stared across the street.

“Mum made tea when she didn’t know what to say. You remember? Bad exam results. Girlfriends. That time I crashed the van.”

Mara nodded.

“I wanted one thing from her kitchen,” he said. “Something I’d actually seen her hold.”

Mara put the clipboard down.

“I’m sorry.”

***

They crossed together.

For the first few steps, nothing happened.

Then the traffic quieted.

Mara smelled toast.

Halfway across, they found a kitchen. Its window stood open above the sink. Their mother’s blue apron hung from a hook, and the radio muttered beside a bowl of oranges.

There was no one in the room.

Tomas touched the back of a chair.

On the stove sat the yellow kettle.

Mara reached for it, then stopped.

“You take it.”

Tomas lifted it by the handle.

It was heavier than she remembered, with a brown stain around the spout and a loose lid that rattled when he moved.

They stayed until the light in the window began to fade.

Then they walked on.

On Bellwether Street, Tomas was empty-handed.

For a moment, he stared at his palm. Mara could not think of anything to say.

He rubbed his thumb against his fingers.

“Still warm,” he said.

The sixth lamp came on.

***

They bought tea from the bakery.

Tomas asked whether she still lived in the same flat. Mara asked about his work. Their answers were awkward and too detailed, full of things that would have been easier to mention years earlier.

At sunset, Mr. Venn returned.

He stopped beside the bridge and watched people crossing. Then, without removing his municipal identification badge, he walked over it himself.

When he came back, he sat down on the curb.

“Tomorrow,” he told Mara, “I’m taking annual leave.”

“How much?”

“I’ll let you know.”

The seventh lamp lit shortly after eight.

The bridge waited for a woman with a shopping trolley to reach the pavement. Then its lamps lowered, its arches folded inward, and Bellwether Street slowly became an ordinary street again.

Mara picked up the small stone bridge.

Tomas held open the envelope.

***

On Monday, Mr. Ilyan helped her establish a new archive category.

Mr. Venn, writing from an undisclosed holiday destination, approved it without requesting revisions.

The official designation was **Temporary Crossings for Unspecified Public Need**. Mara labeled the drawer **UNNECESSARY BRIDGES**, because otherwise people would keep asking her to prove necessity in advance.

The bridge stayed there for seven weeks.

Then, one rainy afternoon, she opened the drawer and found a little stone railway platform, complete with a clock and an empty bench.

She called the cleaner downstairs.

“Any thoughts?”

The cleaner examined it.

“Station Road, probably.”

“There’s already a station on Station Road.”

“Well,” said the cleaner, “perhaps it doesn’t go everywhere.”

Mara found a fresh form.

Under *reason for existing*, she began to write *transport*, then crossed it out.

She left the space blank and fetched the handcart.

samples.result:
# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a brass key, a cup with somebody else’s name on it, and a warning about the third floor.

“Nothing dangerous,” said the director. “But you may hear applause.”

The department occupied an old municipal building between the tax office and a shop that sold only lampshades. Its windows were tall and perpetually dusty. Above the entrance, someone had carved a sentence into the stone, then abandoned it halfway through:

*FOR THE BENEFIT OF ALL WHO*

Mara had applied because the advertisement promised regular hours and no public speaking. Her previous job involved explaining parking regulations to people who believed their circumstances were unique.

“What exactly do we keep here?” she asked.

The director, whose name was Ivo, opened a drawer.

Inside lay a blue mitten with three fingers.

“Things people meant to finish.”

“All of them?”

“Good heavens, no. We have six employees.”

He closed the drawer gently.

“We keep the ones that arrive.”

This seemed to Mara like a distinction designed to prevent further questions. She would eventually learn that it was the department’s only workable philosophy.

Her desk stood beside a window overlooking a narrow courtyard. Someone had begun planting a garden there years ago. Six neat rows of labels emerged from the soil, naming vegetables that had never appeared.

At noon, she washed the borrowed cup.

The name on it was Daniel.

She wondered whether he had left, or simply stopped coming.

---

Things arrived by post, by hand, and occasionally through mechanisms no one could explain.

A half-written cookbook appeared inside the locked stationery cupboard. A staircase leading nowhere materialized overnight in the basement. Every Thursday, the department received one additional sentence of a detective novel whose author had been dead for nineteen years.

The sentences were not especially good.

“We don’t assess quality,” Ivo told her.

Mara’s work was to enter each arrival in a ledger, describe its condition, and assign it a shelf.

Some items were easy.

*One wool scarf, green, approximately two-thirds complete.*

Others required judgment.

*An apology beginning with an explanation of why the writer was actually the injured party.*

“Correspondence?” Mara asked.

“Structural failures,” said Ivo.

There were abandoned business plans, model ships without rigging, lullabies missing their last lines, and thousands of notebooks whose first pages announced ambitious new lives.

One entire room contained language courses.

Another held exercise equipment, though the department had stopped accepting that in March.

What surprised Mara was how tenderly everything had been packed. Even the most hopeless manuscript arrived wrapped against the rain. Even the ugliest clay bowl had been cushioned with newspaper.

People might surrender their intentions, but they rarely did so without ceremony.

On Friday, she found a small envelope addressed simply:

*To whoever can bear to look.*

Inside was a drawing of a horse.

Only the head was finished.

It was a very good head.

Mara stood it against her lamp instead of filing it immediately.

---

The applause began during her second week.

It drifted down the stairwell at four seventeen: a great soft thunder, followed by the unmistakable sound of a crowd rising to its feet.

Mara looked up.

No one else moved.

“Third floor,” said Tomas, who repaired the department’s clocks despite none of them belonging to the department.

“What’s up there?”

“Things that were almost done.”

“That sounds encouraging.”

“Sometimes.”

He was a narrow old man with a watchmaker’s lens permanently lodged above one eyebrow. Before retirement, he had tuned pianos. He now came three days a week because, he said, his apartment was too quiet and the library too warm.

He took her upstairs.

The third floor contained a concert hall barely larger than a classroom. On its stage stood an upright piano. Beside it rested a pair of shoes, polished so thoroughly that they seemed wet.

“There was a woman,” Tomas said. “She practiced for eleven years. Had a recital booked. Invitations printed.”

“What happened?”

“She didn’t go.”

“Why?”

“We don’t usually get the why.”

Mara approached the piano. A sheet of music lay open on its stand. The final measure was blank.

“Does the applause bother you?” Tomas asked.

“A little.”

“It used to bother me.”

“What changed?”

He considered this.

“I stopped assuming they were applauding the performance.”

They stood together until the hall fell silent.

Then Tomas bent down and straightened one of the shoes, which had turned slightly toward the door.

---

A month after Mara arrived, the city announced that the department would close.

The building required repairs. The collection had no measurable public value. The lampshade shop wished to expand.

Ivo read the letter twice, then placed it in the tray marked PENDING, which struck Mara as either defiance or habit.

“How long?” she asked.

“Thirty days.”

“What happens to everything?”

“The instructions say disposal.”

Outside, a delivery van reversed into the alley, beeping cheerfully.

For the first time, Mara found the arrivals irritating. Another box of someone’s abandoned enthusiasm. Another claim on shelves that would soon cease to exist.

She carried it inside with less care than usual.

The box contained a wooden boat.

Not a model. A real boat, somehow folded into a parcel smaller than a suitcase. When she lifted it free, it expanded across three desks, scattering pencils.

Its hull was painted yellow. One side was smooth; the other remained rough timber. A paper label hung from the bow.

*For Mara, when she is old enough.*

She recognized the handwriting before she understood the words.

Her father had been dead for fourteen years.

She touched the yellow paint. Beneath her finger was a ridge where a drip had dried.

She remembered that drip.

She remembered standing in his workshop, asking whether the boat would be ready by summer.

She remembered asking again the following summer.

Ivo appeared beside her.

“Oh,” he said.

For once, he offered no administrative clarification.

---

Her father had been a man of projects.

He built shelves, repaired bicycles, bought seeds, sketched extensions to houses he did not own. He could make a child feel that next Saturday would contain everything missing from the world.

Next Saturday they would test the boat.

Next Saturday they would drive to the sea.

Next Saturday he would explain the stars.

He was loving, funny, and late. Mara had spent years defending the first two qualities against the third, as if affection were a court case in which only one verdict could be returned.

After he died, other people remembered his generosity.

Mara remembered waiting in a coat.

This had made grief feel impolite.

She walked around the boat. On the unfinished side, pencil marks indicated where another plank should go. A small nail had been tapped into place and left standing, waiting for the next blow.

“Can things be claimed?” she asked.

“Certainly,” Ivo said.

“By anyone?”

“By the person they belong to.”

“And how do you establish that?”

He looked at the label.

“Sometimes the evidence is overwhelming.”

She did not claim it.

Instead, she assigned it a number and moved it into the room reserved for domestic inventions.

For the rest of the afternoon she catalogued a half-built bread oven, three incomplete family trees, and a system for organizing kitchen drawers that consisted entirely of a furious preface.

At closing time, she went back to the boat.

It had not changed.

She found this both reassuring and unfair.

---

The next morning, Mara proposed opening the department to the public.

“People can take their things back.”

Ivo glanced at the closure letter.

“The city asked for a disposal plan.”

“This is one.”

“Possibly.”

“We could call it redistribution.”

“That is much better.”

They put a notice in the newspaper. Tomas made a sign. Someone from Records found a kettle large enough to suggest hospitality on an institutional scale.

On Saturday, a queue formed before opening.

The first visitor was a woman looking for a red cardigan she had begun knitting during her pregnancy. Her son came with her. He was thirty-two and carried the kettle inside.

A man arrived for a screenplay and left it there after reading seven pages.

“I was very angry,” he said, almost admiringly.

A girl collected a science fair volcano. An elderly couple reclaimed a dance they had stopped learning when one of them broke an ankle.

The dance required some space.

For several minutes, everyone in the entrance hall moved aside.

Not every reunion was happy.

One woman found a letter from her brother and asked why the department had not sent it years ago.

Ivo explained, quietly, that they were not a postal service.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

She took the letter anyway.

By afternoon, Mara’s voice was hoarse. Her hands smelled of dust and tea.

The shelves were visibly emptier.

For the first time since the closure notice, the work seemed possible again.

---

On the ninth day, Mara’s mother came.

She wore her good coat and carried an umbrella, although there was no rain.

“I saw the notice,” she said.

Mara had not told her about the boat.

Now she led her through the rooms without knowing whether she wanted a witness, an explanation, or someone else to be blamed.

Her mother stood beside the yellow hull for a long time.

“He worked on this after you went to bed.”

“I know.”

“Sometimes until one.”

“I know.”

Her mother touched the unfinished timber.

“He wanted it to be perfect.”

Mara felt the old defense assembling itself around them.

“I wanted it to float.”

Her mother withdrew her hand.

From somewhere upstairs came a few tentative notes on the piano.

“Yes,” she said finally. “You did.”

They stood in the awkward silence that follows when a family’s familiar story acquires a sentence it cannot absorb.

Then her mother opened her handbag.

“I came for something else.”

She produced a receipt dated twenty-three years earlier.

The corresponding shelf held a letter addressed to Mara’s father.

Her mother read it, folded it, and laughed once.

“What does it say?”

“That I was leaving him.”

Mara stared.

“Were you?”

“I was furious. I wrote six pages. Then I went downstairs to tell him instead.”

“What happened?”

“We talked.”

Her mother returned the letter to its envelope.

“Some things aren’t finished because you find a better way to do them.”

She slipped it into her pocket.

---

As the deadline approached, the department changed its rules.

People could adopt things that had never belonged to them, provided they understood that ownership did not include the obligation to fulfill a stranger’s dream.

A teacher took the unfinished horse for her classroom.

A carpenter collected the staircase to nowhere.

“What will you do with it?” Mara asked.

“Make it go somewhere.”

“That seems obvious now you’ve said it.”

The detective novel went to a reading group willing to argue about the ending. The language courses went to a neighborhood center. Most were probably destined to remain incomplete, but they would at least be incomplete in company.

Other items required more caution.

They did not redistribute apologies. Promises, Ivo ruled, could not be transferred without the consent of the person to whom they had been made.

Nor could the department excuse unpaid wages, neglected children, or damage that someone had found inconvenient to repair.

Those files went to offices whose windows were less dusty and whose powers were more concrete.

“An abandoned symphony is one thing,” Ivo said. “An abandoned responsibility is another.”

Mara wrote this on a card beside the entrance.

The applause upstairs grew less frequent.

One afternoon, the polished shoes disappeared. No one saw who collected them.

Tomas tuned the piano for the first and last time.

When he finished, he played a tune Mara almost recognized.

“Is that complete?” she asked.

“Oh yes.”

“How can you tell?”

He lifted his hands.

“Because that’s where I stop.”

---

On the final evening, only a few things remained.

A weather machine that produced drizzle. A portrait with no face. Seventeen introductions to books about discipline.

And the boat.

Mara sat inside it with her knees raised. It smelled faintly of sawdust, despite all the years that should have carried that smell away.

For a while, she tried to imagine finishing it.

She could take a class. Buy tools. Learn the difference between wood that tolerated water and wood that merely looked confident.

She could spend weekends completing the gift.

The thought exhausted her.

Then she tried to imagine destroying it.

That felt like another kind of assignment.

Tomas found her there.

“You don’t have to decide tonight,” he said.

“The building closes tomorrow.”

“The building does.”

She ran a hand along the gunwale.

“If I finish it, it feels like I’m saying it was all right.”

“And if you don’t?”

“It feels like I’m still waiting.”

Tomas leaned against a desk.

“Those are two possibilities.”

“Do you have a third?”

“No. But there are usually more than two.”

After he left, Mara stayed until the courtyard darkened.

Through the window she could see the rows of labels in the empty garden.

BEANS.

CARROTS.

PEAS.

She pictured the boat out there in the sunlight, filled with soil. The idea was almost ridiculous enough to phone her father about.

She sat with that impulse until it passed.

Then she went downstairs to find the handcart and measure the courtyard gate.

---

The lampshade shop kept the courtyard.

Mara negotiated this during the handover, along with access through the side gate and permission to remove the vegetable labels.

The owner agreed.

“I’ve always wanted somewhere to eat lunch.”

They carried the boat outside with help from the carpenter. He drilled drainage holes in the bottom, a procedure that made Mara wince and then laugh.

Her mother brought compost.

Tomas brought seedlings in paper cups.

Ivo arrived with the old brass key, which he insisted should remain with someone who knew what it opened.

They planted lavender, nasturtiums, and strawberries.

Nothing symbolic, Mara told them. Things that would survive the weather.

By June, the yellow hull had begun to fade. Bees moved through the lavender. The lampshade seller ate sandwiches beside the stern and occasionally remembered to water.

Mara visited on Thursdays.

Some weeks she missed.

The garden endured this ordinary imperfection.

One afternoon, a child peered through the gate and asked why there was a boat full of dirt.

“It doesn’t go on the water,” Mara said.

“Is it broken?”

She considered the question.

“It was never finished.”

The child looked at the leaves spilling over its side.

“Looks finished.”

Mara smiled.

From the street came a bicycle bell, a delivery truck, two people disagreeing about directions. Somewhere, someone was beginning something they would not complete.

She picked a strawberry and offered it through the bars.

The child ate it, then pointed to another, still white beneath its leaves.

“Not yet,” Mara said.

# The Museum of Things That Still Work

The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody expected much from Tuesdays.

It occupied a former shoe shop between a pharmacy and a bakery that had recently begun describing bread as an experience. Above the museum door, painted in careful blue letters, were the words:

**THE MUSEUM OF THINGS THAT STILL WORK**

Below them, in smaller letters:

**Please touch. Ask before plugging anything in.**

Mira stopped outside because she was early for an appointment she did not want to attend. In her bag was a folder containing her employment history, arranged to suggest that everything she had ever done had been leading toward the position of Regional Accounts Coordinator.

Across the bottom of the museum window stood seven objects: a kettle, a stapler, a wooden chair, a bicycle bell, a yellow raincoat, a hand-cranked eggbeater, and a stone.

The stone had a label.

**DOORSTOP. MAKER UNKNOWN. APPROXIMATELY 400 MILLION YEARS OLD. STILL UNDER WARRANTY.**

Mira went inside.

A man behind the counter was repairing the cuff of his sweater with green thread. He looked up without appearing surprised.

“Admission?”

“Free,” he said.

“How do you stay open?”

“Cheap rent. Small pension. Unreasonable confidence.”

She glanced around. There were shelves, handwritten labels, a workbench, and three visitors who seemed to have settled in for the morning.

“Is this a real museum?”

The man bit through his thread.

“I hoped someone would tell me.”

---

His name was Len. He had repaired municipal elevators for thirty-eight years, which had given him strong opinions about gravity and weaker opinions about almost everything else.

He showed Mira a toaster manufactured before she was born.

“Perfectly functional,” he said. “Though the left slot requires patience.”

“Doesn’t that mean it’s broken?”

“Only if you’re in a hurry.”

Beside the toaster sat a black telephone with a rotary dial. Its label read:

**CAN CONNECT TWO PEOPLE WHO HAVE SOMETHING TO SAY. ALSO TWO PEOPLE WHO DON’T.**

“Is it connected?”

“Yes.”

“Who calls?”

“Mostly a woman asking for the previous shoe shop. She refuses to believe they’ve closed.”

“What do you tell her?”

“That we still don’t have her size.”

Mira laughed, surprising herself.

She had spent the previous six weeks becoming proficient at presenting unemployment as a period of strategic reassessment. She had also learned how slowly mornings passed when there was no reason to hurry through them.

Here, at least, she was allowed to look interested without proving that her interest would benefit a company.

Len returned to his sweater.

“What’s your appointment?”

“How did you know?”

“You’ve checked the clock four times but haven’t looked at your phone. Usually means an interview or a dentist.”

“Interview.”

“Ah. Would you like to practice?”

She almost said no.

Instead, she squared her shoulders.

“I’m a highly adaptable professional.”

Len considered this.

“Sounds exhausting. What else can you do?”

---

She did not get the job.

The interviewer described the successful applicant as someone whose experience aligned more closely with the role. Mira thanked him with such polished warmth that afterward she felt she ought to invoice him for it.

On Thursday, she returned to the museum.

Len was arguing with a girl of about ten over a pencil sharpener.

“If it eats half the pencil,” the girl said, “it doesn’t work.”

“It produces a point.”

“So does biting it.”

Len turned to Mira.

“We need an independent judgment.”

Mira examined the sharpener, a heavy metal object clamped to the workbench. She inserted a pencil and turned the handle. The machine made an industrious noise, then delivered something resembling a sharpened toothpick.

“The girl is right.”

“Thank you,” said the girl.

“Democracy,” Len said, unclamping it, “has consequences.”

The girl’s name was Jo. Her mother worked next door at the pharmacy. She came to the museum after school because Len allowed homework at the counter and objected to questions only when she asked them during soldering.

Mira stayed for an hour. Then two.

She helped rewrite a label that had become longer than the object it described. She sorted screws into jars, though Len’s system distinguished them by past usefulness rather than size.

When she finally stood to leave, he asked whether she wanted to come back.

“To help?”

“If you like.”

“I don’t know anything about museums.”

“Neither did I. It’s been an advantage.”

---

By the end of the month, Mira had become the museum’s unofficial registrar.

She made a spreadsheet.

Len regarded it with the caution of a man being introduced to a large unfamiliar dog.

“It won’t replace the labels,” she assured him.

“People always say that.”

The collection contained one hundred and forty-three objects, depending on whether a pair of scissors counted as one thing or two. Most had been donated by people who could not bear to discard them but no longer had space to keep them.

There was a sewing machine belonging to a retired bus driver who had made all his daughter’s school costumes. There was a pressure cooker with a replacement handle carved from applewood. There was an alarm clock that had survived a house fire and still rang at six.

Mira began recording the donors’ names.

Then she began recording their stories.

The stories complicated the spreadsheet.

A woman brought in a blue enamel saucepan and said, “My husband made soup in this.”

Under “Additional Information,” Mira typed: *Used for soup.*

The woman remained at the counter.

“He always made too much.”

Mira added: *Large quantities.*

“He never learned to cook for two after the children left.”

Outside, a bus sighed at the curb.

Mira closed the laptop.

“What kind of soup?”

The woman sat down.

Afterward, Mira added a new column to the spreadsheet. She called it “Other,” then deleted the heading and left it blank.

---

The museum’s most controversial acquisition arrived in November.

It was a public bench.

Two council workers carried it through the door, knocking a small piece of plaster loose as they turned it sideways.

“Len?” one asked.

“Depends.”

“Depot said you might take this.”

The bench had oak slats, iron legs, and a brass plaque so weathered that its inscription could barely be read.

“They’re replacing the street furniture,” the worker explained.

“Why?”

“New design.”

“Was anything wrong with this design?”

The worker lowered his end.

“Not a question they’ve asked me.”

They left the bench in the middle of the floor.

Mira walked around it.

“Does it belong in here?”

Len sat down.

“Seems to work.”

Within three days, it became the most popular exhibit.

An elderly man rested there between the bus stop and the supermarket. A courier ate a sandwich on it during heavy rain. Jo stretched across it to read, until Mira pointed out that a public bench should contain some public.

People who had never entered the museum came in because they could see somewhere to sit.

One afternoon, Mira noticed a woman using the bench while waiting for her prescription. She had placed both hands flat beside her, as though steadying herself.

“Would you like water?”

“No, thank you. I just needed a minute.”

She stayed for twenty.

After she left, Mira made a label.

**BENCH. MADE FOR SITTING. NO PURCHASE NECESSARY.**

---

The trouble with the bench began when someone photographed the label.

The photograph traveled farther than anything else in the museum ever had.

For a week, visitors arrived specifically to see it. Some sat down. Others photographed themselves standing beside it, then left.

A local journalist asked Mira whether the bench represented a critique of contemporary urban policy.

“It represents somewhere to sit,” she said.

The headline was:

**TINY MUSEUM TAKES A STAND WITH SEATING**

Len cut it out and pinned it behind the counter.

Then a council officer visited.

She wore a navy coat and carried a tablet. Her name was Anika, and she looked tired in a way Mira recognized from former colleagues who had been given responsibility without authority.

“There may have been a procedural error in the disposal of this asset,” she said.

“The bench?”

“Yes.”

“Do you need it back?”

“Possibly.”

Len put down his screwdriver.

“Will you put it somewhere people can sit on it?”

“I don’t manage street furniture.”

“Who does?”

Anika gave a small, involuntary laugh.

“That depends on the furniture.”

She inspected the plaque, took photographs, and promised to investigate.

At the door, she paused.

“My father used to repair kettles.”

“Does he still?” Len asked.

“No. His hands aren’t steady enough.”

“Bring him in,” Len said. “He can supervise.”

Anika smiled, but Mira could see she was already thinking about her next appointment.

The bench remained, temporarily.

---

Winter made the museum useful in ways its collection had not anticipated.

The windows fogged. Wet coats dripped onto the floor. Len installed extra hooks, then complained that everyone had mistaken the place for somewhere welcoming.

A man came in every Wednesday to wind the clocks.

A nursing student used the workbench to fix the clasp on her bag.

Anika brought her father, who inspected Len’s electrical work with increasing dissatisfaction and eventually requested a chair closer to the sockets.

Mira continued applying for jobs.

Sometimes she received rejections while sitting beside objects that had outlasted three management theories and a currency redesign. This helped less than she thought it ought to.

One evening, she found Len staring at an electricity bill.

“How bad?”

“Manageable.”

She waited.

“With some imagination.”

The museum was not a business. This had initially seemed part of its charm. Now Mira could see that charm did not negotiate with energy suppliers.

“We could charge admission.”

“And stop the people who need twenty minutes on a bench?”

“A donation box.”

“We have one.”

It contained eleven pounds, two foreign coins, and a note reading *Lovely idea.*

Mira picked up the note.

“Can we pay the electricity company with this?”

“Only if they accept lovely ideas.”

They sat quietly.

Then she opened her laptop.

Len watched her.

“That expression,” he said. “Should I be worried?”

“Probably. I’m about to become adaptable.”

---

Mira organized a repair evening.

She printed notices that said:

**BRING SOMETHING BROKEN. WE WILL MAKE NO PROMISES.**

Len approved the second sentence.

She recruited a bicycle mechanic, a seamstress, and a retired physics teacher who claimed competence with lamps but declined all responsibility for computers.

The first evening attracted twenty-seven people, a number that exceeded both expectations and available chairs.

Someone brought a fan in January.

Someone brought a music box that played four notes and stopped.

A young man brought a jacket whose lining had torn. He explained twice that it wasn’t valuable.

The seamstress spread it across her lap.

“Do you like it?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop apologizing.”

Not everything could be repaired.

The fan needed a part nobody could identify. A cheap blender had been sealed in a way that made opening it destructive. The music box remained stubbornly committed to four notes.

But the lamps lit. The jacket recovered its lining. A bicycle left without making the sound its owner described as “a spoon in a nightmare.”

People put money in the donation box.

More importantly, they asked when the next evening would be.

After everyone left, Mira counted the money while Len swept.

“We covered the electricity.”

“For the month?”

“For the month.”

Len leaned on the broom.

“Well.”

Mira waited for him to make a joke.

Instead, he wiped his eyes with his sleeve, then complained that somebody had used the good scissors on wire.

---

In March, the council decided it wanted the bench back.

Anika delivered the news herself.

“There’s good news attached.”

Len folded his arms.

“I distrust attachments.”

“It’s going outside.”

“Where?”

“Here. On the pavement. We have clearance, provided the bakery adjusts its sign.”

The bakery owner initially objected. His sign announced the day’s bread experience, and he considered its position essential to trade.

Then his mother visited, found nowhere to sit while he closed up, and resolved the matter.

The bench was collected for refurbishment.

For nine days, its absence made the museum look as though a tooth had been removed.

When it returned, the iron had been painted dark green and the oak cleaned. The plaque was readable again.

**IN MEMORY OF ELSIE WARREN, WHO LIKED TO WATCH THE WORLD GO BY.**

Nobody knew who Elsie Warren had been.

Mira searched newspaper archives. Len asked old neighbors. Jo proposed that the absence of evidence suggested espionage.

Eventually, a woman in another town answered an email.

Elsie was her aunt. She had worked in a laundry, kept racing pigeons, and possessed a laugh that carried through closed windows.

The woman sent a photograph.

Elsie stood beside a bicycle, squinting at the camera, one trouser leg tucked into her sock.

Mira placed the photograph in the museum window.

That afternoon, two strangers sat on the bench outside and discussed, with evident seriousness, whether rain was coming.

Elsie looked on.

---

By summer, Mira had found paid work at a housing association, three days a week.

The job involved spreadsheets, difficult telephone calls, and occasional opportunities to solve the problem a person actually had rather than the one the form expected.

She stayed at the museum on Thursdays and Saturdays.

There were still bills. Len’s knee grew worse. The toaster finally lost its left slot, and after a small debate they changed its label rather than pretending nothing had happened.

The museum never became famous enough to save itself permanently.

It survived by ordinary methods: standing orders, donated tools, volunteers who remembered their shifts, volunteers who forgot and apologized, somebody buying toilet paper before it ran out.

One Saturday, Jo arrived carrying a wooden box.

Inside lay the pencil sharpener they had removed months earlier.

“I fixed it.”

Len examined the mechanism.

“How?”

“New cutter. Different angle. Also, you’d put one part in backward.”

“An experimental configuration.”

“A wrong configuration.”

They clamped it to the workbench.

Mira inserted a pencil.

The handle turned smoothly. Fine curls fell into the drawer. Out came a clean, modest point.

Jo tried to conceal her pleasure and failed.

“Does it go back in the collection?”

“Of course,” Mira said.

She found a blank card and uncapped her pen.

For a moment, nobody spoke. Outside, the pharmacy door opened. A bus arrived. Someone on the bench shifted to make room for someone else.

“What should the label say?” Mira asked.

Jo took the pen.

**PENCIL SHARPENER. FIXED.**

# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a brass key, a chipped blue mug, and a warning not to complete anything without written authorization.

“Not even a sentence?” she asked.

Her supervisor, Mr. Vale, looked up from his desk.

“Especially a sentence.”

The department occupied the fourth floor of a municipal building that appeared, from the street, to have only three. Visitors reached it by pressing the elevator button marked with a small scratch. Most people never noticed the scratch. Those who did generally assumed it was damage and looked away, embarrassed on behalf of the city.

Mara had found the job advertisement inside a library book.

**CLERK REQUIRED. Must tolerate ambiguity. Pension available.**

At the time, ambiguity seemed preferable to unemployment.

Mr. Vale led her through a room of tall cabinets. Each drawer bore a handwritten label: APOLOGIES, DOMESTIC PROJECTS, EDUCATIONS, JOURNEYS. One entire wall was devoted to NOVELS. Somewhere inside it, a typewriter struck a single key every few minutes.

“What exactly do we do?” Mara asked.

“We preserve what people leave unfinished.”

“Why?”

“Because it has to go somewhere.”

He opened a drawer marked CONVERSATIONS: INTERRUPTED BY WEATHER. Inside lay hundreds of little glass cylinders, each holding what looked like a breath on a cold morning.

He lifted one.

“‘I’ve been meaning to tell you,’” he read from its tag. “‘November fourteenth. Railway platform. Hail.’”

“What was the person going to say?”

“That isn’t our business.”

He returned the cylinder gently.

At her desk, Mara found a ledger, a fountain pen, and a tray containing her first assignment: a half-knitted green sock.

The attached form listed its owner as Mrs. Anika Bell, eighty-three, deceased.

“Do we give it to her family?”

“Not unless they request it.”

“Couldn’t someone finish knitting it?”

Mr. Vale rested both hands on the back of her chair.

“Possibly. But a finished sock would be a sock. At present it is also a Tuesday afternoon, a radio playing in another room, and a woman expecting to have more time.”

He left her with that.

Mara entered the sock’s details in the ledger.

Under CONDITION, she wrote: Good.

After a moment, she crossed it out.

She wrote: Unfinished.

The morning passed quietly. At noon, someone wheeled a trolley between the desks. It carried sandwiches, tea, and a jigsaw puzzle showing a lighthouse. Three pieces were missing.

“Is that department property?” Mara asked.

“No,” said the woman pushing the trolley. “It’s just annoying.”

Her name was Iona. She had worked there twenty-six years.

Over lunch, she explained the practical rules. Do not shake an unfinished argument. Do not read a love letter aloud. If a drawer smells of seawater, call Maintenance.

“And don’t let Vale frighten you,” she said. “He only sounds like that because he’s been here so long.”

“How long?”

Iona considered.

“I’ve never asked.”

***

By October, Mara could distinguish an abandoned ambition from a postponed one by weight.

Abandoned ambitions were surprisingly light. Postponed ones could strain your wrist.

She learned to file half-learned languages in padded envelopes because loose words escaped at night. She learned that unfinished chess games continued developing grudges. She learned that the cabinet of interrupted dances required oiling every Friday, though it contained no machinery.

Most arrivals came through the intake hatch behind her desk.

A scarf.

A dissertation.

A father’s attempt to explain the divorce.

Each arrived accompanied by a form in the same neat handwriting, though nobody knew who completed the forms.

Mara became good at her work.

She had always been good at arranging things. After her mother died, she had sorted the kitchen cupboards by expiration date. After her fiancé left, she had alphabetized the books they had bought together, removing his and closing the gaps.

There was comfort in making one thing follow another.

Every evening, she returned to her flat, cooked something sufficient, and opened the drawer beneath the telephone.

Inside lay a postcard addressed to her brother.

Dear Daniel,

She had written those two words four years earlier.

They had not quarreled dramatically. There had been no slammed door, no unforgivable speech. Instead, during their mother’s illness, a thousand small disagreements had accumulated until ordinary conversation required a kind of strength neither possessed.

Daniel thought Mara had made decisions without consulting him.

Mara thought Daniel had mistaken asking questions for helping.

Both could produce evidence.

After the funeral, he moved north. They exchanged birthday messages for a while. Then they stopped.

The postcard showed a seaside town they had visited as children. On its front, a gull stood on a railing, looking severely disappointed in the ocean.

Each evening Mara looked at Dear Daniel.

Each evening she closed the drawer.

At work, she began noticing how many objects arrived in pairs that never met: a question in one cabinet, an answer three rooms away; a marriage proposal beside a refusal written six months earlier.

“Do we ever reunite them?” she asked Iona.

“Sometimes.”

“How?”

“Usually by accident. Deliberate reunions need three signatures.”

“And accidental ones?”

“A different form.”

In November, the department received a bridge.

It appeared in the intake hatch at eleven seventeen, although the hatch was no larger than a bread box.

For a moment, Mara saw stone arches stretching into mist. Then the bridge folded itself into a space the size of a shoebox and settled on her desk.

Its form read: MUNICIPAL FOOTBRIDGE, EAST BRANCH. CONSTRUCTION SUSPENDED, 1936.

“What happened?” she asked.

“Funding,” said Mr. Vale.

He studied the little arches with an expression she had not seen before.

“Where was it meant to lead?”

“To the other side.”

But when Mara glanced at him, she thought he had nearly said something else.

***

The trouble began with a memo.

It arrived on thick paper bearing the city seal and the phrase OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY REVIEW.

An inspector would visit the department on Monday.

“Is that bad?” Mara asked.

Iona put down her tea.

“The last review merged Lost Causes with Public Complaints. Nobody slept properly for a month.”

Mr. Vale read the memo twice. Then he locked it in his desk.

The inspector arrived carrying nothing but a slim gray folder.

Her name was Ms. Crisp. She wore shoes that made no sound and greeted everyone with the professional warmth of a person confirming an appointment.

“I’m here to understand your outcomes,” she said.

Mr. Vale showed her the cabinets.

Ms. Crisp took notes.

“And how many items do you process each year?”

He told her.

“How many do you resolve?”

“We don’t generally resolve them.”

“Then what does processing mean?”

“Cataloguing. Stabilizing. Preservation.”

“For what eventual purpose?”

Mr. Vale looked toward the long room.

“Availability.”

Ms. Crisp wrote something down.

She spent the morning examining drawers. She asked whether the unfinished symphonies could be completed by the unfinished composers. She suggested selling unfinished houses as development opportunities. She wanted to know why the department retained New Year’s resolutions older than seven years.

At lunch, she declined a sandwich.

By three, she had reached her conclusion.

“The inventory is growing without limit. Your storage model is unsustainable.”

“People keep living,” Iona said.

“Yes,” said Ms. Crisp. “That has been identified as a contributing factor.”

Her proposal was simple.

The department would conduct a general clearance. Items would either be returned to their owners for prompt completion or designated permanently abandoned and destroyed.

“You can’t require people to finish things,” Mara said.

“Of course not. There will be an opt-out box.”

“And if they don’t answer?”

“Nonresponse will constitute abandonment.”

From the wall of novels came the sound of a thousand pages turning at once.

Mr. Vale stood.

“This department exists because a thing may matter without ever being finished.”

Ms. Crisp closed her folder.

“I appreciate that this is an emotional workplace.”

After she left, nobody spoke for a while.

Then Iona said, “Well. We’d better put the kettle on.”

The clearance notices went out that Friday.

By Monday, the city had become strange.

A retired dentist began building the boat he had sketched at nineteen. He laid the keel across his driveway, blocking his wife’s car.

Two former friends met in a café to resume an argument about a borrowed coat.

A woman walked into a university lecture thirty-one years late.

At first, the newspapers called it a renaissance.

Then the complaints started.

People stayed awake trying to remember why they had wanted what they once wanted. Elderly men climbed ladders. Old resentments arrived at doorsteps carrying flowers.

The department’s intake hatch rattled day and night.

For every thing completed, several new things remained undone.

***

Mara found Mr. Vale in the bridge cabinet.

He had placed the little bridge on a table. Mist drifted beneath its arches.

“There was supposed to be a garden on the far bank,” he said.

Mara sat beside him.

“My wife drew the plans. Chestnuts along the path. Benches facing west.”

“Was she an architect?”

“No. A person with opinions about benches.”

He smiled briefly.

“They stopped construction in winter. By spring she was ill.”

Mara looked at the bridge.

“Is that why you work here?”

“I came to inquire about it. They needed someone temporarily.”

“How long ago?”

“Long enough that temporarily has become misleading.”

From the next room came a muffled crash. An unfinished renovation was reacting badly to its clearance notice.

“Can we stop this?” Mara asked.

“Crisp has authority.”

“Who gave it to her?”

“The city.”

“Could we ask the city to take it back?”

“Certainly. There’s an appeals process.”

“How long?”

“Nine to fourteen months.”

The first destruction was scheduled for Thursday.

That evening, Mara opened the drawer beneath her telephone.

The postcard was gone.

In its place lay a clearance notice.

**ITEM: CORRESPONDENCE, SIBLING.**

**STATUS: PENDING DETERMINATION.**

She sat down hard.

At the bottom of the page were two boxes.

COMPLETE.

ABANDON.

For several minutes she stared at them.

Then she turned the notice over and wrote: Neither.

At work the next morning, she gave it to Ms. Crisp, who had installed herself in the conference room.

“That isn’t an available category,” the inspector said.

“It should be.”

“You’ve had four years.”

“I know.”

“How much longer do you need?”

“I don’t know.”

Ms. Crisp tapped the paper against the table.

“There must be a point at which indecision becomes a decision.”

“Maybe. But I can’t tell you the date.”

The inspector looked tired.

For the first time, Mara noticed that the gray folder’s corners were worn soft.

“What have you left unfinished?” she asked.

“That isn’t relevant.”

“Nothing?”

Ms. Crisp said nothing.

Somewhere beyond the wall, the typewriter struck its lonely key.

Finally, she opened the folder.

Inside was a photograph of a room with bare plaster walls. Sunlight fell across an upright piano.

“My daughter wanted me to learn with her,” she said. “One piece. Four hands.”

“What happened?”

“She grew up.”

“Where is she now?”

“Not far.”

Mara waited.

“I thought,” Ms. Crisp said, and stopped.

The intake hatch opened in the next room.

Both women heard it.

Ms. Crisp shut her folder.

“No,” Mara said gently. “You can finish that sentence here.”

The inspector looked at her for a long time.

“I thought there would be an ordinary evening when we could begin.”

Mara glanced at the photograph again. There was a second stool beside the piano, barely visible at its edge.

***

They did not save the department with a speech.

They saved it with paperwork.

Ms. Crisp discovered an obscure provision allowing inventory to be reclassified as civic infrastructure if it served an ongoing public function.

Bridges qualified.

So did reservoirs.

After some discussion, and one exceptionally long lunch, she agreed that certain unfinished things might be described as reservoirs.

Of possibility, Mr. Vale suggested.

“Don’t put that in the official version,” she said. “Put deferred utility.”

The revised proposal established three categories: active, resting, and released.

Owners could request their unfinished things back. They could leave them in safekeeping. They could also let them go, without pretending they had never mattered.

Nothing would be destroyed for failure to answer a letter.

It was not perfect.

There were budget reductions. Two cabinets had to share a drawer. Journeys lost its window.

But Thursday came and went without the furnaces being lit.

On Friday, Iona brought a cake.

The icing read: PROVISIONALLY APPROVED.

Mara took her postcard home.

For three nights, she left it on the kitchen table. On the fourth, she put it in a larger envelope and added a sheet of paper.

Dear Daniel,

I keep trying to find a fair account of what happened, and I don’t think I can. I was angry with you. I expect you were angry with me. Some days I still am, which makes this awkward.

I saw this postcard and remembered you stealing chips from the gulls, which remains the most foolish contest I have ever witnessed.

Would you like to have lunch sometime?

She read it once before she could reorganize it into silence.

Then she posted it.

Daniel replied nine days later.

His letter was short.

He remembered the gulls differently. He had been defending the chips.

Lunch would be good.

They met halfway between their homes, in a town neither knew. The restaurant was too warm, and Daniel had grown a beard Mara disliked immediately.

For twenty minutes they discussed trains.

Then he asked about her work.

“It’s difficult to explain,” she said.

He nodded.

He had always hated it when she said that. She remembered, and began again.

“I look after things people haven’t finished.”

“Like what?”

“Socks. Books. Bridges.”

“Bridges?”

“Occasionally.”

He waited for her to smile. When she didn’t, he tore a piece from his bread roll and considered this.

Outside, a bus struggled around a corner.

Mara wanted to ask whether he had been lonely. She wanted to explain the hospital forms, the calls she had made, the last morning. Instead she asked whether he wanted coffee.

“Yes,” he said. “I’m not in a hurry.”

Back at the department, the postcard’s ledger entry had changed.

Not to complete.

Not to resolved.

In Mr. Vale’s careful handwriting, it said:

**Returned to use.**

# The Museum of Almost

On her first morning as director, Mara found a wooden boat in the museum’s front hall.

It was twelve feet long, painted blue along one side and bare on the other. A stiff brush rested in a jar beside it. The paint in the jar had hardened around the bristles, preserving the angle at which someone had abandoned the work.

There was no delivery receipt.

“Did we order this?” she asked.

Elias, the caretaker, leaned on his mop.

“We don’t order anything.”

“Then who brought it?”

“Usually that becomes apparent.”

Mara had been hired because she had experience with archives, municipal budgets, and declining attendance. The job description had not mentioned mysterious boats. It had also omitted the smell of wet wool that drifted through the building every afternoon, regardless of weather.

She walked around the boat. On the stern, someone had penciled a name beneath the unfinished paint.

*Margaret.*

Her mother’s name.

***

The Museum of Almost occupied a former post office between a dentist and a shop that sold expensive olive oil. Its limestone façade bore the weathered inscription NEITHER SNOW NOR RAIN, after which the remaining words had been removed during renovations.

Inside were seven galleries of unfinished things.

A wedding dress with one sleeve. A chess game abandoned after the thirty-seventh move. The first nine chapters of a detective novel, accompanied by a sealed envelope containing the author’s intended solution.

Mara had opened the envelope during her interview.

It contained the words: *I hoped I would know by then.*

The previous director, a woman named Dr. Bell, had disappeared in circumstances the trustees described as retirement. Her office contained an umbrella, seventeen years of immaculate expense reports, and a note tucked beneath the telephone.

*Do not accept donations from people who are still angry.*

Mara had assumed this was practical fundraising advice.

Now she suspected it was an operational rule.

She found Elias replacing a lightbulb above an unfinished portrait. The sitter had a finely rendered mouth, one complete ear, and no eyes.

“My father was building that boat,” she said.

“I wondered.”

“He died eleven years ago.”

Elias climbed down.

“Then it’s taken its time.”

***

Her father had started the boat when Mara was fourteen. Every Saturday he went into the garage with a mug of tea, switched on the radio, and worked until lunchtime.

By sixteen she had stopped asking when it would be ready.

By eighteen she had acquired a sharpened opinion about men who started things and did not finish them.

He was a surveyor. He could calculate gradients, settle boundary disputes, and explain why a wall had cracked simply by looking at the ground beneath it. Yet the boat remained stubbornly boat-shaped without becoming a boat.

After his death, her mother sold the house.

Mara assumed the buyers had disposed of it.

Seeing it now, she felt irritation before grief. Even here, even after all this time, it was taking up space.

“Can we send it back?” she asked.

“To where?”

“The garage. Wherever it came from.”

Elias considered the hull.

“You can move it to Gallery Three. There’s room beside the unbuilt railway.”

“That’s a model railway.”

“Most of it.”

***

The municipal inspector arrived on Tuesday.

Her name was Sal Venn, and she carried a tablet in a waterproof case. Rain shone on her shoulders. She declined tea, accepted a chair, and asked Mara to describe the museum’s public purpose.

“We preserve unfinished cultural artifacts.”

Sal typed.

“Why?”

Mara had prepared for questions about accessibility, emergency lighting, and the unreliable boiler.

“Because they offer insight into the creative process.”

“Do they?”

“Among other things.”

Sal looked through the office doorway at a display case containing half a knitted sock.

“My aunt has a room full of that.”

The inspection had been triggered by a ceiling leak. Water had entered Gallery Five and damaged an unfinished map of the city, producing three streets that did not exist.

Mara had not mentioned this in her report.

Sal examined the damp plaster. She examined the visitor figures. She examined a fire exit blocked by the first half of a mechanical elephant.

Then she explained the situation.

The museum needed a new roof, electrical work, and a compelling reason to receive public money.

“You have six weeks,” she said.

“Until what?”

“The committee meeting.”

“And if they say no?”

Sal looked apologetic but not uncertain.

“Then we find another use for the building.”

***

That evening Mara stayed late to read the accession registers.

At first they seemed conventional: dates, descriptions, provenance. Gradually she noticed that the dates did not correspond to manufacture or donation.

The wedding dress had arrived forty years after its maker married someone else.

The mechanical elephant had appeared the morning its inventor’s grandson dismantled his workshop.

A single unposted letter had arrived on a day described simply as *too late*.

In the oldest register, written in brown ink, she found a paragraph explaining the collection.

*An unfinished thing may persist in the world long after the hands that began it have let go. Most are absorbed into ordinary life. Some become burdens. A few require temporary shelter.*

Below this, in another hand:

*Temporary is important.*

Mara checked the first accession number.

A stone arch, begun in 1843.

Still on display.

***

She called an emergency trustees’ meeting. Two trustees attended in person; the third joined from a car and repeatedly disappeared whenever his phone slid off the dashboard.

“We need an exhibition,” Mara said. “Something people will come to see.”

“Famous failures,” suggested the treasurer.

“Celebrity shopping lists,” said the trustee in the car.

Mara proposed inviting the public to bring their own unfinished projects. They could tell their stories, contribute to the archive, recognize themselves in the collection.

The trustees liked that recognition cost little.

Elias, who was changing the batteries in the wall clock, did not look pleased.

Afterward he said, “People will bring things they want to get rid of.”

“Yes. That’s how collecting works.”

“Sometimes.”

“We can’t save the museum without visitors.”

He set the clock to the correct time. It immediately lost four minutes.

“You should ask what we’re saving it for.”

***

The exhibition opened on a Saturday.

By noon, a queue stretched past the olive oil shop.

People brought quilts, applications, pottery, business plans, and a language-learning course still wrapped in plastic. A retired electrician arrived with two-thirds of a harpsichord. A woman carried a box labeled TAXES, which Mara declined on the grounds that the museum could not suspend statutory obligations.

Each donor completed a form.

*What is the object?*

*Why was it begun?*

*Why was it left unfinished?*

The third question caused trouble.

People wrote *lack of time*, then crossed it out.

They wrote *circumstances*.

One man sat for twenty minutes before writing, in small capitals, *I FOUND OUT I DID NOT LIKE DOING IT.*

By closing time, Mara had collected eighty-three objects and enough admissions revenue to cover the boiler repair.

She stood among the donations, exhilarated.

Then she noticed the boat had moved.

Its bow now pointed toward the exit.

***

On Monday, a boy came back for a violin.

He was twelve, perhaps thirteen, with a solemn face and a coat too large for him. His mother had donated the instrument along with an exercise book containing six completed lessons.

“She said I’d regret stopping,” he told Mara.

“Do you?”

“No.”

“Then why do you want it back?”

“Because she keeps saying it’s in a museum now. Like that proves something.”

Mara brought him to the intake room.

The violin lay in its open case. A pale rectangle on the velvet showed where its bow had rested.

“Would you like to finish the lessons someday?”

The boy looked at her with exhausted courtesy.

“No. I like swimming.”

Mara handed him the case.

After he left, she retrieved his mother’s donation form.

Under *Why was it left unfinished?* she had written: *He lost confidence.*

Mara put the form in a drawer rather than the archive. She did not know what to replace the answer with.

***

Over the following week, the museum became difficult.

Doors opened into the wrong galleries. The unfinished railway extended across a corridor overnight. Someone discovered a new chapter in the detective novel, but it consisted entirely of the detective walking through rooms, unable to remember what he was investigating.

The donations would not stay where they were placed.

A half-completed degree application appeared on Mara’s desk every morning.

The harpsichord sounded a single note whenever anyone said *potential*.

Elias placed buckets under fresh leaks.

“Is this because of the exhibition?” Mara asked.

“It’s crowded.”

“We have storage.”

“Not that kind of crowded.”

He took her to Gallery Seven, closed since before she arrived. Beneath dust sheets stood hundreds of objects that had never been catalogued.

“How long have these been here?”

“Some longer than I have.”

“Why weren’t they processed?”

“Dr. Bell thought keeping them safe was enough.”

At the back stood a small wooden chair with three legs. Beside it lay the fourth, shaped and sanded, waiting for someone to attach it.

Mara crouched down. There were screw holes in the seat.

For the first time, she wanted to fetch a screwdriver.

***

Instead, she telephoned her mother.

“Do you remember Dad’s boat?”

“Of course.”

“Why didn’t he finish it?”

Her mother was quiet. Mara could hear plates being stacked.

“I don’t think he wanted to.”

“He worked on it for years.”

“He liked working on it.”

“That’s not the same as wanting a boat.”

“No,” her mother said. “It isn’t.”

Mara sat down.

“He told me we’d take it to the lake.”

“We might have. Though neither of us could swim very well.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?”

“About what?”

“About him never finishing.”

Her mother laughed.

“Darling, on Saturdays I had the house to myself. I could read. Your father had his radio. We were both quite happy.”

Mara looked through her office window at the blue-painted hull.

“I thought you must have been disappointed.”

“I was disappointed he died.”

***

The next morning she found an old photograph tucked beneath a loose floorboard in the boat.

Her father stood in the garage, younger than she remembered him. He held a strip of timber against the hull. His mouth was open, probably explaining something to whoever held the camera.

On the workbench behind him were a sandwich, a newspaper, and a vase containing three daffodils.

She studied the flowers.

In all her memories, the garage had been a place of delay. The photograph suggested that her father had been spending his Saturdays somewhere else entirely.

Elias found her sitting on the floor.

“I’ve been thinking about the museum,” she said.

“Dangerous habit for a director.”

“What happens if we finish something?”

“Depends on the thing.”

“What happens if we take it apart?”

“Same answer.”

“And if we let it go?”

He sat beside her, slowly, with one hand on his knee.

“We used to do more of that.”

***

Mara bought tools with the remaining exhibition budget.

The treasurer objected. Tools were not interpretation materials.

“They will be,” she said.

She moved the intake desk into the front hall and changed the forms.

The new questions were:

*Do you want to continue?*

*Would you like someone else to continue?*

*Are you ready to stop?*

There was also a box marked *I don’t know*, which proved essential.

She invited the donors back.

The retired electrician spent three afternoons examining his harpsichord before deciding to salvage the wood. A local school took it for woodworking lessons.

A woman finished the last six inches of a scarf while talking to a stranger who had come to dismantle a model battleship.

The man who did not like pottery smashed his uneven bowls into pieces for a garden mosaic. He wore safety goggles and looked cheerful.

Not everyone approved.

One visitor accused Mara of destroying evidence.

Another asked whether giving up was now a publicly funded activity.

Sal returned to inspect the roof repairs and found twelve people gathered around the three-legged chair.

“Is this an event?” she asked.

“I’m not sure yet,” Mara said.

***

They attached the fourth leg badly.

The chair wobbled.

A joiner named Ruth removed it, explained the problem, and helped a university student fit it properly. The student had donated an unfinished thesis and was not ready to discuss it.

When the chair stood level, everyone applauded except Ruth, who checked the other joints.

Nothing magical happened.

Then Elias removed its accession tag.

The tag crumbled between his fingers.

Across the room, a locked window swung open. Cool air entered the gallery, carrying the smell of bread from the bakery around the corner.

Mara sat on the chair.

It was uncomfortable.

“Probably needs a cushion,” Ruth said.

***

Three days before the committee meeting, Mara worked on the boat.

She did not attempt to finish it. She cleaned out the dust, removed two rusted nails, and sanded a rough edge where visitors might catch their sleeves.

Inside the hull she placed the photograph, protected beneath glass.

The label took longer.

She threw away a version about deferred dreams. She threw away another about the dignity of labor. Finally she wrote:

*Boat built by Daniel Vale between 1989 and 2006.*

*He worked on it most Saturdays.*

*His family believes he enjoyed himself.*

She invited her mother to see it.

Her mother read the label twice, then climbed into the boat before Mara could stop her.

“He kept biscuits under here,” she said, lifting a small hinged seat.

The compartment was empty except for a pencil and a brass screw.

“Well,” her mother said. “Evidently he finished those.”

***

At the committee meeting, Mara showed photographs of the workshops, visitor figures, and estimates for the roof.

She explained the revised collection policy. Objects would be reviewed rather than preserved indefinitely. Some would remain on display. Others could be completed, returned, repurposed, or respectfully dismantled.

A councilor asked how she intended to measure success.

Mara almost said attendance.

Then she described the boy with the violin.

The councilor looked puzzled.

“So you lost an exhibit.”

“Yes.”

“Deliberately?”

“Yes.”

Sal, seated along the wall, made a note.

The funding passed by one vote.

It was less than Mara had requested. The roof would be repaired in stages, and she would have to submit quarterly reports.

Outside, she called Elias.

“We’re staying open.”

“Good,” he said. “Someone’s brought a bridge.”

“A model?”

There was a pause.

“You’d better come back.”

***

By spring, the museum had fewer exhibits and more chairs.

The railway occupied one room instead of three corridors. Its owner’s great-granddaughter came on Thursdays to work out where it should go.

The detective novel remained unfinished, but visitors could borrow pencils and propose solutions. Most blamed the uncle. There was no uncle in the manuscript.

Mara still had difficult days. Donors argued. Grants were refused. The mechanical elephant required an expensive inspection before anyone would agree to switch it on.

Sometimes she sat in her father’s boat to eat lunch.

She liked the smell of the wood, especially when sunlight warmed the hull. From there she could hear people working in the next gallery: a saw, a dropped spoon, somebody asking for help.

One afternoon, a little girl stopped beside her.

“Does it float?”

“I don’t know.”

“Are you going to find out?”

Mara considered this.

“Maybe not.”

The girl ran her hand along the blue paint.

Then she asked if she could get in.
