samples.result:
The first thing my father labeled was the label maker.

He printed LABEL MAKER on a strip of white plastic, trimmed the corners with nail scissors, and stuck it to the gray casing just above the trigger. Then he held it at arm’s length.

“There,” he said.

My mother looked up from her crossword.

“Thank God. I thought it was a duck.”

This was the kind of marriage they had: he secured the world against misunderstanding, and she introduced a little misunderstanding wherever she could.

By the time I left for college, nearly everything in the house had acquired a name. EXTENSION CORD. FLOUR. SPARE KEYS. The drawers in his workshop bore increasingly specialized descriptions: WOOD SCREWS, MACHINE SCREWS, SCREWS—UNCERTAIN.

That last drawer was my mother’s favorite.

“A drawer for doubt,” she said. “Every home should have one.”

After she died, the labels multiplied.

UPSTAIRS LIGHT SWITCH.

WATER SHUTOFF.

POLICY DOCUMENTS.

He labeled the backs of photographs, which was sensible, and then the fronts, which was less so. Under a picture of my mother standing beside a lake, he put ELAINE, LAKE SUPERIOR, 1987.

I knew her name. I knew the lake. I remembered the trip: rain for six days, a cabin that smelled of damp matches, my father insisting the weather was about to break.

When I asked why the label had to go on the front, he said, “You shouldn’t have to turn something over to know what it is.”

I let it go.

He lived alone for another eleven years.

When he died, I took two weeks off work and drove home with cardboard boxes folded flat in the trunk. I had made a spreadsheet. There were columns for keep, donate, sell, discard.

For the first few days, I was efficient.

The towels went to the animal shelter. The canned food went to a church. A man with enormous hands bought the drill press and carried it out as gently as if it were asleep.

I found seven tape measures.

I found the receipt for a toaster purchased before I was born.

In the drawer marked SCREWS—UNCERTAIN, I found a tooth.

An adult molar, wrapped in tissue.

For several minutes I stood in the workshop holding it, hoping some piece of information would arrive to make it an ordinary possession.

None did.

I put it back.

On the fourth day, I began peeling labels from things I wanted to keep.

The lettering on the sugar bowl came off cleanly. The label on the sewing tin left a sticky rectangle. On the bottom of a brass lamp, beneath the expected LIVING ROOM LAMP, I found another strip.

ELAINE LIKED THIS ONE.

I sat down.

I had assumed the labels were there to help me empty the house. Now I wondered how many I had thrown away.

There were others.

Behind the kitchen clock: TEN MINUTES FAST ON PURPOSE.

Inside his good coat: WORE TO YOUR GRADUATION.

Under the small blue dish by the telephone: SHE BOUGHT THIS AFTER WE QUARRELED. I DON’T REMEMBER WHY WE QUARRELED.

His machine had no lowercase letters. Even this came out looking like an instruction.

I began examining everything before I put it in a box.

The dining table had a label underneath, where I used to hide during thunderstorms.

YOU THOUGHT WE COULDN’T SEE YOUR FEET.

On the ladder: THIRD RUNG LOOSE. ALSO I AM SORRY ABOUT THE TREEHOUSE.

I remembered being furious about the treehouse. He had promised to build it one summer, then worked Saturdays through August. By September I had stopped asking. When he offered the following spring, I told him I was too old.

I turned the ladder over and checked the rung. It was loose.

That evening I called my sister.

“Did you know about the labels?”

“Obviously.”

“No. The other ones.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“Look in the freezer,” she said.

At the back, beneath a bag of peas gone solid with frost, was a foil package.

YOUR MOTHER’S LAST GOOD SOUP.

“Don’t eat it,” my sister said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“I know. I just needed to say it.”

We stayed on the phone while I cleaned the freezer. Eventually I put the soup in the trash, then took it out again. My sister listened to the foil crackle.

“You can do it tomorrow,” she said.

On my last morning, I found the label maker in his desk. There was still tape in it.

I tried to think of something worth putting on the house before I left. Every sentence sounded either too grand or like something he would have corrected.

So I packed it.

Months later, my daughter found it in our kitchen drawer.

“What’s this?”

“A label maker.”

“What does it do?”

I showed her. She considered the available world, then slowly pressed out a word, turning the dial with both hands.

She peeled away the backing and stuck the label on my shirt.

DAD.

“There,” she said.

The city employed one person to erase the pencil marks from library books.

Her name was Ada. She worked Tuesdays through Saturdays in a room above the loading dock, where the returns arrived in gray plastic crates. She had three kinds of eraser, a soft brush, and a desk lamp she had brought from home.

Most marks were ordinary: underlines, stars, answers to questions nobody had asked. People wrote *yes* beside ideas they already believed and *nonsense* beside ideas they disliked. In cookbooks, they reduced the sugar. In travel guides, they corrected the price of admission to museums that had since closed.

Ada erased everything in pencil. Ink was somebody else’s problem.

She liked the work. A task could be finished. A page began marked and ended clean.

One Thursday, in a book about repairing household appliances, she found:

*If the noise stops when you open the door, it is probably the fan.*

Below it, in smaller handwriting:

*You always knew what things were called.*

Ada rested the eraser on the desk.

The book smelled faintly of fried onions. Its spine had been repaired with transparent tape, now yellow at the edges. On the facing page, someone had drawn an arrow toward a diagram of a refrigerator motor.

She erased the arrow first.

At lunch, she went downstairs and asked the circulation manager whether there was a rule about personal messages.

“What kind?”

“Notes. Not about the book.”

“Same rule.”

“What if they’re interesting?”

The manager was trying to remove a staple from her sleeve.

“Especially then, probably.”

Ada went back upstairs.

She erased *You always knew what things were called*, brushing the crumbs into her palm. Then she erased the advice about the fan.

On Friday, there was a geometry textbook containing a careful drawing of a horse. The horse occupied the margin beside an explanation of parallel lines. It had an extravagant mane and legs that suggested the artist had heard of horses but never met one.

Ada laughed.

She looked at the horse for another moment, then erased it from the tail forward.

That evening, she bought a notebook.

On the first page she wrote:

*If the noise stops when you open the door, it is probably the fan.*

She left a line.

*You always knew what things were called.*

On the next page, she attempted the horse.

Hers was worse.

Over the following months, the notebook filled with things she could not quite bring herself to discard.

*Too much salt. Use half.*

*This is where I stopped understanding.*

*Ask Martin.*

*Martin says no.*

There were arithmetic calculations on the blank pages of a romance novel, apparently concerning the purchase of a freezer. There was a proposed name for a baby: *Eleanor?* Then, underneath, *too many Eleanors already.*

There was a shopping list in a book about polar exploration.

Eggs. Soap. Pears.

Ada found that one unusually difficult to erase. She copied it at the bottom of a page, though afterward she could not remember which polar explorer had carried it, briefly, across the ice.

In November, a new supervisor visited her room.

He asked about volume, turnaround, and the possibility of volunteers.

Then he noticed the notebook.

“What’s that?”

“Things people wrote.”

“Why are you keeping them?”

Ada had no answer that sounded suitable for a workplace.

The supervisor turned a page.

“Are these names?”

“Some.”

“Don’t include names,” he said. “Could be a privacy issue.”

She went through the notebook that afternoon. She changed Martin to M. She considered Eleanor for a long time, then left her alone.

In January, Ada’s father died.

For three weeks she did not go to work. When she returned, the loading dock was piled with crates, and somebody had moved her lamp.

The first book she opened was a guide to garden birds.

Beside a picture of a wren, someone had written:

*Not this one.*

Beside a sparrow:

*Not this one either.*

The identification stopped there.

Ada turned the pages to the end. Nothing.

She went back to the sparrow. Her father had kept a bird feeder outside his kitchen window, although he disliked the pigeons and knocked on the glass whenever they landed. Once, in hospital, he had asked her whether she was filling it.

She had said yes.

She had forgotten until now.

Ada copied both notes into her notebook, then cleaned the pages. At five, she put on her coat and took the bus to his house.

The feeder hung crooked from its bracket. Rain had hardened the seed in the tray.

She brought it inside, emptied it into the bin, and washed it at the kitchen sink. In the cupboard beneath, behind the furniture polish, she found the bag of seed with a wooden clothes peg closing the top.

She filled the feeder and hung it back outside.

Then she sat at the kitchen table for a while, still wearing her coat, to see what came.

The city employed one person to collect sounds that were no longer being made.

It was not a prestigious position. Mara’s office occupied a former supply closet beneath the licensing department, and her annual budget was smaller than the budget for flags. Nevertheless, every Thursday she took a municipal recorder into the streets and tried to arrive before something ended.

She had captured the last mechanical bell on the number nine tram. The cough of the newspaper press before its conversion to digital. A certain revolving door, admired by nobody, that sighed in three descending notes.

Each recording required a location, a date, and a description.

**Door, revolving. Glass and brass. Reluctant.**

Her supervisor had asked her to remove “reluctant.”

“Not a technical term,” he said.

“Neither is goodbye.”

“That wouldn’t belong on the form either.”

She removed it.

In October, a man came to her office carrying an empty birdcage.

“I understand you preserve things,” he said.

“Sounds.”

“Yes.”

He set the cage on her desk. There was a little wooden swing inside, perfectly still.

Mara waited.

“My wife used to sing while she washed it,” he said. “The cage, I mean. We had a canary. After it died, she kept cleaning the cage. Every Sunday.”

“Do you have a recording?”

“No.”

“Then I’m afraid—”

“I haven’t told you what she sang.”

Mara put down her pen.

The man hummed four uncertain notes. He stopped, frowned, and tried again. The second version was different.

“There was something about a window,” he said.

They spent forty minutes looking through songs on the municipal computer. None was right. At noon, he apologized for taking her time.

“Leave your number,” Mara said.

When he had gone, she found a tiny yellow feather caught beneath the cage’s removable tray.

She put it in an envelope. There was no field for it in the database.

***

That winter the city announced that the sound archive would close.

The letter praised Mara’s dedication, then explained that the recordings could be held by the central library without the continuing expense of a collection officer.

She had six weeks to finish.

For the first five, she worked harder than she ever had. She recorded the shoe repairman’s treadle machine, the loose drain cover outside the swimming pool, the freight elevator at a warehouse scheduled for demolition. She stood in sleet to capture the rattle of a shop’s metal shutter.

On her final Thursday, she took the recorder home.

Her father lived in the downstairs room. He had once repaired watches and now struggled with buttons. Each evening, Mara helped him to the kitchen table, where he inspected the newspaper under a lamp.

He no longer remembered much of what he read, but he disliked being interrupted.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“A recorder.”

“Is it broken?”

“No.”

“Then why have you brought it to me?”

She laughed, and he smiled with the satisfaction of a man who had made a joke on purpose.

She placed the recorder beside the salt.

“What should I say?”

“Anything.”

He considered this.

“Your gutters need clearing.”

“I know.”

“The back one especially.”

“I know, Dad.”

He nodded toward the machine. “Did it get that?”

“Yes.”

“Good. You never listen.”

Afterward, they ate soup. He tapped his spoon twice against the bowl whenever he finished a mouthful. He had always done this. It had irritated Mara for thirty-seven years.

She checked the little red light.

***

On her last afternoon, the man with the birdcage returned.

“I remembered,” he said.

Mara reached for a sheet of paper.

“No, not the song.” He sat down. “The bird hated water. When she cleaned the cage, she put him in a cardboard box. He made such a fuss that she sang to cover him up.”

He was smiling.

“I’d forgotten what a dreadful noise he made.”

She gave him the envelope with the feather. He held it close to his face, then asked whether she had somewhere safe to keep it. His flat was in disorder; he was preparing to move.

They agreed it would go with the recordings to the library.

After he left, Mara packed the equipment. In the bottom drawer she found a recording from her first month: eleven minutes of a station clock being wound.

She had written, in the notes, **Mostly handling noise. Possible deletion.**

She played it.

There was the scrape of the key, then a long pause. A train arrived. Someone nearby asked whether she wanted a cup of tea. She heard her own voice, younger and brisker, saying no, thank you, she was working.

Mara rewound it.

She listened again to the offer.

Then she changed the file’s status to **Retain**, put on her coat, and went downstairs to hand in her keys.

On the morning they came to remove the sea, Nora put the kettle on.

There had been notices, of course. Notices nailed to the harbor wall, notices slipped beneath doors, a public meeting in the school gymnasium where a man with excellent shoes explained that the sea was operating at a considerable loss.

“Not a financial loss,” he said, when people began shouting. “A loss of coherence.”

He showed them several charts.

For years, the tides had been arriving late. Fish were turning up with memories of forests. On three occasions, the horizon had slipped low enough to expose the machinery.

Everyone agreed something needed doing. Nobody had understood that doing something meant taking it away.

Now there were trucks parked along the promenade.

Nora watched a worker in an orange vest unfasten the beach from the water. He worked slowly, with a long-handled tool, lifting the edge and rolling it back. Beneath the sea lay pale concrete marked with the outlines of things that had rested there: anchors, bottles, a bicycle, the curled silhouette of a whale.

The kettle clicked off.

Her husband had been dead eleven years. This was not relevant to the removal of the sea, except that most things were relevant to it eventually.

She made two cups, caught herself, and poured one into the sink.

Outside, a supervisor was arguing with a gull.

Nora carried her tea down to the promenade.

“Where’s it going?” she asked.

The supervisor consulted his clipboard.

“Processing.”

“And after processing?”

“That depends on the assessment.”

The gull made a harsh, derisive sound.

“Exactly,” Nora said.

By noon, they had taken the shallows. Children stood behind temporary barriers watching the rock pools being packed into padded crates. Each pool retained its small arrangement of weeds and anemones. A crab kept trying to climb over the rim of one crate, and a worker kept gently pushing it back with his pencil.

Nora found herself beside Mr. Vale, who had taught mathematics at the secondary school until his retirement.

“They could have started at the other end,” he said.

“What other end?”

He gestured vaguely toward France.

They watched in silence.

Farther out, a fishing boat listed on the exposed concrete. Its owner sat in the wheelhouse, refusing to leave. Two workers stood below him with a ladder and the patient expressions of people paid by the hour.

“Do you suppose we’ll still get the weather?” Mr. Vale asked.

“I expect they’ll leave the weather. It’s difficult to move.”

At three, Nora went home and opened the drawer where she kept things that did not belong anywhere else.

There were foreign coins, a tiny screwdriver, birthday candles, three keys of unknown purpose, and a photograph of her husband standing knee-deep in water. He was holding his shoes above his head, though the water was nowhere near them.

She remembered taking the photograph.

“Why are you doing that?” she had asked.

“In case it gets ambitious.”

She had forgotten the sentence until that moment. Then she could hear exactly how he had said it, including the slightly pompous emphasis he used when he thought he was being funny.

She put the photograph in her pocket.

By evening, most of the sea was on the trucks.

It had been rolled into enormous dark cylinders, secured with straps. Something inside one of them kept shining, and a worker covered it with a tarpaulin.

Only a narrow strip of water remained beside the harbor wall.

Nora approached the supervisor.

“I’d like a little.”

“A little what?”

“The sea.”

He looked tired. There was salt on his excellent shoes. She recognized him then: the man from the meeting.

“We can’t distribute it privately.”

“Why not?”

“It hasn’t been assessed.”

“I’ve lived beside it for sixty-eight years.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

She took an empty jam jar from her shopping bag.

The supervisor looked at the jar, then at Nora, then toward the boat, whose owner had begun playing an accordion.

“Don’t let anyone see,” he said.

She knelt carefully. Her knees were unreliable, and the harbor stones were wet.

The water entered the jar with surprising reluctance. For a moment she felt a tug, as though something on the other side had taken hold of it. Then the jar was full.

“Leave some air,” the supervisor said.

She tipped a little back.

At home, she set it on the kitchen windowsill.

The trucks left after dark. Nora heard them changing gears on the hill.

She had thought the silence would be enormous. Instead, the refrigerator hummed. A motorbike passed. Next door, someone dropped a pan and swore.

The jar stood between a basil plant and the washing-up liquid.

She watched it while she ate her supper. Once, a small wave struck the glass.

The following morning, Mr. Vale knocked at her door.

“Have you looked?” he asked.

Beyond him, people were walking down the street carrying buckets, saucepans, a baby’s bath.

Nora went upstairs for a better view.

All across the exposed seabed, in the hollows and cracks of the concrete, water had begun to gather.

“It might only be rain,” Mr. Vale called.

It hadn’t rained.

Nora went down to the kitchen. She screwed the lid firmly onto the jar and put it in her shopping bag, wrapped in a tea towel.

Outside, Mr. Vale took her arm for the steep part of the hill.

Neither of them said much. They had to watch their footing, and Nora was trying not to spill anything.

The Department of Unused Time occupied the narrowest building on Bellwether Street. From the pavement it looked like a filing cabinet someone had forgotten to push shut.

Mara found it on a Tuesday, between a dentist’s appointment that ended early and a train that never came.

There was a brass plate beside the door.

**HOURS RETURNED, SUBJECT TO AVAILABILITY.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**Please do not bring clocks. They become difficult.**

She put her watch in her coat pocket, which seemed close enough, and went inside.

The waiting room contained three chairs, a fern, and a man holding a birthday cake. Its candles had burned down to blue puddles.

“Have you been waiting long?” Mara asked.

“That’s what I’m here to find out.”

Before she could decide whether he was joking, a woman behind the counter called her forward.

The woman wore a green cardigan with wooden buttons. On her desk stood a glass of water, a stapler, and a small stone labeled **THURSDAY**.

“What sort of time have you lost?”

“I’m not sure.”

“Most people aren’t. We can search by circumstance.”

Mara considered.

“Queues. Meetings. Trying to remember passwords.”

The woman nodded without writing anything.

“And there were eight years with someone who said he wasn’t ready.”

“We get that a lot. Unfortunately, time spent hoping is classified as used.”

“That seems unfair.”

“You can appeal.”

“Does it take long?”

The woman looked at her.

“Right,” Mara said.

A trolley rattled somewhere behind the wall.

“What can you return?”

“Small things, usually. Minutes misplaced between tasks. Afternoons you failed to notice. Occasionally a summer, though there’s a considerable backlog.”

Mara thought of her mother’s kitchen.

It had been demolished three years earlier, after the house was sold. The new owners sent photographs of the renovation, believing she would be pleased. White cabinets. Black taps. The wall where her mother had marked her height was gone.

“I’d like an hour with my mother.”

The woman’s expression changed only slightly.

“We can’t return people.”

“I know.”

“People often say that before asking.”

Mara looked down at the counter. Someone had scratched a tiny boat into its varnish.

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know.”

For a while, the woman searched through drawers. They were much deeper than the desk should have allowed. Mara heard wind in one and cutlery in another. From a third came the noise of children being told to come inside.

Finally, the woman placed a brown envelope on the counter.

“Forty-three minutes.”

“What are they from?”

“A Sunday in November. You were seventeen. You declined to help make bread.”

“I don’t remember that.”

“No.”

Mara touched the envelope. It was warm.

“If I open it, will I be there?”

“You’ll be here. The time will be yours again.”

“And my mother?”

“No.”

“Then what good is it?”

The woman drew the envelope back toward herself.

“I can put it away.”

Mara kept one finger on the corner.

“How much?”

“There’s no charge. But you must use it before midnight.”

***

At home, she put the envelope on the kitchen table.

She answered two emails. She washed a mug that was already clean. She called her brother and asked whether he remembered their mother making bread.

“She was terrible at it,” he said.

“She wasn’t.”

“Mara. You could build a garage with those loaves.”

She laughed, then cried so suddenly that he stopped speaking.

After a moment he said, “Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Want me to come over?”

“No. Thank you. No.”

When they hung up, she opened the cupboard.

Flour. Salt. A sachet of yeast far beyond its printed date.

She went to the corner shop.

By the time she returned, it was raining. She took off her wet shoes, cleared the table, and tore open the envelope.

Nothing shone.

There was no music, no kitchen rising around her, no familiar voice from the next room.

Inside was a square of ordinary paper.

**Begin.**

Mara nearly threw it away.

Instead, she found a recipe.

She tipped flour into a bowl. Added salt. Mixed the yeast with water that was probably too hot, then started again.

Dough stuck to her hands.

She had forgotten that part, or never known it: how thoroughly a thing could resist becoming itself.

She worked it against the table. Folded, pressed, turned. Rain clicked against the window.

Her mother had worn her rings while cooking. Bits of dough would lodge beneath the settings, and she would pick them out with a pin afterward. Mara had found this disgusting at seventeen.

She took off her own ring and set it beside the bowl.

For a moment she wanted to call her brother again. Then the dough caught under her palm, and she turned back to it.

***

The loaf came out crooked and pale on one side.

Mara cut it too soon. The middle dragged against the knife.

She buttered a slice anyway and ate it standing at the counter.

Outside, a bus sighed at the stop. Upstairs, someone dropped something heavy and swore. Her phone lit up with a message from her brother.

**Any good?**

She sent him a photograph.

Three dots appeared.

**Garage material?**

**Garden wall, at most.**

She wrapped half the loaf in a clean towel for him.

The next morning, Bellwether Street contained a dentist, a florist, and a narrow passage between two buildings.

Mara stood at the passage for a while. At the far end were bins and a delivery bicycle chained to a pipe.

She checked her watch. She had twenty minutes before work.

Across the street, the bakery was opening. She went in and asked the woman arranging the window why a loaf might come out pale on one side.

“Your oven, probably. What shelf did you use?”

Mara explained.

The woman listened, then moved two chairs away from a little table.

“Sit down,” she said. “I’ve got a minute.”

samples.result:
The first thing my father taught me to repair was a drawer.

Not a clock, not a bicycle, nothing that rewarded competence by moving. Just a kitchen drawer that stuck every winter and opened too freely in summer, spilling birthday candles and rubber bands onto the floor.

“Wood remembers being a tree,” he said.

This was not a useful explanation. I was nine and wanted instructions.

He turned the drawer upside down on the table. There were pale tracks along its sides where the wood had rubbed itself smooth.

“Here.”

He gave me a stub of candle.

I waxed the runners. We put the drawer back. It opened.

For several days I found reasons to retrieve things nobody needed.

***

Thirty years later, after his funeral, I went through his house with a yellow legal pad.

The pad was my sister’s idea.

Three columns: KEEP, DONATE, DISCARD.

“You need a system,” she said over the phone.

She had children, a bad knee, and a job that required her to use the phrase “capacity planning.” She would come on Saturday. Until then I had the system.

I began with the kitchen.

Six mugs. Four ordinary, one commemorating a bank that no longer existed, one with a handle he had repaired using a small metal bracket and two screws.

I held the repaired mug over the DISCARD column.

He had owned a drill bit fine enough to make those holes. Somewhere in the house, I would have to find it and decide what to do with that, too.

I put the mug back.

***

In the garage, jars of screws stood beneath a shelf of useful-looking pieces of wood.

My father labeled everything, but his labels anticipated a reader who already knew what he meant.

GOOD WIRE.

OTHER HINGES.

DO NOT USE.

The last was on a biscuit tin containing what appeared to be perfectly usable bolts. I did not trust them.

There was a cardboard box marked BITS FROM THINGS.

Inside were a brass wheel, a blue plastic lever, three springs, and the little door from a toy ambulance I had owned.

I remembered the ambulance but not losing the door. I remembered making its siren noise under the dining table while my parents tried to listen to the weather forecast.

He must have found the door afterward. Perhaps he had meant to fix it that evening.

I sat on his work stool. One leg was shorter than the others, and he had corrected this with a folded square of sandpaper taped around the foot.

Even his repairs needed repairs.

***

At noon, the woman next door knocked.

She carried soup in a saucepan.

“I didn’t know what you’d have unpacked,” she said.

“I’m packing.”

“Yes, of course.”

Her name was Mrs. Alvarez. She had lived beside him for eleven years. I knew her mostly as a voice asking him, during our telephone calls, whether he wanted anything from the shops.

She looked past me toward the hall.

“He fixed my gate in March.”

“He liked fixing things.”

“He didn’t like my gate.”

That surprised a laugh out of me.

“He said it had been hung by an optimist.”

We ate soup at the kitchen table. Mrs. Alvarez told me about the gate, her grandson’s bicycle, a lamp with an unreliable switch.

Then she said, “He talked about you.”

I looked down at my spoon.

“He said you make maps.”

“I work on routing software.”

“Yes,” she said. “He wasn’t sure what to call it.”

I had explained my work to him several times, usually while doing something else. He asked questions about delivery vans. I corrected him: our largest customers operated freight networks.

Now I wished I had let us talk about vans.

***

That afternoon I found his notebook.

Most pages contained measurements.

Window, back room: 43⅝.

Alvarez gate: lift ¼.

There were shopping lists and telephone numbers. Near the middle, on a page otherwise blank, he had written:

Ask about the maps.

I read it standing up.

Then I sat down.

I could picture him writing it before one of our Sunday calls, putting the notebook beside the telephone. I could not remember whether he had asked.

***

When my sister arrived, she found the legal pad on the table.

Under KEEP I had written:

notebook  
blue bowl  
photographs  
mug?

The other columns were empty.

“You’ve been busy,” she said.

“I made a start.”

She picked up the mug and examined its bracket.

“God, Dad.”

She put it down carefully.

We worked together through the afternoon. She was better at throwing things away, though she quietly pocketed a cheap vegetable peeler I had already put in the rubbish.

At five, the kitchen drawer stuck.

She pulled harder.

“Lift the left side,” I said.

It opened with a wooden complaint.

We took it out and laid it upside down on the table. My sister found the birthday candles. I rubbed one along the runners while she held the drawer steady.

There was a new scrape near the back. We looked for its cause and found a screw projecting from the cabinet.

She fetched a screwdriver from the garage.

We were keeping those.

***

The house sold in November.

Before we handed over the keys, I opened the kitchen drawer once more. It slid easily, empty now except for a stub of yellow candle.

I left that in the corner.

Then I went back, took it out, and put it with the spare keys and appliance manuals, where somebody might actually find it.

There was a man in our building who practiced applause.

Every evening at six, just as the pipes began knocking with everyone’s dinner water, he would clap for twenty minutes. Sometimes slowly, with the solemnity of a visiting dignitary. Sometimes in quick, delighted bursts. Sometimes there was a pause followed by a tremendous renewal, as though someone had returned to the stage.

He lived directly below me.

For three weeks I hated him without knowing his face.

I was studying for an examination I had already failed twice. My desk stood over the place where, I imagined, he kept his chair. At six I would be reading the same paragraph about municipal drainage, and beneath me a roomful of invisible people would apparently learn that the war was over.

I tried earplugs. I moved to the kitchen. Finally, I went downstairs.

He opened the door wearing a cardigan with one sleeve neatly pinned at the elbow.

This complicated my complaint.

Behind him, on a table, was a wooden contraption: a hinged arm, a pedal, and what looked like a padded leather paddle.

“Yes?” he said.

“I’m upstairs.”

“Ah.”

“The noise.”

He glanced back at the apparatus.

“I can do it earlier.”

“What is it?”

“A hand.”

I looked again.

“My daughter made it,” he said. “She works in theatrical properties. Mostly swords. You’d be surprised how many swords they get through.”

He showed me how it worked. His foot pressed the pedal, raising the padded piece. His remaining hand met it.

Clap.

The sound was ordinary. That seemed, somehow, the strangest part.

“Is it for exercise?” I asked.

“No. I go to things.”

He pointed toward a noticeboard crowded with tickets.

School concerts. Amateur plays. A lecture about bats. A poetry reading at the library.

“My wife used to handle this side of things,” he said, nodding toward his missing arm.

I must have looked confused, because he demonstrated: one hand held out toward an absent person.

“She’d lend me hers. We got quite good.”

I said I was sorry, and he said thank you, and neither of us specified for what.

“I’ve been practicing for our grandson’s recital. First time I’ll take the thing out.” He bent to adjust a strap. “It has to sit on my knee without sliding. And I don’t want to get carried away and stamp on the pedal. Makes an awful bang on a wooden floor.”

We settled on five-thirty.

For the next month, his applause became part of my timetable. I ate something before it began. When it stopped, I made coffee and opened the drainage manual.

I passed the examination in November.

Coming home, I found him in the lobby, attempting to carry a bag of oranges and retrieve his keys.

“How did it go?” he asked.

I hadn’t realized he knew the date.

“I passed.”

He put the oranges down.

There was a brief, awkward interval in which his hand moved, then stopped.

“Hang on,” he said. “Come upstairs.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know where I keep the biscuits, too.”

So I followed him.

He gave me three biscuits on a plate, settled the machine across his knees, and applauded me for perhaps ten seconds. I stood by the table with my coat on. I had spent years imagining the relief of passing, and now I found I was embarrassed enough to laugh.

He laughed too, which spoiled his rhythm.

Afterward, I asked about the recital.

“Saturday.”

“Ready?”

“Mechanically.”

The following week, I knocked to ask how it had gone.

He said his grandson had played beautifully, then admitted that the boy had stopped halfway through and asked to begin again.

“Did they let him?”

“Of course.”

“And the hand?”

“Dropped it getting out of the taxi.”

He showed me a crack along the wooden base. His daughter was coming to repair it on Sunday.

“Did you manage?”

“Oh, there were plenty of people.”

He said it lightly, but I thought of him sitting among all those busy hands with his own resting on a broken machine.

I nearly offered to go with him next time. Then I worried that this would be an enormous offer, involving years of school concerts and lectures about bats, and said nothing.

At my door, I reconsidered.

I went back downstairs and asked whether there was anything on before Sunday.

He consulted the noticeboard.

“Thursday. Local history. The old railway station.”

“I could do Thursday.”

“It may be quite dull.”

“That’s all right.”

He took a pencil from beside the telephone and wrote my name on the ticket.

We attended eleven things together that winter. The railway lecture was excellent. The poetry was not. At a production of *King Lear*, he leaned over during the interval and whispered, with unmistakable professional interest, “Those are her swords.”

His daughter fixed the machine. He brought it along, folded in a canvas bag, but usually left it there.

We got quite good.

The city hired a man to remove the names from things that no longer existed.

It was not a prestigious job, but it came with a pension and a bicycle.

Every morning, Emil received a list: a demolished cinema, a drained pond, a street absorbed into a shopping complex. He would ride out with his tools and take down the signs. Brass plaques went into one sack, enamel into another. Stone required paperwork.

His predecessor had lasted forty-three years.

“Don’t get interested,” she told him on her last day. “That’s how you end up keeping things.”

For eleven months, Emil followed her advice.

He removed the name of a bakery without wondering about the bread. He unscrewed a sign reading MERCY LANE from a wall that now enclosed a private car park. He scraped the words PUBLIC BATHS from a window behind which accountants sat in rows, wearing headphones.

Then, on a Thursday in November, he was sent to remove the name of a bridge.

The bridge was still there.

He checked the work order.

**HALFPENNY BRIDGE. NAME OBSOLETE. REMOVE ALL MUNICIPAL REFERENCES.**

Below this, someone had added:

**Structure to remain.**

Emil leaned his bicycle against the railing.

The bridge crossed a narrow canal. There were weeds in the mortar and a glove on one of the posts, its fingers stiff with frost. Two brass plates bore the bridge’s name, one at either end.

An old woman stood in the middle, feeding nothing.

She had a paper bag. Every so often she reached into it and made a scattering motion, but Emil could see nothing falling.

“Birds gone?” he asked.

“Years ago.”

“What are you feeding?”

She folded the bag shut.

“Is that your business?”

“No,” he said. “Mine’s the signs.”

He showed her the work order. She read it carefully, holding the bottom of the page between two fingers.

“They stopped charging the halfpenny in 1906,” she said.

“That would explain it.”

“Would it?”

Emil looked at the bridge again. It was only a bridge, and the plates were held on by ordinary screws.

He took out his screwdriver.

“My husband proposed to me here,” the woman said.

He paused.

“I said no.”

“Oh.”

“Then I proposed to him here the following spring. He asked whether I was certain. I told him not to spoil it.”

Emil put the screwdriver into the first screw.

“What was his name?”

“Daniel.”

The screw was old and came free with a small cry.

That afternoon, instead of taking the brass to the depot, Emil brought it home.

He lived above a pharmacy in two rooms that smelled faintly of cardboard. He washed the plates in his kitchen sink and laid them on a towel.

HALFPENNY BRIDGE.

Without the bridge underneath them, the words looked oddly helpless.

He put one on the mantelpiece. The other went beneath his bed.

After that, he began to keep things.

A blue enamel street sign. A bronze dedication to a school garden. The wooden nameboard of a ferry that had been dismantled upriver.

He told himself he was saving the city disposal fees.

By February, he had nowhere to put his shoes.

By March, he was interested.

He started visiting the archives after work. He learned that Mercy Lane had been named not for the virtue but for a laundress who owned three houses there. He found a photograph of the public baths on opening day: children lined up with towels, a councillor holding scissors, everyone except the councillor blurred by movement.

He looked for Daniel.

There were too many Daniels.

When he next saw the woman on the bridge, he asked her surname.

She told him, then frowned.

“You haven’t put him on a list?”

“No.”

“Good. He hated committees.”

Emil admitted he had kept the signs.

“Both of them?”

“Yes.”

“What for?”

He had expected her to approve. He was embarrassed by how much he had expected it.

“I didn’t think they should be melted down.”

She looked towards the bare stone at the end of the bridge.

“Well,” she said, “they’re not doing much good in your flat.”

The following morning, Emil returned with his tools.

He fitted the first plate loosely, then went to the other end and fitted the second. Once both were straight, he tightened the screws.

A cyclist rang her bell. A delivery driver asked whether the canal path led to the hospital. Nothing else happened.

At the depot, Emil marked the work order incomplete.

“Reason?” asked the clerk.

“Bridge still in use.”

The clerk turned the form over, looking for a box that would accommodate this. Eventually she wrote it in the margin.

That evening, Emil began sorting the things in his flat.

Most could not go back. He knew that now. The ferry was gone; the bakery wall was rubble. He wrapped those signs carefully and wrote to the city museum.

But Mercy Lane’s wall remained.

He set the blue sign beside the door, put four screws in his coat pocket, and found his shoes.

The first thing the sea returned was a yellow glove.

It lay on the harbor steps with its fingers full of sand. Mara found it while unlocking the ferry office, shook it out, and hung it on the railing. By noon, three people had recognized it.

“My father’s,” said the baker.

“My daughter’s,” said a woman waiting for the mainland boat.

“Mine,” said a boy who had never owned gloves.

Mara left it where it was.

The next morning there was a teaspoon, a bicycle bell, and a photograph of a woman standing beside a horse. The woman’s face had washed away. The horse looked remarkably pleased with itself.

By Friday, the harbor steps were crowded.

Not with treasure. There were no gold coins, no jeweled swords, none of the things the council chairman mentioned when he called the newspaper. Instead, the sea delivered spectacles, hair clips, a cracked casserole dish, fourteen keys, and a wooden ruler bearing the name of a school that had burned down thirty years earlier.

People came carrying shopping bags.

They bent over the objects with the embarrassed concentration of adults searching for something beneath a restaurant table.

Occasionally someone cried.

Mostly they said, “Well, would you look at that.”

Mara kept the ferry running.

She sold tickets through the little window and told passengers that yes, the afternoon crossing was still scheduled, and no, the objects were not included in the fare. When the newspaper reporter asked what she thought was happening, she said the sea was clearing a cupboard.

He printed that beneath a photograph of someone else.

On the ninth day, it returned a door.

Blue paint. Brass handle. Three shallow scratches near the bottom.

Mara knew it before she reached the steps.

Her father had painted that door every other summer, choosing the same blue from the same shop and then complaining that they had changed the mixture. The scratches were from a dog they had owned for six months. The dog had run away during a thunderstorm. For years afterward, her father stepped outside whenever he heard barking.

The house itself was gone.

Not taken by the sea. Sold, renovated, sold again. Mara had driven past once and seen a white wall where the entrance used to be.

She stood looking at the door until the first ferry sounded its horn.

“Want a hand?” asked Tomas, the deckhand.

“No.”

He waited.

“Yes,” she said.

They carried it into the ferry office and leaned it against the wall behind the timetable.

For the rest of the morning, Mara worked with her back to it.

At eleven, someone knocked.

Three quick taps.

She turned so sharply that her chair struck the radiator.

The blue door stood where they had left it. Beyond its edges she could see the timetable, the damp patch on the plaster, the cable leading to the electric kettle.

Again: three taps.

Her father’s knock. Impatient, even when he was arriving somewhere he had been invited.

Mara put both hands flat on the counter.

Outside, a man was arguing about whether a returned umbrella belonged to his wife. The printer needed paper. The kettle clicked off.

“Not now,” she said.

The knocking stopped.

That evening she stayed after the last crossing. She swept the floor twice. She counted the money. She cleaned a ring of tea from beneath her mug, although it had been there since November.

Then she faced the door.

She had spent twelve years becoming someone who could speak about her father without stopping midway through a sentence. She could remember his faults now, and had even begun to repeat one of his better jokes. She did not know whether she could bear to hear him tell it.

“What happens if I open it?” she asked.

Nothing answered.

“Are you actually there?”

A small sound came from the other side: a cup being set into a saucer.

Her father had drunk his tea from a saucer when it was too hot. Mara had found this disgusting at fourteen and charming at thirty, though she had never told him either thing.

She approached the door.

The brass handle was cold.

She rested her fingers on it without turning it.

“I was angry,” she said.

The harbor ropes creaked outside.

“That last day. I wasn’t busy. I could have come.”

She waited, ashamed of how readily she had offered this to a door. She had never said it to her sister, who still apologized for not calling her sooner.

Then a voice, muffled and ordinary, said, “I know.”

Mara sat on the floor.

After a while, she laughed once. Then she cried, awkwardly, with her sleeve pressed beneath her nose.

The handle did not move.

By morning the door was gone.

In its place stood a small brown teacup with a chip beside the handle.

Tomas found Mara asleep at her desk. He put his coat over her shoulders and opened the ticket window himself.

The sea returned things for another week, then stopped.

People disagreed about what it meant. The council commissioned a plaque. Someone stole it before the unveiling, which many considered appropriate.

Mara took the cup home.

Sometimes she used it. Sometimes she left it in the cupboard for months.

Once, washing it, she nearly dropped it. She caught it against the side of the sink and stood holding it tightly while the tap ran.

Then she rinsed it, dried it, and put it on the shelf with the others.

The town kept its spare time in a building beside the railway station.

It was not a bank, although newcomers often mistook it for one. There were brass handles on the doors and a clock above the entrance, but the clock had no hands. Inside, a woman named Ada sat behind a wooden counter, accepting minutes.

People brought them in all sorts of containers.

A schoolboy arrived with eleven minutes in a jam jar: the remainder of a canceled spelling test. A doctor deposited half an hour that had opened unexpectedly between appointments. Once, a man carried in three entire days wrapped in a blanket. He had been stood up at the altar and did not want to discuss it.

Ada issued receipts.

“What happens to it?” the schoolboy asked.

“It keeps.”

“Does it go bad?”

“Only if you spend too long wishing it were a different kind.”

He looked at his jar. The minutes inside moved like small fish.

“Can I have it back?”

“Of course.”

“Not yet,” he said, and pushed it toward her.

***

There were rules.

You could deposit only time you had genuinely been given. You could not bring the hours you stole from sleep, or the afternoon you spent avoiding a difficult conversation. Ada turned away many such offerings.

“This isn’t spare,” she would say gently. “You owe it to someone.”

You could withdraw your own time whenever you liked.

You could also donate it.

The donation shelf stood behind the counter, beside a fern that had been green for sixty years.

Most donations were small: five minutes, a quarter of an hour. People left them without ceremony. A tired mother. A delivery driver. An old woman who said she had more Tuesdays than she needed.

Ada never asked why.

***

One November evening, a girl came in carrying nothing.

She was perhaps seventeen, though worry had made a poor job of counting her years.

“My father,” she said.

Ada waited.

“The hospital says tonight.”

Outside, a train passed without stopping. The glasses on the shelves gave a faint, bright shiver.

“How much do you need?” Ada asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s usual.”

“Does it make people well?”

“No.”

The girl looked down.

Ada brought a small blue cup from the donation shelf.

“What does it do, then?”

“It gives you time.”

The girl stared at the cup for a long while. Then she took it carefully in both hands.

***

Afterward, she came back.

It was morning. Rain had darkened the shoulders of her coat.

“Did you use it?” Ada asked.

“Yes.”

The girl set the empty cup on the counter.

“Was it enough?”

“No.”

Ada nodded.

“But he told me where he put the seeds,” the girl said. “For the garden. I thought they were in the shed, but he said mice would get them there. They’re in an old biscuit tin above the fridge.”

She touched the handle of the cup.

“He made me promise not to plant all the beans at once.”

Ada reached for a cloth and dried a little rain from the counter.

“I wrote it down,” the girl said.

***

Ada had worked at the building for forty-three years.

She had inherited the position from a man called Mr. Vale, who had explained the ledgers, the shelves, the difference between a moment and a minute.

“A moment,” he had said, “doesn’t fit reliably into anything.”

On her first day, Ada had asked whether employees received an allowance.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“You’ll be tempted to take some anyway.”

She had been twenty-six then, and disliked him for saying it.

Now she was sixty-nine. In her handbag she carried a receipt dated the year before she began work: forty minutes from a train delay.

She had been saving them for something.

For years she had imagined an emergency. Then a journey. Then an afternoon with her sister, who lived by the sea and kept asking her to visit.

Her sister had died in March.

The receipt remained.

***

On the first warm day of spring, Ada put a sign on the door.

BACK IN FORTY MINUTES.

She took her deposit in a plain glass bottle and walked to the park.

A groundskeeper was repairing a bench. Two children argued over a bicycle. Beside the pond, a young man rehearsed something under his breath, stopped, and began again.

Ada found a dry place on the grass.

For a while she held the bottle between her knees. She had forgotten to bring a book. At work, there were cups to wash and a ledger waiting for its new page.

She loosened the stopper.

A dog came over and inspected her shoes. Its owner apologized. Ada said it was all right.

When the woman had gone, Ada lay back, awkwardly, with her handbag beneath her head.

Above her, among the new leaves, a bird was pulling at a length of string caught on a branch.

Ada watched until it came free.

The city hired a man to remove the names from benches.

Not the plaques. Those remained: small rectangles of brass attached with screws that resisted rain, frost, and the occasional determined child. His job was to remove the names themselves.

The council had discovered that people were reluctant to sit on benches dedicated to strangers. They felt watched, or indebted, or vaguely as though they had entered someone else’s living room.

“It’s a utilization issue,” his supervisor explained.

The man’s name was Ellis. He had previously repaired clocks at the railway station, until the clocks were replaced by screens.

He was given a bicycle, a box of tools, and a map.

On Monday, he removed **MARGARET BELL, WHO LOVED THIS VIEW**.

The view was a duck pond containing no ducks and one orange traffic cone. Ellis stood there for a while before beginning. Then he knelt, applied the solvent, and worked the letters away with a soft cloth.

The brass beneath was brighter.

By lunchtime, Margaret Bell had become **WHO LOVED THIS VIEW**.

By two, there was only the view.

***

At home, Ellis kept the names in a notebook.

He wasn’t required to. The council maintained a spreadsheet, but its records contained only bench numbers, locations, and dates of completion.

His notebook contained other things.

**Arthur Singh. Beloved husband. Bench facing bakery.**

**Nina and Jo. Forty-three happy years. Broken slat.**

**For Daniel, who always stopped here. Nothing nearby.**

He found that last one troubling.

Nothing nearby: no river, no garden, no playground. Just a stretch of pavement between a pharmacy and a shuttered travel agency.

He sat on Daniel’s bench after finishing it.

People passed carrying groceries. A bus sighed at the curb. In the upstairs window of the pharmacy, someone watered a plant.

Ellis stayed until five.

***

On Thursday, a woman caught him removing her father.

“Excuse me,” she said.

Ellis lifted the cloth from the plaque.

She was wearing running clothes and holding a leash. At the other end stood a dog with the cautious expression of a retired accountant.

“That’s my father.”

Ellis looked down.

**PETER VALE, 1941–2018. HE MADE THINGS GROW.**

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“What are you doing?”

He explained the utilization issue.

The woman listened without interrupting. The dog sat.

When Ellis finished, she said, “He was terrible at gardening.”

Ellis glanced at the plaque again.

“Killed everything. My mother wrote that. She meant people, I suppose.”

“I haven’t started the name yet.”

The woman looked toward the trees.

“He used to bring sandwiches here. Egg sandwiches, even in hot weather. We told him it was dangerous.”

Ellis waited.

“He never listened.”

She laughed once, then tightened her grip on the leash.

“Do you have to do it today?”

“No,” Ellis said.

This was not strictly true, but he could make it true by going somewhere else.

***

That evening, he turned to a fresh page.

**Peter Vale. Egg sandwiches.**

He considered adding the gardening, but decided against it.

***

By the third week, Ellis had begun taking longer routes.

He arrived at benches when people were likely to be sitting on them. If a bench was occupied, he was permitted to postpone the work.

He became knowledgeable about lunch breaks, school dismissals, and the movements of dog walkers.

He learned that the bench outside the library belonged, in practice, to a young man who cried into his phone every Tuesday.

He learned that the one near the tennis courts supported three women who brought folding cushions and spoke about their husbands with immense, affectionate contempt.

He learned that Daniel’s bench caught the last direct sunlight in the neighborhood.

At four forty-seven, light slipped between the pharmacy and the travel agency and warmed the wood for eleven minutes.

Ellis timed it.

He still had his old watch.

***

His supervisor called him in.

“You’re falling behind.”

“Yes.”

“Is there a problem with the materials?”

“No.”

“The equipment?”

“No.”

The supervisor rotated a pen between her fingers.

Ellis noticed that her office contained no photographs. On the windowsill stood a cactus so brown it might have been made of paper.

“Do you ever sit outside?” he asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Where?”

She stopped turning the pen.

“What does that have to do with anything?”

“Nothing,” Ellis said.

She sighed and gave him until Friday to catch up.

***

On Friday morning, Ellis returned to Margaret Bell’s bench.

The pond had ducks now. The cone remained.

He opened his notebook, then his toolbox.

The letter punches were his own. He had used them years ago to mark replacement clock parts. He arranged them on the cloth beside him.

He couldn’t restore all the lettering. The punches were too large, and the polished area too narrow.

He chose a place along the bottom edge of the plaque and tapped carefully with his hammer.

**MARGARET.**

It took longer than he expected. The G was crooked.

At the next bench, he added **ARTHUR**.

At the next, **NINA + JO**.

By Daniel’s bench, his supervisor was calling. He let the phone ring.

He had finished the name and was putting away the punches when an old woman stopped beside him.

“Is the paint wet?”

“No paint.”

“Can I sit?”

“Of course.”

She lowered herself onto the bench with both hands braced against the wood. Ellis moved his toolbox.

For a while they watched the pharmacy window.

Then the sunlight arrived.

The woman closed her eyes.

“Oh,” she said. “That’s nice.”

Ellis sat beside her, his notebook open on his knee, and did not write anything down.

The municipal clock stopped at 3:17, and for the first time in forty years, nobody called Martin.

He waited beside the telephone until four.

Then he put on his coat, took his tools, and walked into town.

The clock stood above the old library, which was now a place where people rented desks. Through its tall windows he could see young people wearing headphones, each seated before a small luminous rectangle. They looked like monks engaged in a religion that required excellent posture but seldom achieved it.

At reception, a woman asked whether he had booked a room.

“I’ve come about the clock.”

She looked at the clock on her computer.

“The other one,” he said.

“Oh. Right.”

She made a phone call. He examined a bowl of green apples so polished they appeared to be a statement about apples rather than something to eat.

A man arrived wearing shoes without socks.

“We were actually discussing this,” the man said. “Whether it’s necessary to maintain it.”

“It’s stopped.”

“Yes. Whether that’s a problem.”

Martin had brought several screwdrivers, a small oil bottle, and the key to the clock chamber. He had brought nothing suitable for this conversation.

“It tells the time.”

“Everyone has the time.”

Above them, beyond the refurbished ceiling and the air ducts, the mechanism waited. Martin knew its noises: the dry click before release, the weight descending in its shaft, the slight complaint of a bearing he had meant to replace last spring.

“I could take a look,” he said.

The man consulted his phone.

“As long as there’s no charge.”

***

Inside the tower, the air smelled of dust and old grease.

Martin stood still until his breathing settled. The stairs had become steeper over the years, despite remaining precisely the same stairs.

The fault was simple. A pin had worked loose and lodged where it ought not to be. He found it, freed it, and held it in his palm.

“That’s all you are,” he said.

From below came the muffled sound of a meeting.

He could repair the clock in twenty minutes. Ten, if his hands behaved. Then he could go home, wash the oil from his fingers, and eat the soup his daughter had left in the refrigerator, labeled TUESDAY, as if he might otherwise attempt to eat Thursday.

Instead, he sat on the wooden stool.

There were names carved beneath its seat. He knew because he had carved one himself at nineteen. His predecessor had caught him doing it.

“If you want your name on something,” old Bell had said, “make something.”

Then Bell had turned the stool over and shown him his own name.

Martin reached beneath the seat. His fingers found the letters without difficulty.

***

At five, footsteps sounded on the stairs.

The receptionist appeared carrying two mugs.

“I thought you might want tea.”

“Thank you.”

She handed him one and looked around.

“I’ve worked here eight months. I didn’t know all this was up here.”

“Where did you think the clock was?”

“On the outside.”

He smiled, and she did too.

She watched him retrieve the loose pin.

“Is it expensive?”

“No.”

“Can you fix it?”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to?”

He turned the pin between his fingers.

“They don’t seem to mind if I don’t.”

She set her mug on the windowsill and peered through a gap beside the clock face.

“My bus stop’s down there,” she said. “I look up when I’m waiting.”

“You have a phone.”

“It’s usually in my bag.”

He took a small pair of pliers from his case.

“Could you hold this?”

She came over and steadied the inspection lamp while he worked. Her sleeve brushed the great brass wheel.

“Careful there,” he said. “It’ll move.”

***

When the clock started, she jumped.

The sound filled the chamber: one click, another, then the familiar sequence, uneven for a moment before settling.

Martin watched the repaired joint through several cycles.

The woman looked pleased.

“Should I tell someone?”

“Tell the man downstairs it’ll need a proper service before winter.”

“Will you do it?”

“If he asks.”

She nodded as though this were a perfectly workable arrangement.

They finished their tea. Martin packed his tools, leaving the lamp until last.

At the foot of the stairs, she asked his name.

“Martin.”

“I’m Leah.”

She wrote both names on a note beside her keyboard: his with a telephone number, hers beneath *clock service—October*. Then she gave him a sheet of paper for an invoice.

“He said no charge,” Martin told her.

“He says that about everything. Put down what it costs.”

***

Outside, Martin stopped across the road and looked up.

The minute hand advanced.

Below it, a boy was trying to persuade a reluctant dog past the butcher’s. Someone dropped a bag of oranges. Two people bent to help and bumped their heads.

Martin checked his watch against the clock.

Then he went home to Tuesday’s soup, carrying his empty flask and an apple Leah had insisted was real.

The town hired a man to listen to the bridge.

It was an old bridge, older than anyone’s grandmother, built from gray stone and a kind of confidence no longer available locally. It crossed a river that was usually shallow enough to embarrass a bridge, except in March, when the water rose and everyone remembered why their ancestors had bothered.

The man’s name was Ellis. He had no particular qualifications, but neither had the other applicants.

“What would you listen for?” the council asked.

“Changes,” he said.

This impressed them because it was both sensible and inexpensive.

They gave him a folding chair, a notebook, and a small brass badge that said MUNICIPAL LISTENER. Each morning he sat beneath the central arch. He listened to the river, the tires overhead, the tiny settling noises of stone. At noon he ate a cheese sandwich. At four he went home.

For the first three months, his reports were brief.

*Monday: Nothing unusual.*

*Tuesday: Nothing unusual.*

*Wednesday: A shopping cart passed downstream. Otherwise normal.*

The council was pleased. Here, finally, was a public service producing reassuring results.

Then, one Thursday, Ellis heard someone say his name.

Not loudly. Not mysteriously, either. It sounded like a person in another room who needed a jar opened.

“Ellis.”

He got up and walked around the arch.

Nobody.

He sat down.

“Ellis.”

He looked at the bridge.

“Yes?”

A truck passed overhead. Dust drifted from a seam in the stone.

“Your sandwich,” said the bridge. “There’s an ant.”

Ellis inspected his lunch. There was indeed an ant, negotiating the crust.

“Thank you.”

“Of course.”

He moved the ant to the grass.

That afternoon, his report read:

*Thursday: Minor insect activity.*

He did not consider this dishonest. The form had no section for conversations.

***

The bridge turned out to be interested in ordinary things.

It asked whether people still danced at weddings. It wanted to know what had happened to the horses. Ellis explained engines, badly, and the bridge listened with the politeness of someone who had already grasped the essentials.

“Explosions,” it said.

“Small ones.”

“And you sit beside them?”

“More or less.”

The bridge considered this.

“The horses must be relieved.”

Sometimes it asked about people Ellis did not know.

A woman with yellow gloves. A boy who had dropped a silver cup into the river. Two brothers who used to cross together and then, for many years, separately.

“I don’t remember their names,” the bridge said.

“Did you ever know them?”

“No.”

“Then you haven’t forgotten.”

The bridge was quiet for the rest of the morning.

Later it said, “That is a useful distinction.”

***

Ellis had been married once. His wife, Mara, had died four years before he became a municipal listener.

He did not tell the bridge immediately. It learned by asking why he always made two sandwiches and brought only one.

“I put the other in the refrigerator,” he said.

“For tomorrow?”

“Usually.”

“Does it keep?”

“Not especially.”

The river moved around a branch caught between two rocks.

After a while, Ellis said, “I know I could just make one.”

“I didn’t ask that,” said the bridge.

He liked it better after that.

***

In November, an engineer arrived wearing clean boots and carrying instruments in padded cases.

Ellis watched her attach sensors to the stone.

“Any unusual sounds?” she asked.

“Define unusual.”

“Cracking. Grinding. Sharp reports under load.”

“No sharp reports.”

She glanced at his notebook.

“What exactly do you write down?”

“Changes.”

She nodded, much as the council had.

For two days she measured, tapped, frowned, and entered numbers into a tablet. On the third day she sat beside Ellis beneath the arch.

“It needs work,” she said.

“How much?”

“A lot.”

“Will they do it?”

She looked up at the underside of the roadway.

“They might replace it.”

That evening, Ellis stayed after four.

“You heard?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Are you frightened?”

“I don’t know,” said the bridge. “What does frightened feel like?”

Ellis thought.

“Like trying to prepare for something by imagining it repeatedly.”

Water ticked against the stones.

“Then yes.”

***

The council held a public meeting.

People loved the bridge, provided loving it did not significantly affect taxes or traffic. They called it irreplaceable, then asked what a replacement would cost.

Ellis stood at the back with his badge pinned to his coat.

When public comments opened, he approached the microphone.

He had prepared a speech about memory. He had written phrases like *shared inheritance* and *the fabric of this community*. Reading it over, he had been embarrassed to find he sounded exactly like a man asking for money.

So he folded the paper.

“I spend every day under that bridge,” he said. “The engineer says it can be repaired.”

Someone asked how he could justify the expense.

“I can’t,” Ellis said. “I wouldn’t know how. But I’d like us to get an estimate before we decide.”

The council agreed to get an estimate.

It was a smaller victory than he had hoped for on his walk to the meeting, and a larger one than he had expected while waiting to speak.

***

The work began in April.

Ellis’s chair had to be moved beyond the safety barriers. He disliked the new spot; the bank sloped, and one of the chair’s feet sank into mud. Between machinery and running water, he could hear nothing from the arch.

He still came each morning.

One day the engineer brought him a flat piece of timber to put beneath the chair.

“Better?” she asked.

He tested it.

“Much.”

When she left, he opened his notebook. He recorded the delivery of stone, the weather, and a loose bolt he had noticed in the temporary fence.

Then he unwrapped his sandwich.

From somewhere beneath the scaffolding came a voice, faint but distinct.

“What have you got today?”

“Cheese.”

“Again?”

“It’s what I like.”

“Fair enough,” said the bridge.

The city hired a man to listen to the bridge.

Every morning, before traffic thickened, he descended a ladder bolted to the eastern pier and sat inside the steelwork with a thermos of coffee. He listened for a change in pitch, a new rattle, anything that might require an engineer.

His name was Emil. On municipal forms, his occupation was Acoustic Infrastructure Technician. His daughter told people he was a musician.

“What instrument?” they asked.

“The bridge.”

He had tried to correct her once, but she was seven and delighted by the idea, so he let it stand.

For nineteen years, the bridge said approximately the same thing.

In winter it rang. In summer it groaned. Rain produced a complicated ticking, and the first bus of the morning always made a loose plate tremble near the western shore.

Then, on a Tuesday in October, Emil heard three knocks.

He took the cup away from his mouth.

They came again.

Three measured blows, somewhere deep inside a sealed support.

He reported them. An engineer arrived at eleven, wearing white shoes that were unsuitable for the ladder.

“Thermal contraction,” she said.

“Possibly.”

“You disagree?”

“I’ve heard it contract.”

She arranged a scan anyway. The report found no structural defects.

The knocking returned the next morning.

This time, Emil knocked back.

He used the handle of his screwdriver. Three blows against a beam.

The answer came at once.

Two.

He sat very still.

Above him, thousands of people crossed the river, each carrying some urgent private thing: an apology, a sandwich, the suspicion of being unwell. A cyclist stopped to retie a shoelace. The river moved beneath them all.

Emil knocked once.

Once came back.

That evening he called his daughter.

She was twenty-six now and lived in a city where the bridges were newer.

“Dad,” she said, “are you getting enough sleep?”

“Yes.”

“Because last time you heard something strange, there was a pigeon in your kitchen.”

“That was different. I saw the pigeon.”

He asked whether she remembered telling people he played the bridge.

“No,” she said, then, “Wait. Yes. You were annoyed.”

“Not very.”

After they hung up, she sent him a photograph of her dinner. He enlarged it with two fingers. Some green vegetable he couldn’t identify. A blue plate he remembered buying her when she left home.

Over the following weeks, Emil developed a system.

One knock meant yes. Two meant no.

He asked whether someone was trapped.

Two.

Whether someone was injured.

Two.

Whether he should call for help.

A long silence.

Then two.

He bought a mechanic’s stethoscope and pressed it to the steel. Beneath the traffic noise he heard something like water moving through a pipe, though the plans showed no pipe there.

“Are you part of the bridge?” he asked.

One.

He did not report this.

Instead, he began bringing a second cup.

He knew it was foolish. He left it beside him anyway, filled with coffee that cooled untouched while he worked.

In November, the city announced the bridge would be replaced.

There were renderings. There were consultations. The new design included dedicated cycle lanes, improved flood clearance, and programmable lighting. Emil looked carefully through the proposal and could find little to object to.

He read the announcement aloud beneath the roadway.

“Did you know?”

One.

“Are you afraid?”

Two.

He was relieved, then oddly embarrassed by his relief.

The next morning, a question occurred to him.

“Have you been knocking all these years?”

One.

He put his thermos down.

“I’m sorry.”

There was no answer.

After that, he stayed longer. At first he tried to explain why he might have missed it: the traffic, his ear protection, the difficulty of distinguishing one sound among so many. Eventually he stopped explaining.

He told it about his daughter. About his wife, who had died nine years earlier. About the replacement washing machine, which made a noise during the spin cycle that he distrusted on professional grounds.

Sometimes it answered. Mostly it listened.

On his final morning, Emil brought no coffee.

The road above had been closed. Without traffic, the chamber sounded unfamiliar. He could hear his coat brushing the ladder, the little catch in his breathing.

He sat in his usual place.

“I don’t know what to ask,” he said.

A knock came from the support beside him.

Then another, farther away.

Then another.

The sound travelled westward, pausing at each span. Emil followed it as far as the maintenance walkway allowed. At the locked gate, he gripped the mesh and listened.

From the other side of the river came three faint blows.

He laughed once, startling himself.

Then he went back for his tools.

His daughter met him at the eastern end. She had driven through the night to be there. While he took off his hard hat, she looked at the barriers and the silent roadway.

“Did it say anything?”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t have to believe me.”

“I know.”

He handed her the hat while he fastened his bag.

They crossed by the old pedestrian ferry, restored for the duration of the works. Halfway over, his daughter moved closer to the window to photograph the bridge.

Emil stayed where he was, his palm resting on the worn wooden seat.

Under his hand, the ferry shuddered as its engine took the current.

He waited, listening.

The clock repair shop opened on a Tuesday, in a street that had never contained a clock repair shop before.

This was not, by itself, unusual. Streets change. A bakery becomes a pharmacy; a pharmacy becomes a place where people pay to break plates. But the shop occupied a space between two buildings that had previously shared a wall.

Its sign read:

**MINOR ADJUSTMENTS**

Beneath that, in smaller letters:

**No refunds on time already spent.**

Mara noticed it because she was late.

She was usually late by seven minutes. Not six, not eight. Seven minutes had become the small, persistent debt she owed the world. Her friends had learned to account for it. Her employer had stopped making jokes.

In the window stood a single clock with no hands.

She went inside.

A man sat behind a desk, peeling an orange in one continuous ribbon. He wore a green waistcoat and the expression of someone who had heard every possible complaint about Tuesdays.

“My watch is slow,” Mara said.

“Is it?”

She checked her phone.

“No. Apparently not.”

“Then we’ve saved you some money.”

She should have left. Instead, she looked around. Shelves covered the walls, holding kitchen timers, carriage clocks, cheap plastic alarm clocks, and a grandfather clock small enough to fit in a coat pocket.

“What do you repair?”

“Mostly misunderstandings.”

“About clocks?”

“People rarely bring me clocks.”

He offered her a piece of orange. She declined.

“I’m always seven minutes late,” she said.

“Yes,” he replied, as though she had finally given him her name.

He opened a ledger.

“When did it start?”

“I don’t know. Years ago.”

“Most people say that. Think of the first person who minded.”

“My mother.”

“And did she?”

Mara looked at the handless clock in the window.

Her mother had minded lateness intensely. She had believed that arriving on time was a form of good manners available even to people who could afford nothing else.

“Appointments are promises,” she used to say.

Now she lived in a room overlooking a car park. Some days she knew Mara. Some days she called her by the name of a woman who had died before Mara was born.

“The first person,” the man repeated gently.

Mara sat down.

There had been a school concert. She was nine. Her mother had promised to come, but the chair beside Mara’s father remained empty.

Afterward, her mother arrived smelling of rain and hospital soap. She was a nurse then, always being asked to stay, always saying yes.

“Only seven minutes,” her father had said in the car.

Mara remembered the remark because it was untrue. Her mother had missed the whole concert.

She had been seven minutes late for the end.

“That’s ridiculous,” Mara said.

The man finished peeling the orange.

“Quite possibly.”

“You’re saying I’ve been late for thirty years because of a concert?”

“I haven’t said anything of the sort. You asked what I repair.”

Outside, a bus passed through a puddle. Water struck the window, then ran down the glass.

“Can you fix it?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Seven minutes.”

“I don’t understand.”

“I’ll need you to spend them somewhere.”

He took a brass timer from the shelf. It was shaped like an egg and warm when he placed it in her palm.

“Wind it when you get there.”

“Where?”

But someone had come in behind her, carrying a calendar wrapped in a towel. The man rose to help.

***

Her mother was watching a nature documentary with the sound off.

A fox moved through snow.

“You’re late,” her mother said.

Mara checked the time. Seven minutes past three.

“I know.”

Her mother turned back to the screen.

Usually, Mara filled these visits. She brought biscuits, sorted laundry, asked about lunch, adjusted the flowers. She narrated the weather and the traffic. When conversation failed, she spoke more quickly.

Today she sat.

“What have you got?” her mother asked.

“A timer.”

“Are we cooking something?”

“No.”

“Good. I’ve just eaten.”

Mara wound the brass egg.

For the first minute, she worried that she was wasting the visit.

For the second, she studied her mother’s hands. The swollen knuckles, the wedding ring, the tiny blue mark where a pencil had pierced her skin as a child.

During the third minute, her mother said, “You look tired.”

“A little.”

“You should sit down.”

“I am sitting down.”

“Oh. Yes.”

In the fourth minute, Mara wanted to ask about the concert. She could describe the hall, the borrowed white blouse, the song whose second verse she still remembered.

But her mother was watching the fox.

During the fifth minute, her mother reached for her hand.

Her grip was unexpectedly firm.

In the sixth, Mara began to cry.

Her mother glanced over, concerned but not alarmed.

“Did something happen?”

“Not today.”

“Well,” her mother said, and rubbed her thumb across Mara’s fingers.

The timer rang.

“Oh, switch that off,” her mother said.

Mara did.

Neither let go.

***

The shop was gone when she returned.

Between the pharmacy and the dry cleaner stood an unbroken wall, stained by an old drainpipe. Mara knocked once, feeling foolish.

Nothing happened.

She kept the brass timer on her kitchen table.

She still ran late sometimes. The bus failed to come; she misplaced her keys. Once she simply did not want to go to dinner and took too long admitting it.

But when she visited her mother, she stopped checking the clock.

Sometimes they talked. Sometimes Mara folded laundry while her mother slept.

Once, arriving early, she stood outside the room and heard her mother singing. It was a song Mara knew, though she hadn’t heard it in years.

She waited in the doorway until the verse was finished.
