The city opened a lost-and-found for things that were not objects.

It began as a clerical mistake. A woman filling out a municipal form wrote that she had lost her patience on the number 14 bus. The clerk, who had been instructed to reject no claim without review, assigned it a tracking number.

Three days later, someone brought in a small, warm parcel wrapped in a transit map.

“Found this under a seat,” he said. “Thought it might belong to somebody.”

Inside was the woman’s patience.

She recognized it immediately. It was thinner than she remembered.

After that, the city found a basement, hired two people, and printed some leaflets.

***

Mara took the evening shift because she had trouble sleeping and because the work required no references. Her previous employer had described her as insufficiently enthusiastic about growth.

“What kind of growth?” the interviewer asked.

“Quarterly.”

He nodded and gave her a ring of keys.

The basement smelled of wet wool. There were shelves for convictions, drawers for missed opportunities, and a refrigerated cabinet for things people had said in anger but still meant.

Youth arrived occasionally, though usually it was somebody’s idea of youth rather than the actual thing. Mara learned to tell the difference. The idea was loud and smelled of expensive soap. The real thing was awkward, hungry, and worried about its skin.

Mostly, people brought in small losses.

A retired mechanic recovered his ability to enjoy Sundays. A teenager claimed a laugh she had stopped using after someone imitated it. A man collected the feeling that his brother would call, then returned it a week later without explanation.

Mara did not ask questions unless the paperwork required them.

“Approximate date of loss?”

“Would you recognize it if shown?”

“Did you look for it anywhere else?”

That last question upset people more than she expected.

***

One Thursday, a boy arrived carrying nothing.

“I found a way home,” he said.

Mara looked up from an inventory of misplaced confidence.

“Whose?”

“I don’t know.”

“Where did you find it?”

“Behind the supermarket. Near the bins.”

He held out his hands. Between them was a narrow strip of afternoon: pavement, a low wall, somebody cooking onions. A dog barked beyond the edge.

Mara fetched a tray.

The boy laid the way home down carefully. It extended itself a little, revealing a gate with peeling green paint.

“Will someone come for it?”

“We’ll put it in the system.”

“What if they don’t know it’s gone?”

Mara had no procedural answer.

“We keep things for a long time,” she said.

After he left, she moved the tray away from the fluorescent light.

***

Most items grew quieter in storage.

Certainty softened. Old ambitions stopped scratching at their boxes. A grudge left beside a radiator became, over several months, an account of what had happened.

But the way home grew.

By December, its pavement reached the edge of the tray. By January, there was rain in it, though the basement remained dry. Mara could hear a radio through an open window.

She entered updates in the database.

*Additional identifying feature: kitchen radio.*

*Additional identifying feature: loose paving stone.*

*Additional identifying feature: voice calling from another room.*

She never wrote down what the voice said.

***

Her father had been dead for eleven years.

When people asked, she said they had not been close. This was accurate in the way that saying a house had no roof was accurate. It did not describe what happened when it rained.

He had repaired bicycles in the kitchen. He had kept screws in jam jars and money in books he disliked, confident nobody would open them. He had been capable of remarkable gentleness toward broken machinery.

Their last conversation concerned a ladder.

She had lent it to a neighbor. He said she should have asked. She said he treated every object as if it had greater rights than she did.

Neither had apologized.

The neighbor still had the ladder.

***

In February, Mara took the tray off the shelf.

She set it on the floor and watched the little road settle against the concrete. At its far end, the green gate shifted in the wind.

She recognized the broken latch.

Recognition should have arrived sooner. She understood that now. She had been cataloguing the evidence of a place she did not want to identify.

The radio played a song her father used to interrupt by whistling the wrong notes.

Then his voice came from the kitchen.

“Mara? Hold this a minute.”

She stood so quickly that her chair fell over.

There he was, beyond the gate, beyond the window. Not visible. Busy with something. Assuming she was nearby.

She put one foot on the pavement.

It held.

For a moment she smelled bicycle grease, onions, the damp cloth left beside the sink.

Then she stepped back.

The road remained.

***

In the morning, her coworker found her sitting beside the tray.

“Are you claiming that?”

“I don’t know.”

He hung up his coat.

“You can take it home while you decide.”

“Is that allowed?”

He considered the shelves, the drawers, the forms awaiting signatures.

“I think we made most of this up.”

Mara laughed.

They found a shallow cardboard box and packed towels around the tray. Her coworker held the door while she carried it upstairs.

Outside, the city was beginning its ordinary work.

At the bus stop, Mara shifted the box against her hip and took out her phone.

She still had the neighbor’s number.

She typed, *Hello. This is Mara. Do you happen to have my father’s ladder?*

Then she waited, holding the road level.

The city employed one person to look after the things nobody had named.

It was a modest position. The salary arrived on time, the office had a window, and there was no uniform beyond a pair of soft-soled shoes. The shoes were important. Some of the things were easily startled.

Every morning, Mara unlocked the office beneath the eastern bridge and checked the overnight deliveries.

Usually there were three or four.

The feeling of recognizing someone from behind and realizing, before they turned, that you were wrong.

The particular silence left in a kitchen after a refrigerator stops humming.

A small, persistent hope attached to an otherwise unremarkable Thursday.

These arrived in different containers. Feelings generally came in brown envelopes, silences in padded boxes. Hopes had to be weighed down with something. Once, someone had sent one in a biscuit tin with a brick on top.

Mara’s job was not to name them.

That was stated clearly in her contract.

**Items are to be preserved in their original condition. Classification must not constitute definition.**

She sorted them by the effect they had on the office.

Things that made the window seem farther away went on the upper shelves. Things that made her remember water went in the blue cabinet. Anything that caused the room to feel as though someone had just left it was stored near the radiator.

She had been doing this for nineteen years.

Then, on a Tuesday, a boy arrived carrying nothing.

He stood in the doorway with his hands held carefully apart.

“I’ve brought something,” he said.

“I can see that,” Mara said, although she couldn’t.

“Where should I put it?”

“Let’s find out.”

She cleared a space on her desk. The boy lowered his hands.

Nothing changed.

Outside, a bus crossed the bridge. A loose screw in the window frame gave its usual little rattle.

“How long have you had it?” Mara asked.

“Since Sunday.”

“Did you find it somewhere?”

The boy nodded.

“At my granddad’s.”

“Was it his?”

“I don’t know.”

Mara took out an intake form. There were boxes for approximate size, preferred light, and whether the item had been known to recur.

“What happened on Sunday?”

“We were making a birdhouse.”

She waited.

“He let me use the drill. Then we had lunch. Then he fell asleep in his chair.”

The boy looked at the empty place on the desk.

“He’s not dead,” he said quickly.

“All right.”

“People keep thinking that when I tell it.”

“What happened after he fell asleep?”

“Nothing. I was waiting for him to wake up.”

Mara put down her pen.

“And while you were waiting?”

The boy frowned with the effort of being exact.

“I looked at his hands.”

The office grew very quiet. The refrigerator in the adjoining kitchenette continued to hum, but Mara could no longer hear the traffic overhead.

“His hands were just there,” the boy said. “On the chair. And I thought about how he’d been a boy too. And somebody must have taught him the drill. Or something before drills.”

“Yes.”

“And I didn’t like it.”

Mara nodded.

“But I did like it.”

She opened a drawer and took out a shallow wooden tray lined with green felt.

“Try this.”

The boy lifted the thing from the desk. This time Mara saw the slightest resistance in his wrists, as if he were raising something out of water.

He set it in the tray.

A knot in the wood darkened.

“Is it dangerous?” he asked.

“No.”

“Will he be all right?”

“I don’t know.”

The boy rubbed one thumb along the other. Mara let him.

At last he asked, “Can I visit it?”

“Of course.”

After he left, she carried the tray through the storeroom.

It did not belong on the upper shelves. The window remained precisely where it was. The blue cabinet wouldn’t close with the tray inside, though there was ample room.

Near the radiator, the thing became so heavy she had to sit down.

She rested the tray on her knees.

She thought of her mother peeling an orange in one long spiral. She had not remembered that in years: the orange turning, the peel lengthening, her own impatience to be handed a piece.

Mara stayed there until the radiator cooled.

Then she made room on her desk.

The boy returned the following Saturday.

They examined the tray together. Neither could see anything, but he seemed satisfied.

“We finished the birdhouse,” he said.

“Did you put it up?”

“He says we picked the wrong tree. We’re moving it tomorrow.”

He reached toward the tray, then stopped.

“Can I take it back?”

“It’s yours.”

“I thought you had to keep things here.”

“Only until someone comes for them.”

She found a box wide enough for the tray and packed it with tissue. The boy held it against his chest while she opened the door.

“Keep it level on the stairs,” she said.

That evening, Mara called her mother.

They talked about the price of oranges, the repairs to the bridge, a neighbor’s unreasonable dog. For a while, her mother put the phone down to look for a receipt.

Mara waited.

She could hear drawers opening at the other end.

The last repair shop in the city had a sign that read:

**WE FIX THINGS THAT STILL MATTER.**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**YOU DECIDE.**

People brought in the usual things at first. Lamps. Watches. A toaster that burned a small, precise cathedral into every slice of bread.

Then someone brought a snow globe with no snow.

“It used to have a little house,” the woman said.

“What happened to it?”

“I don’t remember.”

The repairman held the globe up to the window. Inside, the water was perfectly clear.

“Leave it with me.”

He was not a magician. This is important. He had a soldering iron, three kinds of glue, and knees that hurt when it rained. His name was Emil. He ate lunch out of the same blue container every day, though the food inside varied according to his optimism.

He opened the snow globe carefully. He cleaned it. From a scrap of cedar, he carved a house small enough to disappear beneath his thumbnail. He painted the door green.

When the woman returned, she looked at it for a long time.

“That wasn’t the house,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“No,” she said. “This one is nice.”

She took it home.

After that, the requests changed.

A man brought a cassette tape labeled SUMMER, although the case was empty.

A child brought a stone split neatly in two.

“What happened?” Emil asked.

“I wanted to see inside.”

“And now?”

The child arranged the halves on the counter.

“Now I have.”

Emil glued the stone back together. He showed the child how to hold it up to the light so the seam was visible.

“Will it break again?”

“Possibly.”

The child considered this, then paid him with a button and a piece of wrapped candy that had become part of its wrapper.

Emil put the button in the till.

Across the street, a new building rose. Its windows did not open. On the ground floor, a bright showroom sold household objects designed to be replaced before they could grow familiar.

One afternoon, a young woman from the showroom came into the repair shop carrying a kettle.

“Don’t tell anyone,” she said.

The handle was loose.

Emil tightened it.

“How much?”

“Nothing. It was a screw.”

“I should buy a new one, shouldn’t I?”

He filled the kettle at the sink, plugged it in, and waited. They listened to the water gathering itself toward a boil.

“There,” he said.

She laughed, though he had not meant to be funny.

Winter arrived. Emil put a little electric heater beneath the workbench. Customers began staying longer than their repairs required.

One Tuesday, nobody brought anything broken.

They came anyway.

The woman with the snow globe brought oranges. The child brought another stone, this one intact, and asked Emil to keep it that way. The young woman from the showroom brought paper cups.

Emil looked around his crowded shop.

“I have work to do,” he said.

“We know,” said the woman with the oranges.

So he worked.

He replaced the spring in a music box. He cleaned the contacts of a radio. He persuaded a stubborn drawer to travel the last half inch home.

Around him, people talked. Someone complained about the weather. Someone else said the city had been colder when she was young. The child, sitting on the floor, sorted loose washers into families.

At five, Emil turned the sign to CLOSED.

Nobody noticed.

He could have asked them to leave. Instead, he went upstairs to his apartment and returned with another chair.

Years later, when the shop was gone, people disagreed about what had become of it.

Some remembered a rent increase. Others said Emil had retired to the coast. The child, grown tall by then, insisted there had been a farewell party, although nobody could recall who had attended.

The showroom across the street became a pharmacy, then a place that sold expensive bowls.

For a while, nothing marked the repair shop except four holes in the brick where the sign had been.

Then someone put a bench beneath them.

It was secondhand. One leg was shorter than the others. If you sat at the wrong end, it rocked.

The following morning, a small wedge of cedar appeared beneath the short leg.

Nobody saw who put it there.

It held.

The Office of Unfinished Things occupied the second floor above a bakery, which meant that every unresolved matter in the town smelled faintly of bread.

People came carrying what they could.

A woman brought a blue sweater with one sleeve. A boy brought a letter addressed to his father, who lived three streets away but might as well have lived underwater. An old musician arrived with the first seven notes of a song, humming them into his cupped hands.

Mara, the clerk, received each item without comment.

“Will you finish it?” people always asked.

“No,” she said. “We keep it safe until you can.”

This disappointed almost everyone.

There were other offices, people said, in larger towns, where trained professionals would finish things for you. They would write the last chapter, make the apology, decide whether to stay. Some even claimed there was a man in the capital who could end a grief in an afternoon.

Mara gave these stories the attention she gave the weather: enough to know what people were bringing in with them.

Then she opened a drawer.

***

The office had more drawers than its dimensions reasonably allowed.

There were narrow drawers for interrupted sentences and deep ones for abandoned studies. A cedar cabinet held friendships that had stopped not with a quarrel but with the words *We should do this again soon.*

Plans for gardens occupied the sunny wall.

Promises required careful handling. Mara wrapped them in plain paper and tied them loosely. A promise bound too tightly could become an obligation, which was heavier and much harder to store.

Every evening, she checked the labels.

Every morning, something had moved.

The unfinished song once turned up among the letters. A half-built cradle spent a week beside a plan to sail around the world. Mara suspected that unfinished things sought company according to principles she had not yet understood.

She put them back, though sometimes she waited a day.

***

One Thursday, a man arrived carrying nothing.

This was not unusual. Some of the largest deposits were invisible.

“What would you like to leave?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

She slid the intake form across the counter.

“Start with your name.”

He wrote *Elias* in a hand so careful it seemed he was copying someone else’s handwriting.

“And the nature of the item?”

He looked toward the window. Across the street, a workman was painting a door yellow.

“I was going to be different,” he said.

Mara waited.

“When I was young. Not famous. Nothing like that. I just had some ideas about the kind of person I would become.”

“Which ideas?”

“I thought I’d have people over.”

She glanced at him.

“For dinner,” he said. “I used to notice things in shops. A big table. Plates that didn’t match. I thought I’d learn to cook a few things well.”

“Do you cook?”

“A little.”

“And do people come?”

He shook his head.

Mara brought out a small wooden box.

“Will it fit?” he asked.

“We’ll see.”

He rested his hands on either side of it. For a moment, she thought he would change his mind. Then his shoulders lowered.

The box made a quiet sound, like a chair being pulled away from a table.

“Can I get it back?”

“Yes.”

“What if it’s too late?”

“The office doesn’t determine that.”

For the first time, he smiled.

***

Mara herself had never made a deposit.

She considered this professional discipline.

At home she kept a suitcase beneath her bed. Inside were a map, a pair of walking shoes, and a photograph of her sister standing beside the sea.

On the back, her sister had written:

*Come in September. The water is still warm.*

There had been several Septembers since then.

First their mother had needed help. Then the bakery’s roof had leaked into the office. Then a September arrived when nothing much was wrong, but Mara had not bought a ticket, and by the time she called, her sister had made other plans.

They still spoke on Sundays. The invitation had not been withdrawn. It simply wasn’t mentioned anymore.

***

In November, the baker downstairs died.

For three days the building smelled of nothing.

Mara had not known how much she depended on the ovens starting before dawn, the trays striking the counter, the baker shouting up the stairs whenever a parcel arrived for her.

His daughter came to open the shop on Monday. She burned the first batch of rolls.

Mara went downstairs.

“I don’t know what I’m doing,” the daughter said.

“Neither did he, at first.”

“Did you know him then?”

“No.”

The daughter laughed, unwillingly, and wiped her face on her apron.

They ate two of the burned rolls standing at the counter. Inside, they were still good.

***

That afternoon, Mara took her suitcase to the office.

She set it beside the intake desk and looked for the right drawer. Travel plans belonged along the west wall, but none of those drawers would accommodate the case.

She could remove the contents, of course.

Instead, she opened it on the floor and tried on the walking shoes.

They were stiff. She walked between the cabinets, past the cradle and the garden plans, until the leather began to warm.

Then she telephoned her sister.

“Would December be inconvenient?”

“For what?”

“A visit.”

Her sister was quiet long enough that Mara sat down.

“The water will be freezing,” she said at last.

“I know.”

“How long can you stay?”

***

Before closing, Mara pinned a notice to the door announcing that the office would be shut for one week.

Elias was coming up the stairs as she finished.

“I’d like my box,” he said.

She fetched it without asking why. But he told her anyway: he had invited his neighbor to supper. He was making soup.

Mara handed him the box.

“Is that enough?” he asked.

“You’ll probably want bread.”

He looked downstairs, where the bakery lights were still on.

“Yes,” he said. “I will.”

samples.result:
The town hired a man to wind the clock after the clock had stopped needing winding.

This was not an oversight. The council knew perfectly well that the new mechanism was electric. They had approved the expense, argued about the expense, and eventually hidden the expense under “pedestrian improvements,” because everyone agreed that pedestrians benefited from knowing the time.

But Arthur had wound the old mechanism every Thursday for thirty-one years, and nobody wanted to tell him.

So each Thursday he climbed the tower carrying his brass key.

At the top, he opened the little door in the casing, put the key into a hole that no longer connected to anything, and turned it twelve times. Then he sat on the wooden stool beside the window and ate an orange.

Below him, the town went about its business.

There was the florist putting buckets on the pavement. There was a bus performing its difficult turn. There was a boy who walked to school looking backward, as though expecting something interesting to arrive just behind him.

Arthur watched them all.

He knew the clock was electric.

He had helped install it.

***

For a while, the arrangement embarrassed him. He considered resigning. He wrote a letter on the back of a gas bill, then copied it onto clean paper.

*Dear Council Members,*

*In light of the recent improvements—*

He disliked “in light of.” It sounded like someone explaining why a swimming pool had closed.

He tried again.

*As my services are no longer—*

That was worse.

He put the letter in a drawer.

The following Thursday, he climbed the tower.

Halfway up, on the forty-third step, he found a small blue glove.

At the top, he saw that the florist had not put out her buckets.

He ate his orange and thought about these things.

On his way home, he returned the glove to the school and stopped at the flower shop. The florist, whose name was Lena, had hurt her shoulder moving a sack of compost.

Arthur carried out the buckets.

“You’re early,” she said.

“The clock’s fast.”

“Is it?”

“No.”

She laughed, and he found himself pleased out of proportion to the joke.

***

After that, he began to notice more.

The loose slate on the bakery roof. The delivery van that blocked the crossing every Thursday at nine. The old woman in the green coat who came to the square with an envelope, sat beside the postbox for an hour, and took the envelope home again.

Some things he mentioned. Some he left alone.

He told the baker about the slate.

He asked the delivery driver to move six feet forward.

He did not ask the woman about the letter.

Instead, when winter came, he brushed the snow from her end of the bench.

His employment continued to appear in the council accounts as “clock maintenance.”

***

In March, a new council clerk discovered the arrangement.

She was twenty-six, wore excellent boots, and believed that most institutional problems could be solved by finding the correct spreadsheet.

She invited Arthur into her office.

“I’m trying to understand your duties,” she said.

“Of course.”

“You wind the clock.”

“Yes.”

“Which is electric.”

“Yes.”

She set down her pen.

For the first time, Arthur felt sorry for someone who was about to dismiss him.

“I do have the key,” he offered.

“That isn’t quite the same as having a function.”

“No,” he said. “I suppose it isn’t.”

Outside her window, two men were attempting to carry a sofa through the door of the tax office. Neither seemed willing to be the one who walked backward.

The clerk followed his gaze.

“That’s been going on for twenty minutes,” she said.

“They’ll need to take the feet off.”

“I told them that.”

“Ah.”

They watched a little longer.

“What do you actually do up there?” she asked.

Arthur considered telling her about the buckets, the slate, the bench. But listed aloud, they seemed either too little to mention or too grand a claim.

“I look out,” he said.

***

The following Thursday, she came with him.

She was breathing hard by the forty-third step but refused his offer to stop.

At the top, Arthur performed the twelve unnecessary turns. He was acutely conscious of how long they took.

Then he gave her the stool.

From the street, the square was a place to cross. From the tower, it was possible to see where everyone was trying to go.

The bus arrived. The florist opened. A man stopped to tie his shoe, forcing three people to change direction around him.

Arthur took an orange from his pocket.

“Do you always bring one?” the clerk asked.

“Yes.”

He began peeling it, catching the pieces of skin in his hand.

Below, the boy who walked backward came into the square. A smaller child was hurrying after him, dragging a schoolbag by one strap.

“Oh,” Arthur said.

“What?”

“Nothing. I’d wondered.”

He split the orange and offered her half.

She took it.

***

The clerk changed the entry in the accounts.

The next Thursday, Arthur found a carbon copy waiting beneath the tower door.

*Clock inspection and observation of the square: one hour weekly.*

He folded it into his coat pocket and began the climb.

On the forty-third step, he stopped to get his breath. Then he went on.

The city hired a man to remove the weeds from its clocks.

Nobody remembered when the weeds had started growing. At first, a little grass appeared between the numerals of the station clock. Then dandelions opened in the courthouse dial, and a vine wound itself around the minute hand above the public library.

The clocks still worked, mostly. But the library began losing seven minutes a day, and people were arriving late to things with books in their hands.

The man’s name was Emil. His previous job had involved actual gardens. He accepted the position because the pay was better and because, at fifty-eight, he was tired of kneeling.

He had not considered the ladders.

Every morning, he wheeled a cart through the city. Inside were pruning shears, a trowel, several soft brushes, and a flask of tea. At the station, he climbed thirty feet and pulled chickweed from the space between eleven and twelve. At the courthouse, he clipped the dandelions before they could seed.

The work was pleasant in ways he hadn’t expected. Up close, the clocks made small, companionable noises. From the pavement they appeared stern and absolute, but behind their faces they were full of hesitations: clicks, catches, the faint scrape of something trying its best.

In his third week, he found a strawberry growing at half past four.

He ate it.

This was against regulations, probably, though no regulations had yet been written.

It tasted warm, despite the cold morning.

That afternoon, he remembered the name of a dog his family had owned when he was six.

“Biscuit,” he said aloud on the bus.

The woman beside him moved her shopping bag.

Soon there were raspberries on the post office clock and a pear no larger than his thumb on the tower beside the river. Emil put the pear in his pocket. By lunchtime it was ripe.

After eating it, he remembered his mother teaching him to whistle. They had stood at the kitchen window, neither of them succeeding. He had forgotten that she couldn’t whistle either.

He began keeping a notebook.

**Station: chickweed, no apparent effect.**

**Courthouse: dandelion. Bitter. Remembered blue bicycle.**

**Library: mint. Remembered argument with Daniel. Would prefer not to repeat.**

He did not write down the argument.

Daniel was his brother. They hadn’t spoken in eleven years, although Emil sometimes composed brief, reasonable speeches to him while washing dishes.

The mint brought back something inconvenient: Daniel had been crying before Emil arrived. In all Emil’s subsequent versions of the afternoon, his brother had merely been angry.

He closed the notebook.

By summer, the clocks were becoming difficult to manage.

Roots pressed against gears. Bees gathered around the hospital tower. A sunflower emerged from the face of the municipal clock and turned, all day, away from the time.

People complained.

The city gave Emil an assistant, a young woman named Noor, who had studied mechanical engineering and needed rent money.

“Why don’t we seal them?” she asked.

“With what?”

“Something plants can’t grow through.”

Emil gestured toward a birch sapling coming out of a drainpipe.

Noor considered it.

“Fair enough.”

She was better at the ladders. Emil was better at persuading roots to let go.

They worked together for six weeks before she caught him eating a blackberry from the fire station clock.

“Are those safe?”

“So far.”

She held out her hand.

An hour later, sitting on the curb, she said, “I remembered my father without his beard.”

Emil poured her some tea.

“I’d forgotten he ever looked like that.”

“Yes,” Emil said.

They sat until the tea was gone.

In September, an inspector came. He wore a white helmet on the pavement and asked whether the vegetation posed a structural risk.

“Eventually,” Noor said.

“Can it be eradicated?”

“Probably.”

Emil looked at her.

The inspector made a note.

That evening, Emil telephoned Daniel.

When his brother answered, Emil discovered that none of his reasonable speeches contained an opening sentence.

“Hello?” Daniel said again.

“It’s me.”

“I know.”

Outside Emil’s kitchen window, rain struck the fire escape.

“I’ve been doing a strange job,” Emil said.

After a moment, Daniel asked, “Strange how?”

They spoke for nine minutes. Emil knew because he watched the kitchen clock. When they hung up, he left the dishes where they were and sat down.

The city eventually replaced the old clock faces with sealed units. Emil helped remove the roots; Noor supervised the installation. The clocks kept excellent time afterward.

On the last day, Emil found a small green tomato behind the courthouse dial. He carried it home in his lunch tin and set it on the kitchen windowsill.

Daniel was coming on Sunday.

By Saturday, the tomato had turned red. Emil picked it up, then put it back beside the salt. He would slice it in half when his brother arrived.

The city hired a man to remove the names from benches.

Not the plaques. Those stayed: small brass rectangles polished by weather, each with four empty screw holes where another life might eventually be attached. His job was only the names.

He carried a battery-powered grinder and a folded towel. He worked early, before the dog walkers, because people disliked the noise and sometimes asked questions.

The first bench belonged to Miriam Vale, who had loved this view.

He looked at the view. A pond, mostly. Three ducks. Beyond it, the back wall of a supermarket.

He ground away MIRIAM VALE.

The second bench belonged to Arthur and Jean, together always.

That took longer.

By eleven, he had finished six benches and eaten a sandwich. He brushed the crumbs from his trousers into his hand, then carried them to a bin. Feeding the birds was prohibited.

His name was Daniel. No one had asked for it all morning.

*

The work order said renewal initiative.

His supervisor had explained that the memorial leases had expired. Families could renew them, but many letters came back unopened. Some of the benches were older than Daniel. Some of the people who had paid for the plaques now needed plaques themselves.

“What if somebody asks?” Daniel had said.

“Tell them they can contact the office.”

“What if they’re upset?”

“Give them the number.”

He had written the number on the inside of his glove.

*

On Thursday, a woman arrived while he was working.

She wore a yellow raincoat although the weather was clear, and she carried a paper bag darkened at the bottom by grease.

“You’ve missed a bit,” she said.

Daniel stopped the grinder.

A shallow groove remained near the edge of the plaque. Part of a W.

“I haven’t finished.”

“Whose was it?”

He consulted the sheet clipped to his toolbox.

“Walter Bell.”

“Oh,” she said. “Walter.”

“Did you know him?”

“No.”

She sat on the far end of the bench. Daniel waited for her to move.

“Do you need the whole thing?” she asked.

“Not exactly. But there’s dust.”

She opened the bag.

“Chips?”

He looked at her, then at the bag.

“They’re still warm.”

He took one.

For a while they sat without speaking. Across the path, a child was trying to persuade a small dog to climb onto a much larger dog.

“Would you remember it?” the woman asked.

“What?”

“Walter Bell. If you didn’t have the paper.”

“I don’t know.”

She folded down the top of the bag and left it between them.

*

That evening Daniel bought a notebook.

On the first page he wrote:

Miriam Vale  
Arthur and Jean  
Walter Bell

He could remember three of the other names. For the rest, he took the work orders out of his van.

He did not copy the dates or the inscriptions. The names were what he had been told to remove, so the names were what he kept.

There were fourteen by the end of the week.

He put the notebook in his kitchen drawer, under the takeaway menus.

*

In November, his supervisor noticed.

“What’s that?”

“Notebook.”

“I can see that.”

Daniel closed it.

“Are you keeping records?”

“Just the names.”

“Why?”

He had no answer ready. He wished the woman in the raincoat had been there. She might have explained it, or at least offered his supervisor a chip.

“I don’t use them for anything,” he said.

His supervisor sighed.

“Make sure it doesn’t slow you down.”

*

Winter came. The grinder batteries drained faster in the cold.

Some plaques were too deeply engraved to smooth without ruining them. Daniel removed those whole and fitted blank replacements. He wrapped the old ones in his towel so their corners wouldn’t scratch the tools.

By February he had a box of them in the van.

He asked at the depot where they should go.

“Metal recycling,” the stores manager said.

Daniel carried the box home.

His kitchen drawer no longer closed properly. He moved the notebook to the shelf above the kettle and put the plaques in the cupboard beneath the sink. Whenever he needed washing-up liquid, he had to shift Walter Bell.

*

In March, the woman in the yellow raincoat returned.

Daniel was kneeling beside a bench dedicated to a man who had apparently loved three things: his family, cricket, and this park, in that order.

“You’re still at it,” she said.

“Another month.”

“And then?”

“Fences, probably.”

She sat down.

After a moment he told her about the notebook and the box.

“Does anybody ever ask for them?” she said.

“They don’t know I’ve got them.”

“You could tell the office.”

He shook his head.

“Yes,” she said. “They might make you stop.”

He loosened the last screw. She held out her hands, and he passed her the plaque.

It was heavier than she expected.

*

They put up one notice on the library board.

**OLD MEMORIAL PLAQUES**

**Some plaques removed from park benches are available to families. Please ask at the desk.**

The librarian agreed to keep the box for a month. Daniel left his number.

Only one person called.

She was looking for her grandmother, Miriam Vale.

“I thought it would be there forever,” she said.

Daniel told her he was sorry.

“No, I should have answered the letter.”

He brought the plaque to the library on Saturday. There were grinding marks across it, and almost nothing of the name remained.

The woman ran her thumb over the brass.

“I can still see the M.”

Daniel couldn’t, but he let her show him.

She wrapped it in a scarf before putting it in her bag. Then she asked which bench it had been.

He drew her a little map on the back of an overdue notice.

“Facing the pond,” he said.

“Yes,” she said. “That sounds right.”

The first thing the sea returned was a blue plastic chair.

It arrived on a Tuesday, upright in the shallows, as if someone had just stepped away to fetch a drink.

Mara watched it from the seawall. She had come down to eat her lunch where nobody would ask how she was managing. An egg sandwich, an apple, tea in a flask with a lid that always leaked. The chair rocked gently.

At low tide she went out and brought it home.

There was nothing mysterious about a chair washing ashore. She reminded herself of this while scrubbing tiny shells from its legs. People lost things from boats. Storms took things from gardens. The world was full of unsecured furniture.

She put it in the kitchen.

The next morning, the sea returned a bicycle.

Not hers. Hers had been green, with a basket that leaned to the left. This one was red and much too small. She left it beside the public steps. By noon it was gone.

On Thursday there were seventeen oranges.

On Friday, a door.

People began to gather.

The door lay flat on the sand, its brass knocker bright and dry. A man from the council said it was a navigational hazard, though it was nowhere near the water. Two teenagers carried it up the beach and propped it against the shelter.

Someone knocked.

Everyone laughed, except the person who had knocked.

Nothing happened.

By Sunday, the beach was crowded.

The sea returned a wedding veil, three unopened tins of peaches, a wooden leg, and a piano stool. Each object arrived alone. A wave would break, spread its white fingers over the sand, and withdraw, leaving something behind.

The local paper called it a phenomenon. The national papers called it a mystery. A professor explained currents on television while standing beside the wooden leg.

Mara stopped going down at lunchtime.

She knew what people were beginning to hope.

At the grocer’s, Mrs. Vale bought two bottles of her husband’s favorite beer. He had been dead eleven years.

A little boy waited with a dog lead.

The man who ran the amusement arcade came to the beach in a suit.

Nobody spoke about these preparations. They discussed tides, weather, the possibility of a wreck somewhere beyond the headland.

On Monday, the sea returned a yellow mitten.

Mara saw it on the news while washing a plate. She turned off the television with wet hands.

Her son’s mitten had been yellow.

So had thousands of mittens. There were factories that made nothing else.

She finished the plate. She washed the cup beside it, though it was clean.

At four in the morning, she went to the beach.

Others were already there, spaced along the seawall with blankets and flasks. They made room without looking at her.

For a long time, nothing arrived.

Then a wave brought in a teaspoon.

A woman near the steps began to cry. Her companion put an arm around her, and the woman shook it off.

When daylight came, Mara walked home. On the kitchen floor, beneath the blue chair, lay a small heap of sand she had somehow missed.

She sat down.

For seven years she had kept her son’s room exactly as he had left it, except for dusting. She had thought this was a way of refusing what had happened. Lately it had begun to feel like something she was doing to him: making him remain twelve, making him keep the same books, the same narrow bed, the same dislike of mushrooms.

At nine, she opened his wardrobe.

She did not empty it.

She took out one shirt.

It was an ugly shirt, patterned with orange flames. He had loved it. She had hated it and let him wear it for the school photograph.

She held it against herself, then folded it and put it in her own drawer.

That afternoon, she bought mushrooms. At the last moment she also bought a packet of the biscuits he liked.

The sea went on returning things for another six days.

A typewriter. A cracked green bowl. One roller skate.

No one came back.

Eventually the crowds thinned. The television vans left. The boy with the dog lead stopped appearing, and someone took down the handwritten notices taped to the shelter.

Mara kept the chair.

In summer she carried it outside and sat in the small patch of shade behind her house. It was uncomfortable. One leg was shorter than the others, and she wedged a folded envelope beneath it.

Sometimes a neighbor joined her. They drank tea and talked over the fence about ordinary things: a blocked drain, the price of tomatoes, whether the swifts had arrived earlier that year.

When the chair finally split across the seat, Mara tried to repair it with wire.

The repair lasted three weeks.

Then she borrowed her neighbor’s car and took it to the dump. She stood beside the plastics skip for a while before lifting it over.

On the way home, she stopped at the beach.

There was nothing on the sand but seaweed and a tennis ball, which she threw for somebody else’s dog.

The clock in the repair shop had no hands, but people checked it anyway.

They came in carrying lamps, kettles, radios, the small domestic betrayals that accumulate in a life. Before explaining what had gone wrong, almost everyone glanced at the clock.

“About half past,” the repairman would say.

He was usually right.

His name was Emil. He had inherited the shop from a woman who had inherited it from her brother, who had won the lease in a card game and spent forty years pretending he knew how to fix things. Eventually, he did.

Emil believed this was how most professions began.

One wet Tuesday, a girl brought him a doorbell.

Not the button, or the transformer, or the mechanism in its yellowing plastic box. She brought the sound.

It was inside a jam jar.

Emil put down his screwdriver.

“Who took it out?”

“My mother.”

“Does she know you have it?”

The girl watched a bus pass the window. Its passengers were lit from within, like people in an aquarium.

“She said to throw it away.”

Emil held the jar to his ear. Two notes sounded faintly through the glass. The second had a little crack in it.

“Nothing wrong with that.”

“I know.”

“Then what do you need?”

The girl took the jar back and held it against her coat.

“I need it to be something else.”

***

There were procedures for this, though Emil had never seen them written down.

You could shorten a sound, stretch it, remove a troublesome frequency. You could make a whistle less piercing or take the rattle out of a recorded breath. Changing what a sound *was* generally proved more difficult.

“What did you have in mind?”

“A bird.”

“Which bird?”

“I don’t know any.”

“A bicycle bell?”

She shook her head.

“A teaspoon against a cup?”

“That would be all right.”

He found a claim ticket in the drawer.

“Friday.”

“How much?”

“Bring the jar lid. It’ll get dusty.”

***

After she left, Emil set the doorbell beside a toaster awaiting a new spring.

At six he locked the shop. At seven he ate bread and cheese at the workbench. At eight, when the street had emptied, he unscrewed the jar.

The sound came out carefully.

Two notes.

Then the shop was full of a man taking off his shoes.

Emil could not see him. There were no ghostly footprints, no shape in the dust. But there was the unmistakable presence of somebody trying not to wake a household: the weight shifted onto one foot, the coat held close so its keys would not jingle.

The man hesitated.

Then everything stopped.

Emil sat still for a while. Eventually he tipped the jar on its side, and the sound went back inside.

He screwed on a spare lid.

***

On Wednesday he tried a cup from the cupboard above the sink.

It was thick and white, with a hairline fracture near the handle. He struck its rim with a teaspoon.

A modest, useful note.

He opened the jar and worked through the morning, adjusting, listening, starting again.

By noon, the doorbell had become the sound of a teaspoon against a cup.

But behind it was still a man taking off his shoes.

Emil tried a different cup.

Then a glass.

Then a little brass bowl someone had left as payment years before.

Each sound made room for the same arrival.

***

The girl returned on Thursday.

“You said Friday,” Emil said.

“I know.”

She stood just inside the door, dripping onto the mat.

“Is it done?”

“The sound is changed.”

“Can I hear?”

He tapped the cup.

She closed her eyes.

Outside, a lorry reversed with three indignant beeps.

“No,” she said.

“I thought not.”

She wiped her nose with her sleeve.

“He used to forget his keys.”

Emil waited.

“Even when he hadn’t forgotten them, sometimes. He’d ring so I could let him in.”

“How long?”

“Since January.”

It was October.

Emil turned the cup by its handle.

“Your mother took the sound out because it hurt her.”

The girl nodded.

“And you kept it.”

Another nod.

Rain ticked against the window.

Finally she said, “Could you make it so he comes all the way in?”

Emil looked at the tools laid out on the green cloth. Small pliers. Fine brushes. Instruments for faults he understood.

“No.”

The girl pressed her lips together. He let her be angry.

***

They tried something else.

Emil found a wooden box that had once held a set of precision weights. He lined it with felt and fitted a small brass catch.

The girl chose the original two notes.

Together, they put them inside.

“Will it escape?” she asked.

“Not with the catch shut.”

“Will it wear out?”

“I don’t think so. Bring it back if it does.”

She opened the box once before leaving.

The bell rang. Somewhere very close, a man balanced on one foot, loosening a shoe.

She shut it again.

***

On Friday her mother came to pay.

She stood at the counter holding the box. Emil prepared an explanation, but she only asked whether he had anything smaller.

“Small enough for a drawer,” she said. “This one catches.”

He trimmed the corners while she waited.

When he handed it back, she ran her thumb over the smooth wood.

“Thank you.”

After she left, Emil swept up the shavings. He ate his lunch and repaired the toaster.

At three, a man came in with a broken desk fan.

He glanced at the clock.

“About half past,” Emil said, and reached for a claim ticket.

The town hired a man to listen to the bridge.

This was cheaper than repairing it, and considerably cheaper than replacing it, and the man, whose name was Ellis, had a reputation for hearing things accurately.

He had once told a mechanic that a bearing was failing in a machine on the other side of a wall. He could distinguish rain in the gutters from rain in the leaves. For thirty-one years, he had known whether his wife was asleep by the sound of her turning a page.

The job came with a folding chair, a thermos, and a form.

The form had three boxes:

**NORMAL**

**UNUSUAL**

**URGENT**

Beneath them was a small space labeled **DESCRIPTION**.

“Most days,” said the town engineer, “you’ll tick normal.”

“What does normal sound like?”

The engineer glanced at the bridge.

“You’ll get the hang of it.”

*

The bridge was older than anyone who used it. Trucks crossed it reluctantly. Teenagers crossed it fast. On cold mornings, it made a noise like someone trying to remember a name.

Ellis sat beneath the eastern approach, where the riverbank offered a dry shelf of earth. He brought sandwiches wrapped in paper and a pencil he sharpened with a pocketknife.

At first, everything sounded urgent.

A school bus passed overhead and the entire structure uttered a long metallic complaint. A cyclist struck a loose plate with a sound like a dropped baking tray. Around noon, with no traffic at all, something deep inside the bridge went *tok*.

Ellis ticked unusual.

Under description he wrote:

*Single tok. No apparent cause.*

The engineer phoned him that evening.

“What kind of tok?”

“A short one.”

“Could it have been a bird?”

“It could have been a very solid bird.”

There was a silence.

“Keep listening,” the engineer said.

*

By the third week, Ellis knew the bridge’s habits.

It disliked the first frost but settled down afterward. Its western joints rattled more when the river was high. The eleven-ten gravel truck produced a descending series of notes that Ellis began anticipating at eleven-oh-eight.

He learned that something could sound terrible without becoming worse, and that sometimes a change was barely audible.

He made a separate note of this on the back of a form. Then he crossed it out. It seemed like the sort of thing a person wrote before making a serious mistake.

*

People stopped to speak with him.

They wanted to know if the bridge was safe.

“I’m listening,” he said.

They generally found this reassuring, though he had not meant it to be.

A woman walking a terrier asked whether he listened with equipment.

“Sometimes the chair.”

She looked at him.

“You can feel a vibration through the legs.”

“Oh,” she said. “Of course.”

After that, she greeted the chair as well as Ellis.

*

At home, he ate at the kitchen table and left the radio off.

His wife had been dead for eighteen months. Her library books were still on the small shelf by the door, except they were no longer library books. He had paid for them.

The librarian had understood without making him explain.

Occasionally he opened one at the place she had marked. A receipt from a garden center lay halfway through a novel. Six terracotta pots. One bag of compost. A plant identified only as *perennial, assorted*.

He could not remember which plant it had been. In spring, he had stood in the garden trying to work it out, embarrassed by how little attention he had paid when she brought things home.

*

In November, a girl began visiting the riverbank after school.

She was twelve, perhaps thirteen, and carried a trumpet case.

“Are you allowed to be here?” Ellis asked.

“Are you?”

“I’m employed.”

“That doesn’t always mean allowed.”

He conceded this.

She sat on a stone and watched the water. For several afternoons, neither of them said much.

Then she asked, “What are you listening for?”

“A change.”

“How do you know it hasn’t changed while you were home?”

“I don’t.”

“That seems like a problem.”

“It’s one of several.”

She nodded as though this confirmed something about employment.

*

One Thursday she opened the case.

“I’m bad,” she warned him.

“That’s all right.”

“No. I mean actually.”

Her first note startled a duck into flight.

She lowered the trumpet.

Ellis looked at the departing duck.

“You’ve got an audience response.”

She laughed, then tried again.

For twenty minutes she played fragments of a tune Ellis almost recognized. When the gravel truck approached, he raised a hand. She stopped while it crossed, then resumed.

She came back the next day, and the next.

*

In December, Ellis heard a new sound.

It was a faint scrape after each heavy vehicle had passed. He waited for three trucks, checked unusual, and called the engineer.

The inspection took two days. A bearing needed attention. The bridge closed for a week.

On Monday, Ellis returned to his chair. The girl arrived at four.

“Did they fix it?”

“The part they found.”

She unpacked her trumpet.

Overhead, a car crossed smoothly enough. Ellis made a note, put down his pencil, and listened to her play the tune all the way through.

This time he recognized it.

He waited until she finished before telling her.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I’d break the link between the circumstances of your birth and the possibilities of your life.

Not make everyone the same. Just make it so that being born poor, in a war zone, or into a hated minority doesn’t quietly decide how safe you’ll be, how long you’ll live, or whether your talents ever get a chance.

There would still be difficulty, disagreement, and luck. But fewer lives would be narrowed before the person living them had any say.
